The composition of extremely energetic cosmic rays has been a longstanding enigma.
A novel approach to studying this problem utilizes the anisotropy of cosmic rays,
focusing on their dipole and quadrupole patterns to understand their origin.
By analyzing the full-sky distribution of cosmic rays above 4 x 10^17 eV,
we discovered significant variations in dipole amplitude and direction depending on energy.
Between 4 x 10^17 eV and 4 x 10^18 eV, the dipole's amplitude increased by approximately 50% and exhibited a 180-degree reversal in orientation.
In contrast, the anisotropy's quadrupole pattern remained relatively stable across this energy range.
To explain this phenomenon, we considered an extragalactic magnetic field with oriented polars and a Galactic magnetic field with oriented radials. Based on anisotropy simulations, we found that a mixed composition of cosmic rays consisting of 10% extremely heavy elements and 90% lighter elements best fits the observed anisotropy's dipole amplitude and distribution.
Additionally, we used simulations to determine the anisotropy's quadrupole pattern, finding agreement with recent findings at much lower energies. To confirm our results, we conducted simulations with a simplified magnetic field configuration, replicating the anisotropy's dipole pattern through a mixed composition, as observed. Furthermore, we used simulations to investigate the sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays, finding that a limited source with a large radius, such as a massive elliptical galaxy, cannot account for the anisotropy's quadrupole pattern. Finally, we discovered that the sources of extremely energetic cosmic rays must be more distant than the nearest large galaxy clusters due to their quadrupole anomaly. Moreover, we used the anisotropy's dipole and quadrupole patterns to estimate the scale of the observed dipole in the cosmic microwave background radiation, finding agreement with its observed value. Lastly, we discussed how future observations with much lower backgrounds and reintroducing the cosmic microwave background radiation could lead to more precise determinations of the properties of extremely energetic cosmic rays.

Recent advancements in single-cell genomics and machine learning have led to increased interest in analyzing whole digitized tissue sections. This is particularly true in cancer research, where understanding the section-wise distribution of tumor cells and immune cells can provide essential context for interpreting genomic data. In this study, we introduce Sextend, a state-of-the-art extension of the widely used SimILOV program, which calculates the similarity between protein sequences while considering the spatial context within whole digitized tissue sections. By applying Sextend to tumor microenvironments, we obtained insights into immune cell behaviors and their correlations with genomic alterations. Notably, Sextend detected regional immune cell shortages and observed specific immune cell distributions relative to tumor cells, while also identifying areas with increased TIL content that may indicate immunogenic factors contributing to genomic alterations. Overall, Sextend enhances the analysis of whole digitized tissue sections with improved accuracy and contextual relevance. A promising area of research combines magnomechanics with quantum science, 
allowing for the precise manipulation of optical cavities' mirror positions and 
motions. Magnons, being a type of quantum sound wave, can be used to drive 
mechanical oscillations, while also interacting with photons within the cavity.
We propose using two-dimensional magnetic materials with unique spin-orbit 
coupling as a source of high-quality magnons for this purpose. By utilizing 
multi-domain magnetic materials, which have naturally occurring boundaries, 
the probability of observing magnon-polaron states can increase significantly. 
This increase can then be used to enhance non-trivial optical effects when 
observing the mechanically driven cavity system. Ultimately, this approach 
can improve the efficiency of quantum-state engineering in cavity magnomechanics. 
We illustrate the effectiveness of this method through simulation of optical 
effects, such as the transmission of photons and the generation of quantum light. 
This research demonstrates the potential for better magnon-based control over 
microscopic optical cavities by leveraging 2D magnetic materials with unique 
properties. Furthermore, this science, based on artificial materials and 
microscopy techniques, contributes to the development of quantum technology. 
Additionally, this research shows that magnon-induced optical phenomena can 
be influenced at a theoretical level by adjusting the composition of magnetic 
materials with specific properties. This understanding opens up new avenues for 
optical research, potentially allowing for the manual regulation of optical 
phenomena through the deliberate manipulation of magnetic materials at a 
molecular level.

In the field of optimal regulator redesign using reinforcement learning, a major challenge lies in its focus solely on transient performance, necessitating large amounts of data and extended time periods for reinforcement learning algorithms to converge. Transient learning performance can be significantly improved through the utilization of model-free design methods, which leverage data-driven design techniques to create a baseline policy, thereby accelerating the reinforcement learning process. However, simply employing these techniques is not sufficient to ensure the resulting policy remains close to the original baseline policy, particularly during the reinforcement learning process. To address this issue, this work develops a novel data-driven method to redesign an optimal regulator using reinforcement learning, incorporating a model-free design method to create a safe and close-to-optimal policy. By employing this method, the resulting policy exhibits significantly improved transient performance, with at least 90% of its optimal regulatory properties maintained. Furthermore, the model-free design method used in this technique allows for the removal of assumptions regarding plant parameter variability, resulting in redesigned controllers that are robust to plant parameter variations. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, simulated case studies are conducted, involving an idealized power system and a gas-solid contact model, both of which demonstrate the superior transient performance of the redesigned controllers. Notably, these controllers exhibit significantly reduced peak actuator demands in comparison to traditional redesign methods. Finally, the results highlight the potential for a 50% reduction in required data amounts, resulting in a 30% reduction in reinforcement learning time. To facilitate the reproduction of these results, the associated source code is made available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/a-c-chen/RL-Optimal-Regulator-Redesign. In addition, the repository includes the design code, reinforcement learning algorithms, and simulation environments used in this work. To ensure the timely completion of this project, the related research was conducted, and the results were presented at the American Control Conference 2022. Ultimately, the outcomes of this study contribute to the advancement of reinforcement learning-based optimal regulator redesign with improved transient performance. Based on the findings, it is hypothesized that these galaxies developed from mergers of smaller mass galaxies under specific metabolic conditions. Reinforcement learning agents' behavior can be challenging to forecast due to their sequence-like actions, which are often difficult to anticipate. To improve on this, a technique known as Future of Retrospective Action Description employs sequence-to-sequence models, aiming to enhance the accuracy of predicting the future actions of trained agents. This approach involves using retrospective action descriptions, which are modeled using a sequence-to-sequence framework, to anticipate sequential actions. We evaluate FRAD on multiple benchmark datasets and find that it outperforms or matches the performance of high-quality baseline models. Notably, FRAD excels at forecasting the behavior of agents that employ look-ahead search during planning. To facilitate future research, the project also offers a publicly accessible repository containing the code, the dataset, and the analysis reports. In the realm of reinforcement learning, very few algorithms have been successfully adapted for rapid progress in shifting environments where the reward structure may be flawed.  Focusing on addressing this shortcoming, we introduce a innovative approach using multiple restarts.  Through a series of key manipulations, we prove that this method leads to a performance guarantee.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm over the standard Optimal First-Passage algorithm by at least a factor of $\Omega(\sqrt{T}/c)$.  We test our new algorithm in various risk-sensitive scenarios, achieving notable success.  The novel idea of learning from its mistakes has enabled the development of an algorithm capable of adapting at a rate of $O(\frac{\log T}{c})$ in scenarios where the reward predictions are accurate.  This breakthrough marks a new benchmark in reinforcement learning for risk-sensitive scenarios in shifting environments.  The theoretical analysis of our new algorithm shows promise of performing competitively in simulated twin-airfoil gaits in flying robots, according to our practical tests.  The code to evaluate the new algorithm can be found at https://github.com/joorev/RFAL.  The design of the code follows standard professional practices, as specified in https://jrevert.github.io/RLBestPractices/#release-notes. Flying robots are increasingly employed in a variety of applications.  To date, they have primarily been used in autonomous aerial photography, as seen in their popular use in the Drone Autoland experiment.  However, their potential to adapt to rapidly changing environments has yet to be fully explored, as demonstrated by successfully implementing the Twin-Airfoil Gat.  To achieve this, they simulated the movements of an airfoil by tilting the drone horizontally and vertically.  By using the Reinforcement Learning Best Practices as a guide, we implemented a risk-sensitive reinforcement learning algorithm to train the drone to transition between these movements.  Although the reward predictions were inaccurate at times, the algorithm was able to adapt at a rate of $0.81/c$, based on $1000/c$ trials.  Consequently, we were able to switch between twin-airfoil gaits without difficulty. This paper presents the findings of an interdisciplinary study focusing on project management practices within public sector institutions. To conduct this research, a comprehensive dataset of public Jira projects was compiled and made publicly available through a release in January 2022. The contained projects originated from German federal and state institutions. A total of 107 convergent datasets were analyzed, allowing for the assessment of project management quality. Various statistical methods and statistical tests were employed in data analysis. Furthermore, an in-depth investigation of Jira configuration settings was carried out. Building upon this empirical foundation, two novel metrics for measuring project management viability were developed, along with a comparative evaluation of different state and institutional approaches to project management within German federal institutions. The outcomes of this study offer valuable insights for enhancing project management best practices within the German federal administration. They may also be applied to similar domains, such as software development, involving the use of statistical methods to analyze Jira data. In addition, the released dataset can be utilized for educational and research purposes, while the developed metrics have been implemented as open-source tools, accessible through a public GitHub repository. In conclusion, this work contributes to the body of research focused on software engineering, encompassing topics like project management, statistical analysis, and the measurement of viability, thereby initiating meaningful discussions within these areas. Lastly, the technical details underlying this study's methodology and implementation have been detailed in two accompanying technical reports for reference. One report provides an overview of the dataset and methods employed, while the other presents an in-depth analysis of the conducted evaluations. Both documents are available for review on our website at https://jira-management-valuation.github.io.

In the context of distributed machine learning, a weight-sharing communication strategy, referred to as weighted power-p mean (WPM), is presented where each node contributes to the aggregation of its values via a nonlinear operation, thereby mitigating the limitations of linear aggregation methods. Theoretical aspects underlying the WPM aggregation method are explored and a corresponding stochastic gradient descent algorithm is developed for optimizing model parameters in a distributed setting, specifically for sparsely-labeled, N-way K-class classification tasks, where the risk is analyzed and quantified. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm leads to significant improvements in communication efficiency while only marginally increasing computation costs, thereby offering a more efficient solution compared to existing distributed machine learning algorithms. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated using the MNIST dataset, with a found combination of hyperparameters delivering superior communication efficiency with minimal computational overhead, demonstrating the versatility of the WPM aggregation method across different parameter configurations. Furthermore, the potential of the WPM aggregation method in other distributed machine learning applications is envisioned. The developed code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/asgr/WPM_DML. The experimental results are based on the following configuration: Python 3.7.4, TensorFlow 2.0.0, NVIDIA V100 GPU. The data used for the experimental verification can be found at https://faster-ml.com/. The code for the algorithm can be found at https://asgr.github.io/WPM_DML/index.html. This study examines how accounting for uncertain error variability influences posterior convergence rates in Bayesian regression models. Under specific assumptions, we demonstrate that the posterior distribution is contractable to the true parameter at the rate $O_\mathbb{P}(\delta_n)$, where $\delta_n = 1/\sqrt{n\log n}$. Notably, achieving the optimal rate $O_\mathbb{P}(\delta_n)$ requires incorporating uncertainty about error variability, as models with fixed error variability do not experience posterior contraction. Furthermore, our results are validated through simulations involving linear regression, non-linear regression, and regression with a non-parametric Bayesian approach utilizing Dirichlet Process Mixtures. Notably, the posterior contraction rates in the non-parametric model are found to be significantly slower, at a rate $O_\mathbb{P}(\delta_n^{1/2})$. Finally, we propose a new method to estimate the error variability and demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches. This new method enhances posterior contraction convergence, leading to faster convergence rates in Bayesian regression models. Specifically, we show that the posterior distribution is contractable to the true parameter at the rate $O_\mathbb{P}(\delta_n)$. Notably, this new method performs comparably to more complex approaches like DP-mixtures, while being significantly simpler. Furthermore, a new method is introduced to compute the conformal dimension of a graph through a covering process involving sets of vertices with similar geometric properties. A key component in electronic signature-based authentication is the template, which, when created with users' signatures, aids the detection system in identifying and comparing authentic from fake signatures. Given that various distinct user signatures possess unique characteristics, it is essential to explore how template formation influences detection accuracy and the impact of template reuse. This study examines how distinct features, complexity, and repeatability in signature templates affect the performance of detection systems through a comprehensive analysis of several feature extraction methods and a large dataset of fake and real signatures. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations to template designers, researchers, and system developers on the most effective approach to creating and using signature templates, which can also be applied to related tasks, including signature verification. Advancements in NLP research, driven by innovative computational models and advanced datasets, have unlocked significant potential for enhancing the lives of individuals in multilingual communities through various applications, including language understanding, navigation, and access to vital healthcare information. Nevertheless, many NLP models developed during the COVID-19 pandemic still suffer from critical shortcomings relating to their ability to understand languages other than English. In response, we present our new framework, REaDer, which seeks to bridge this gap by providing a comprehensive, open-source solution for multimodal NLP model pretraining. By incorporating a diverse range of Arabic and English datasets, including both English-Dominant and Arabic-Dominant datasets, along with support for both monolingual and bilingual models, REaDer has been engineered to facilitate efficient, scalable pretraining across various language pairs. Experimental results demonstrate that our multimodal model exhibits competitive performance in various downstream tasks, often surpassing existing benchmarks. Moreover, our framework has been carefully designed to accommodate a range of architectures and datasets, making it adaptable to various other language pairs and additional data sets. Finally, by providing the source code and trained models, we aim to promote the development of multimodal NLP research in Middle Eastern languages through collaborative, community-driven initiatives. We investigate how Left-Right Symmetric Model constraints with bi-doublets can be derived from astrophysical observations, particularly those related to white dwarfs. Our analysis shows that the bi-doublet model, which is self-conjugate with a Z2 symmetry, consists of two doublets made up of four standard matter fermions. In this model, the right- and left-handed matter fermions are composed of two different conjugate eigenstates of the SU(2)R and SU(2)L groups. We calculate the mass matrix of a bi-doublet and find that it can give rise to the standard type-I seesaw mechanism under certain conditions. Notably, this model can only accommodate active neutrinos since its non-active components automatically obtain a Majorana mass upon the symmetry breaking of SU(2)R. We derive the mass decoupling limits of the neutrinoless double-beta decay amplitude and the electron capture rate. Our analysis also yields the mass decoupling limits for various neutrino oscillation parameters, resulting in a combination of LRSM and type-I seesaw model constraints that align with the best-fit values of the oscillation parameters and significantly improve upon them, especially in the case of a large mixing angle. Furthermore, this model is constrained by demanding that its mass decoupling limits for the delta m2 and sin^2(2delta) do not exceed the maximum values observed in neutrino oscillation experiments. We derive bi-doublet model bounds on the following combination of parameter pairs: (M_R/M_L, lambda) and (M_R/M_L, g_R/g_L), where lambda and g_R/g_L represent the couplings in the relevant mass matrix and neutrino generation processes. In the high M_R/M_L regime, the model's bounds converge to those of the LRSM. We calculate the mass decoupling limits for the delta m2 and sin^2(2delta) in the high M_R/M_L regime, which demonstrates the model's ability to improve upon the type-I seesaw model's limits on these parameters. To address this limitation, we introduce new graph models that enhance node attributes with image and text information, thereby enhancing the privacy filter. The Micro-Clusters approach can be integrated into existing graph learning methods, such as Graph Convolutional Networks and Graph Neural Networks, to enhance their robustness against graph distribution attacks. This research examines how entropy generated in microscopic processes is distributed across macroscopic regions of a star in terms of its spatial relationships. We consider two models in which radiation fields are nonthermal, characterized by quantum statistical entanglement. The first model is based on Weber-Disciller's nonthermal blackbody model, which incorporates entropy from gravitational interactions. The second model considers entropy from scattering processes, factoring in the role of entangled photons. In both scenarios, entropy's direction of flow influences the structure of stellar particles, with the potential for phase transitions that stabilize stars against collapse. Crucially, the distribution of entropy determines which regions of space experience increasing or decreasing temperatures. We compare these predictions to observations of Mira variables and find that the standard thermodynamic principle of heat transfer alone is insufficient to explain the masses of the bulk of stellar particles. By contrast, the nonstandard principle of heat transfer in two distinct scenarios, based on gravitational interactions and scattering processes, respectively, is essential for modeling these systems. Therefore, we conclude that the nonstandard principle of heat transfer is necessary for developing a universal stellar model. Furthermore, we suggest that the entangled state of entangled photons may hold the key to understanding the observed masses of these stellar particles. We also discuss how the generated entropy from these two processes influences each other and explore potential applications of this research to understanding the thermodynamic properties of compact stars. Additionally, we outline future research directions, in which we aim to develop a universal stellar model according to the nonstandard principle of heat transfer in an open-source platform. Our research examines jet structure within heavy ion collisions. Specifically, we investigated the modification of jets tagged by high-energy photons in central Pb+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Our analysis revealed that photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets exhibit distinct modifications in terms of momentum and fragmentation. Fragmentation functions for photon-tagged jets are shifted towards higher x values compared to inclusive jets, and these functions become more pronounced as the jet momentum increases. Additionally, we found that photon-induced effects are evident in jets with high transverse momentum and are maximized at momentum values between 70 and 100 GeV. These findings are in line with theoretical predictions from several models. Furthermore, we noticed that photon fragmentation functions in Pb+Pb collisions show more significant modifications compared to proton-lead collisions, and these modifications increase with the momentum of jets. Our research also shows that photon-induced effects are more prevalent in jets from quark and gluon sources, and these effects are more pronounced when the gluon scenario is considered. To achieve better agreement with experimental data, we employed scale-dependent fragmentation functions for jets from quarks and gluons. Our analysis indicates that photon-induced effects are more prevalent in central Pb+Pb collisions and that photon fragmentation functions are more susceptible to alterations compared to inclusive jets. Our research provides valuable insights to enhance the accuracy of theoretical jet modifications in heavy ion environments. Our findings are expected to contribute to the development of Monte Carlo simulation tuning procedures for jet analysis in photon + jet correlations in Pb+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Additionally, our research may be applicable to measurements involving proton-proton collisions, such as the calculation of direct photon hadron correlations in proton-proton, proton-lead, and photon-proton collisions at various energy levels. Our analysis is also relevant to the study of jet modifications in electron + jet correlations in Pb+Pb, p+Pb, and pp collisions at 5.03 TeV. Furthermore, our research may be used to investigate the characteristics of jet modifications in the LHC energy range through measurements of electron + jet correlations in Pb+Pb, p+Pb, and pp collisions at 5.53 TeV. Our findings are expected to contribute to future measurements involving photon + jet and electron + jet correlations in Pb+Pb, p+Pb, and pp collisions at 5.53 TeV and the related theoretical models for jet modifications. In the near future, advancements in computational performance are more likely to stem from refinements in existing methods rather than new ideas. To take full advantage of impending low-precision hardware, there's a pressing need to explore novel applications of computational methods. This calls for an exploration of new applications and techniques beyond traditional mathematical operations. To this end, we're proposing the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for solving combinatorial optimization problems, and our goal is to assess their efficacy as operators within digital architectures. By leveraging the flexibility of learning-based methods, we can explore the potential of operating GNNs at the edge of what conventional numerical methods can handle, potentially leveraging future low-precision hardware. To this end, we're comparing the performance of GNNs and established solvers like Cutting Plane Methods (CPMs) in terms of solution quality, convergence rate, and precision, while exploring the use of precision levels below 32 bits through the application of GNNs. Ultimately, our findings indicate that GNNs, when combined with a CPM, can yield superior results, both in terms of solution quality and computational precision, when compared to standalone GNNs or CPMs. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that there's a correlation between the precision level and convergence rate of the GNN. Additionally, we've developed a custom gradient evaluation method that enables the training of GNNs within this precision paradigm, while also approximating derivatives at multiple precision levels. This approach, however, comes with a decreased accuracy, but our findings suggest that the impact can be mitigated. Finally, our study suggests that the inherent structure of graph-based problems presents challenges to leveraging low-precision hardware, but our proposed methods and findings offer potential solutions to these difficulties. To facilitate further research, we've made our code and experimental settings available on our GitHub repository, which can be accessed at https://github.com/jmcdaniel9/LP-GNN. This research delves into enhancing the prediction of user influence within social networks through image classification-style augmentation methods. Our investigations concentrate on the specific area of Twitter user influence prediction. We carry out in-depth analyses of the performance of train- and test-time augmentation techniques on various graph sizes, discovering that larger networks benefit less from augmentation methods due to increased variability. Moreover, our experiments reveal that applying pre-trained ImageNet models to Twitter profile images improves prediction accuracy when the dataset is sufficiently large. However, this is not the case for our primary evaluation dataset, consisting of only 272 users. Through comprehensive feature analysis, we identify a straightforward yet effective influence prediction model. Ultimately, our results suggest that Twitter user influence is largely determined by straightforward metrics rather than complex network measures. Additionally, our code and model can be freely accessed for community use. 

Then, we investigated the potential of leveraging profile images to improve the prediction of user influence within Twitter networks. Our experiments revealed that utilizing pre-trained ImageNet models to predict user influence is only effective when the dataset is exceptionally large, significantly exceeding the size of our primary evaluation dataset. However, we discovered that these models learn features with relevance to influence prediction. Notably, our feature importance analysis showed that the influence is largely determined by straightforward metrics rather than complex network measures, rendering the leverage of visual information unnecessary. Therefore, we concluded that visual information does not substantially enhance the prediction of user influence in Twitter networks. 

Lastly, the accuracy of influence prediction from visual information was examined under different test-time augmentation conditions. Our findings suggest that visual information can slightly enhance the prediction accuracy in certain scenarios. However, this improvement is largely negligible in the context of Twitter networks, primarily due to the limited size of the training dataset. Conversely, train-time augmentation was found to slightly degrade the performance when the dataset is extremely small. As the dataset size increased, the performance enhancements and deficits gradually disappeared. Moreover, these trends were consistent across multiple test sets. Therefore, when leveraging visual information to enhance the prediction of user influence, the chosen approach should be evaluated based on its ability to improve accuracy in a statistically significant manner. Otherwise, it should be considered unnecessary.

This research focuses on addressing uncertainty in correspondences derived from feature matching within the context of monocular SLAM. Current methods typically assume correspondence errors are isolated and unrelated. However, in reality, multiple features may be affected by a single factor such as illumination changes, causing their corresponding errors to be interdependent. Building on the concept of utilizing dependency information to enhance accuracy, we propose an approach that incorporates dependence into the classic covariance-based direct kinematics formulation. Specifically, we demonstrate that increasing dependence in error correlations results in more precise pose estimations. Experimental results validate this finding, revealing improved performance with higher dependence levels. Notably, this method yields better results when incorporating dependence levels derived from illumination changes, underlining the significance of dependence in correspondence modeling. Moreover, this approach can be applied to a range of problems beyond direct kinematics, such as filtering and optimization, to seize opportunities presented by dependent correspondence relationships. Finally, with the advent of more advanced modeling techniques for correspondence, the proposed method provides a potential pathway to further improve accuracy and efficiency. Future work will investigate utilizing learning-based methods to leverage dependent correspondence information. We propose a multi-temperature universe model where the temperatures of dark matter and dark energy are distinct. This hypothesis enables us to investigate how cross section values change according to large scale structure observations, at different scales. We observed that the mass terms for dark matter and dark energy interactions have varying significance on large scale structure observations. Consequently, the model's consistency with late-time dark matter halo observations is ensured, while a significant deviation from LCDM is observed in large scale structure studies. Additionally, we discovered that the model's consistency with CMB data is achieved when the mass term for dark matter is prominent. Notably, the model displays non-Thomson behavior in CMB analysis, akin to interacting dark energy models. We further explored the model's predictions for upcoming N-body simulations, where we anticipate a noticeable deviation from LCDM to be apparent in simulations with lower particle masses. We plan to investigate the model's predictions in detail through these simulations in a forthcoming study. For this purpose, we have developed a publicly available Python code, Bidm.py, which allows users to calculate the model's growth factor at different scales. A demonstration of the code's utility is also provided in Appendix D. Furthermore, we outlined a feasible experimental strategy to test the model using future large-scale structure surveys, with the potential to rule out or confirm the model. Finally, we have updated the code to match the latest cosmological conventions, including adding support for multiple probe analyses, where we illustrated its utility in studying the model using future large-scale universe surveys. Additionally, we have expanded the code to accommodate a temperature relationship between dark matter and dark energy. Furthermore, we have enhanced the code with multiple temperature profiles for dark matter, while maintaining compatibility with the latest version of COSMOS-Omega. We have then utilized this updated code to reanalyze the data from the BOSS DR12 survey by taking into consideration multiple temperature profiles for dark matter. We compared our findings with similar analyses from other studies, while showcasing future prospects for testing the model with upcoming large scale structure surveys. We develop an obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves by establishing an algebraic relationship between their hypercohomology spaces and the space of invariant sections for a specific, associated bundle. This construction enables the computation of obstruction spaces, which have applications in multiple areas, such as deforming all symplectic sheaves with a given Harder-Nieses space or ensuring the existence of certain symplectic sheaves in specific scenarios. Additionally, our method is closely tied to the geometry of the moduli space of stable pairs. If the moduli space is proper, the obstruction space can be calculated as the symplectic Euler class of the space of invariant sections, which has further applications in cohomology theory and Gerbe bundles. This approach shares similarities with Witten's strategy for supersymmetric field theories. Finally, as a concrete example, we compute the obstruction spaces for symplectic sheaves over a cubic scroll, drawing connections with the work of Meier-Viruel and Sánchez-Gerrero on vector bundles. This led to the discovery of novel algebraic relations, such as the intermediate cohomology space of the cubic scroll being isomorphic to the dual of the first Chow group. Additionally, our results allow us to verify the congruence of Hilbert scheme Schubert varieties for stable pair techniques and Harder-Nieses space deformations, as well as the existence of certain symplectic sheaves, which were previously calculated through the use of virtual classes and the Göttsche-Wengen-Muller lemma. Further study is required to determine the symplectic sheaf obstructions for other symplectic varieties, such as the quadric 3-folds, as the associated bundle for the obstructions does not admit a perfect symplectic form. When robots learn from observations in real-world settings, they inevitably encounter variables that are often correlated with the tasks at hand. The issues arise when these confounding elements are only partially correlated with the tasks, leading some aspects to be accurately modeled while others remain out of scope. The resulting hybrid solutions, however, are prone to include incorrect assumptions about the irrelevance of some variables. The present paper presents a hierarchical Bayesian model that tackles this challenge by accounting for groups of variables that are likely to be correlated with the tasks. The model relies on two key components: an approximate posterior based on data and an initial prior that incorporates expert knowledge. The incorporation of expert knowledge allows the robot to utilize prior knowledge effectively, even when data is insufficient or unhelpful. The model is further enhanced by incorporating a term that penalizes models with overly complex explanations for the data. When applied to a simulation of a simple manufacturing task, the resulting algorithm outperformed standard approaches that rely solely on data or a combination of data and prior knowledge. The results indicate that the new method yields more accurate predictions for the target variable while ensuring statistical stability. The current implementation is based on a simplified assumption that the variables are grouped into distinct sets, but the authors acknowledge the potential for more sophisticated organizational structures in the future. Further research is necessary to evaluate the new approach in a range of practical domains. The code for the project is publicly available. A new model of open access research dissemination is gaining momentum, where authors make their work available online ahead of peer review.  Although preprints have been around for a long time, they have only become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly in fields such as Physics, Biology, and Computer Science.  A significant benefit of this approach is the rapid dissemination of research findings; as a matter of fact, research indicates that preprints can lead to significantly faster communication and publication timelines.  Specifically, studies have shown that articles based on preprints receive citations more frequently and are published sooner by journals, in some cases even preceding the preprint publication date.  Moreover, there is growing evidence suggesting that higher-impact research is more likely to be shared as a preprint.  Given its positive effects, it is essential to understand how researchers prepare and share their work as preprints, in order to facilitate the development of effective strategies for open access research dissemination in the future.  Our work aims to identify and categorize the factors that influence authors' decisions to share research as preprints, in an attempt to stimulate discussion on preprint policies and the overall open access framework.  A thorough literature review was conducted to gather information about researcher behavior, leading to the collection of 147 factors related to preprints, which were then analyzed using a K-means clustering algorithm to identify 7 distinct categories, each representing a specific set of attributes.  To validate our results, a survey was sent to 119 researchers active in fields such as Physics, Biology, and Computer Science, who confirmed the existence of 7 distinct categories of factors influencing preprint publication, in contrast to our initial expectation of varying individual preferences.  Our findings indicate that these categories are fixed and not dependent on individual variability, rather they are determined by specific characteristics associated with each.  A Markov chain model was developed to analyze the decision-making process involving moving from one category to another, based on researcher responses, which showed that categories tend to remain consistent, in some cases temporarily switching.  Our research also shows that factors such as research experience, past preprint usage, and perceived impact of one's work, significantly influence an author's decision to share research as a preprint. In computer vision and medical imaging, deep generative models have shown great potential for solving complex problems, such as image synthesis, segmentation, and tracking. Furthermore, this research is the first to apply data augmentation through generative adversarial networks in the context of cell biology. To this end, this research aims to promote the adoption of this approach in the computer vision and medical imaging communities. In terms of future work, the researchers aim to expand the applicability of this approach to a broader range of cell types and to explore its potential for synthesizing images in the computer vision domain. We introduce a Newtonian version of the Ecological Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithm as a straightforward alternative to the Langevin ECMC method. In three-dimensional dipolar models, the ECMC algorithm falls into the category of over-damped dynamics that can induce dynamical arrest. Our key innovation is the ECMC algorithm with Newtonian acceleration, which aims to overcome this limitation. To ensure general applicability, we formulate the new method in a way that applies to any potential energy function. Our simulations demonstrate that the Newtonian ECMC algorithm successfully mitigates dynamical arrest in three-dimensional dipolar models and also outperforms the Langevin ECMC method in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, we find that the equilibrium correlation functions of the Newtonian ECMC variant closely resemble those of the overdamped ECMC algorithm. Lastly, our simulations include a three-dimensional model of superconducting granules that demonstrates the versatility of the Newtonial ECMC algorithm in capturing the dynamics of complex inductive phenomena. Our findings also highlight the advantage of this algorithm in reducing the number of lattice sites where the electric field is updated, thus leading to computational savings. Specifically, we show that the intermediate ECMC regime can be achieved with fewer updates to the electric field than the overdamped ECMC algorithm. Our research thus establishes the Newtonian ECMC algorithm as a faster and more efficient alternative to the Langevin ECMC method that is particularly effective in three-dimensional dipolar models. Data augmentation has been effectively utilized to enhance vision-based deep learning models, yet its impact when applied to audio data remains largely unexplored. In this study, various data augmentation methods for sound processing are investigated and evaluated in the context of sound event detection (SED). An existing model, which won the 2019 DCASE challenge, is utilized for this purpose, and both source and overlay augmentation techniques are applied to the training data with evaluation conducted on the corresponding development sets. The findings demonstrate that applying source augmentation methods results in significantly improved performance, with the combination of time-stretch and pitch-shift augmentation yielding the highest accuracy in multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, using the original unaugugated data in addition to the overlay method with the stretched and pitch-shifted data also leads to improved outcomes, and the integration of these findings contributes to the enhancement of the existing model. The improved model exhibits enhanced efficacy in tasks involving polyphonic sound event detection and its application as a distillation method to simplify and train a more robust model that can handle multiple signal characteristics. To address this gap, we establish a rigorous mathematical framework for the superposition principle, allowing for a more precise understanding of its scope. By revisiting the traditional definition of superposition, we uncover additional nuanced interpretations. Utilizing a formal algebraic structure, we prove that the superposition principle is linked to the linearizability of systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate how various applications rely on distinct aspects of the principle, leading to a more subtle appreciation of its significance. By formalizing the superposition principle, we open the door to exploring its generalization to multiple qubits and explore its potential for further innovation. We're developing a new technique to create spectral profiles from time-frequency data by using level sets that incorporate both minimum variance estimation and signal detection principles. This method can be viewed as an optimization problem with two constraints: one related to signal subspace and the other related to detection statistic calculation. To solve this problem, we reformulate the constraint on detection statistics as a non-degenerate Riemannian manifold and apply a gradient descent method to optimize the objective function. Once this optimization problem is solved, we can calculate various spectral characteristics such as power spectral density, signal-to-noise ratio, and detection threshold. To assess our technique, we simulate multiple simulations based on several signal models, including a sinusoidal signal, a chirp signal, and a Bessel Bump function, under different noise conditions. The results show that our proposed method performs well compared to existing techniques in terms of accuracy and computational speed. Additionally, we apply spectrogram-based level sets to detect and estimate sinusoidal signals within background noise. Our technique demonstrates significant detection and estimation capabilities and achieves better results than traditional level sets, especially in situations where noise patterns resemble the desired signal. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on actual radar data collected from an AN/ALQ-107 radar system. The results show that our technique can successfully detect and estimate sinusoidal signals within the spectrum of the radar signal, even at relatively low signal-to-noise ratios. The estimated frequency and amplitude of one such target are accurate to $\pm 0.42$ Hz and $\pm 0.35$ dB, respectively. Finally, we modify our level-set method to handle multiple target spectrograms by applying a technique that incorporates spectral features and detection statistics, resulting in successful detection and amplitude estimation of multiple sinusoidal signals. The technique demonstrates excellent overall performance, with average frequency and amplitude accuracy of $\pm 1.02$ Hz and $\pm 2.45$ dB, respectively. The technique's effectiveness is also demonstrated on actual radar data collected from an AN/ALQ-107 radar system. The technique successfully detected and estimated multiple sinusoidal signals within the spectrum of the radar signal. The estimated frequency and amplitude of the targets are accurate to $\pm 1.04$ Hz and $\pm 2.28$ dB, respectively. The technique demonstrates the potential to be applied to more complex target spectrograms in the future. The techniques developed in this research have been implemented in C++ and publicly available on the Git repository https://github.com/wasim-j-ullah/LevelSets

We analyze a category of synchronized clusters in complex networks that arise from nonlinear systems exhibiting cluster synchronization. By generating a set of observables based on network node outputs, we create a dynamic system whose equilibrium states correspond to cluster configurations. Through a novel application of switching theory in hybrid systems, we develop a method for determining the number of synchronized clusters in a network. Additionally, we employ observability analysis to assess whether each cluster configuration is reachable and to calculate the dimension of the equilibrium manifold. These theoretical approaches are illustrated with numerical examples. Furthermore, we propose a special class of networks, called C-labeled networks, in which the cluster configuration can be precisely determined based on a simple visual inspection of the inter-cluster edges. Ultimately, we establish a relationship between the degree distribution within synchronized clusters and the condition for the absence of chimeras in such clusters. Our work provides a theoretical framework for detecting and characterizing cluster synchronization in complex networks. We have created a specialized Python module, 'Simulator for Artificial Reality' (SAR), to enhance virtual reality experiences by incorporating high-fidelity physical simulations. The new module enhances existing VR capabilities by adding advanced simulations of physical systems, such as gravity, motion, and interaction, which can be customized to model various phenomena. The integration of SAR with existing VR tools allows for seamless interaction with simulated phenomena, enabling users to explore and interact with virtual objects affected by simulated physical processes. For example, when wearing VR headphones, users can observe how gravity pulls them towards the ground, while also feeling simulated gravitational forces. Additionally, the module includes simulations of free-falling motion and customized gravitational fields, which can be set to mimic real-world phenomena, such as walking through a staircase or experiencing unusual gravitational fields. To facilitate access to these enhanced VR experiences, the SAR module includes detailed documentation and step-by-step examples demonstrating how to use its functions. Our goal is to provide researchers with a versatile tool to develop innovative VR applications that go beyond traditional observation to engaging interactions with simulated physical processes. For a broader size range, the transition shifted towards size-independent behavior. Studies of heavy black hole detection in future colliders have primarily focused on the formation of heavy black holes through the collision of identical light particles. However, nature may have created heavy black holes through different processes, such as the collapse of massive objects. To improve the accuracy of heavy black hole mass spectrum predictions in these scenarios, we use effective field theory to analyze the scattering of a Higgs boson and a heaviest known particle, and then apply these predictions to heavy black hole creation in various theories, including supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and a string theory-inspired scenario. Our findings show significant differences in the mass spectrum of heavy black holes formed either by a heavy particle or a light particle, and even the lightest possible particle in certain theories, leading to a higher cross-section in the light particle scenario. Consequently, a lighter minimum mass for heavy black hole detection is achievable, shifting from approximately 2-3 thousand TeV to a range of 500-700 TeV. If detected, the observed distribution of heavy black holes would also bear a distinct resemblance to those predicted in theories, including supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and a string theory-inspired scenario, allowing for a greater theoretical bias in the interpretation of future heavy black hole observations. Generally, a better agreement with non-supersymmetric theories, such as a string theory-inspired scenario with a high scale, may be seen; yet, a better agreement with a theory is possible if the mass of the heaviest known particle is close to its predicted value. Finally, in a scenario where a high scale applies to both the mass of the heaviest known particle and a related parameter, significant discrepancies in the mass spectrum of heavy black holes formed either by a heavy particle or a light particle, and even the lightest possible particle, are seen, leading to a higher cross-section in the light particle scenario, most notably for lower masses. Consequently, a lighter minimum mass for heavy black hole detection in this scenario is achievable, ranging from approximately 2-3 thousand TeV to a range of 500-700 TeV. The significant majority of genetically influenced traits display discordant pairs of alleles at associated single nucleotide polymorphisms, with a more severe variant often being detrimental and the less severe one being beneficial, having no effect, or occurring less frequently in the population. It has been hypothesized that the less severe variant of a severe allele is more similar in sequence to the optimal variant, and less similar to the detrimental variant. We developed a novel scoring system to assess the likelihood of a less severe variant being more similar to an optimal variant, and less similar to a detrimental variant, and tested it on 468 well-documented severe and less severe pairs of alleles associated with genetically influenced traits in humans. In this research, we examine 2-designs featuring a prime power number of points, which can be broken down into prime power sets. Our findings indicate that if a 2-design possesses a non-trivial automorphism group, its prime power point set count must be a power of the respective prime number. We then identify a finite desgin possessing a non-trivial automorphism group with a prime power point count of $p^2$, as well as another design with a $p^3$ point count. If a non-trivial automorphism group 2-design has a prime power point count greater than $p^2$, its order must be a multiple of the next prime number. Using this insight, we find a non-trivial automorphism group 2-design with a $p^4$ point count. We conclude that finite non-trivial automorphism group 2-designs with a prime power point count may have a point count of $p^k$ for some positive integer $k$. Our research also includes the development of a polynomial equation, which we use to solve for the possible values of $k$. We use the obtained information to classify all finite non-trivial automorphism group 2-designs with a prime power point count. We also provide an example of a finite non-trivial automorphism group 2-design with a $p^5$ point count and identify a candidate for a 2-design with a $p^6$ point count. We further investigate infinite non-trivial automorphism group 2-designs, which may have a prime power point count, and find that a non-trivial automorphism group 2-design with an infinite prime power point count must have an order that is a power of the respective prime number, leading to the identification of infinite non-trivial automorphism group 2-designs with a $p^k$ point count for positive integers $k$. We also provide infinite examples of non-trivial automorphism group 2-designs with a $p^2$ and $p^3$ point count. Additionally, a non-trivial automorphism group 2-design with an infinite number of points that has a $p^2$ point count must have a $p$-component that is a Hamming code over a prime field, which cannot happen, a non-trivial automorphism group 2-design with an infinite number of points that has a $p^3$ point count must have a $p$-component that is a extended Hamming code

We have derived general mathematical expressions, based on informational entropy, that can be applied to the study of electronic systems under a variety of influences, including spatial constraints, electronic influences, and thermal effects. We have initially demonstrated the utility of our framework by investigating two specific situations. We have examined how spatial constraints impact the electronic structure of small islands, such as quantum dots, in the limit where the island size is significantly smaller than the Kondo screening length, and found that Coulomb correlation effects are relatively minimal in this context. Our approach provides a versatile tool for the investigation of confined electronic systems under a variety of influences. High-precision line-of-sight velocity measurements for individual stars within wide binary star systems are challenging to obtain. We developed a maximum likelihood method to calculate the one-dimensional velocity dispersion of these binaries utilizing line velocity data, which are readily available and often obtained from spectroscopic analysis. By integrating a Gaussian velocity distribution, this new approach provides a minimum variance estimation of velocity dispersion. We assessed its performance using simulated data, analyzing the impact of signal-to-noise ratio, line velocity dataset size, and stellar mass. Additionally, we examined the line velocity dispersion analysis of six binary star systems through their entire lifetime, considering the effects of binary mergers on their internal dynamics. We compared our results with earlier studies and the standards of the binary population synthesis framework by van Helmond {\it et al.} (2021). We observed that using line velocities improves the measurement accuracy of velocity dispersion. Our analysis revealed relatively low velocity dispersions in these binaries, which are consistent with the expected outcomes of the binary population synthesis framework, with a recent trend of decreasing dispersion over time in binary evolution. Additionally, we discovered relatively low velocity dispersions in binary systems undergoing dynamical evolution. Furthermore, we analyzed the internal dynamics of the binary system that consists of the stars HIP 41010/40795 and discovered it exhibits a higher velocity dispersion than most of the other binaries, potentially indicating a higher likelihood of it undergoing binary mergers in the future. Lastly, we would like to recommend that future research should concentrate on obtaining high-precision line-of-sight velocity measurements for individual stars within wide binary star systems, which is crucial in further investigating the internal dynamics of these binaries. Also, as well as using line velocities, other methods such as astrometric parameters should be employed in the analysis of internal dynamics of binaries. In a multiplicative linear logic framework, proof structures can be translated into graph formats by introducing nodes that represent contraction and expansion operations. The method of graph format visualization allows us to derive the logical content of proof formats as properties of their graphs. The concept of ideal representations generalizes the idea of sound and weakly sound proofs in the graph format. Specifically, ideal representations preserve the logical content of prems and conclusions within the proof structure. Notably, ideal representations maintain the duality between!-introduction and -introduction, a property not previously documented in the literature. The development of ideal representations offers an alternative method to graph visualization for determining the logical validity of proof structures. Moreover, ideal representations enable the construction of proof structures that violate the free contraction property while maintaining consistency with their logical content. The work presented here introduces the concept of semi-ideal representations, which preserve the logical content of nested!-introduction within the proof structure. Additionally, semi-ideal representations maintain the free contraction property and do not compromise the logical content of weakly sound proofs. The research provides an algorithmic solution for constructing semi-ideal representations from linear graphs that support contraction. The theorem proves that a semi-ideal representation exists for any linear graph that involves contraction. The construction of semi-ideal representations offered by the theorem is strong in the sense that it generates representations that are dual to!-introduction and -introduction, as well as weakly sound for -introduction. The research also shows that semi-ideal representations, which preserve the free contraction property, can be utilized to derive weakly sound cut-elimination theorems from a pre-cut-elimination technique initially developed in the literature. The general approach presented in the research is likely applicable to other resource-based proof structures that incorporate a weakening operation equivalent to!. Additionally, the research maintains the distinction between the concept of soundness and weak soundness, demonstrating that these two notions are distinct within the framework of multiplicative linear logic as visualized through graph formats. The difference between these concepts is exemplified through the use of a simple proof structure that is weakly sound but not sound. The research contrasts its findings with those of earlier studies on resource-based proof structures for multiplicative linear logic with an internal weakening rule, as well as with those of earlier studies on the relationship between graph formats and the duality between!-introduction and -introduction. In a prior study, successful synchronization predictions of Bitcoin and Bitcoin-derived time series were achieved using deep learning models, extending applications of synchronization analysis beyond traditional neuroscience and cryptography applications. This work builds upon those results by applying synchronization analysis to major cryptocurrency pairs and their predictions. Converting price time series into network representations similar to neuronal connections, and feeding them into deep learning models, enabled synchronization predictions with notable accuracy. By leveraging this technique, potential hidden patterns in interdependent cryptocurrency relationships might be uncovered, providing profitable trading opportunities and enhancing investment decision-making strategies. The chosen cryptocurrency pairs were Steem vs. Bitcoin and Ripple vs. Bitcoin, and their synchronization performance was compared with that of Steem vs. Ripple and Steem vs. Bitcoin vs. Ripple, utilizing three distinct models. The results demonstrated that the applied method effectively predicts synchronization in the majority of tested scenarios, even when the lengths of the time series were significantly reduced to 50 data points. Therefore, this technique might be utilized for manual synchronization analysis and as a basis for developing automated trading algorithms. The code and data used for this study are openly available on GitHub, allowing for Reproduction and verification of the results. The provided dataset includes daily closing prices of the mentioned cryptocurrency pairs, and the code for the synchronization predictor can be found at https://github.com/damir7902/Synchronization-prediction-in-cryptocurrencies. The main contributions of this research are as follows: 1) Synchronization analysis was applied to cryptocurrency pairs, and their predictions were successfully achieved, even with reduced dataset lengths. 2) A comparison of three deep learning models revealed that the Bi-LSTM-ANN and the CNN-Bi-LSTM performed more accurately than the LSTM-ANN model in predicting synchronization. 3) A combination of deep learning and synchronization analysis provided profitable trading opportunities in cryptocurrency markets. The outcomes of this study may be extended to other domains, such as extended financial time series, and could contribute to the development of artificial general intelligence, characterized by broad cognitive capabilities and ease of transfer. The potential applications of this technique might also be transferred to neuroscience, cryptography, and other fields that utilize synchronization analysis. The primary constraints of this research were its reliance on dataset variability and the chosen network representation, as the code and data provided allow for verification and potential improvements of the results. Future studies can utilize this technique in various domains by replacing the used dataset with time series from the respective field, and modifying the network representation to better fit the domain in question. Traditional click-through rate models often rely on linear combinations of features, but they may not adequately capture the impact of visual aspects of ads. To address this limitation, this study introduces a novel deep learning model that incorporates visual features into click-through rate predictions. The proposed model leverages a learned visual feature embedding from multi-scale convolutional neural networks, combining it with textual characteristics encoded by a linear combination of weighted terms, to formulate a unified prediction function. By incorporating graphical representation methods, the study uncovers a profound understanding of the model's structural properties, revealing how the proposed model improves click-through rate predictions and outperforms existing methods on benchmark datasets. Notably, the model achieves a 4.0% relative improvement in area under the ROC curve on the Yahoo! Dataset and a 6.5% relative improvement in mean absolute error on the Amazon Dataset. Real-world business processes are often limited by restrictions on the simultaneous execution of tasks, making concurrency relevant in Business Process Management (BPM). However, concurring operations' outcomes are unpredictable, leading BPM systems to rely on flexible process models, allowing partial and probabilistic descriptions of business processes. This study explores the semantic differences between simultaneous executions of tasks with and without upper limits on the number of concurrent operations. While unrestricted concurrency results in process semantics defined by partial equality, adding a limit leads to a distinct semantics, differing from partial equality, even with multiple equality relations. This research investigates the properties of such process semantics, demonstrating that they satisfy pre-order and closedness, but not always weak monotonicity. Additionally, it introduces a formula for calculating the maximum number of concurrent operations allowed in a process. Nonetheless, determining if a process can execute a given number of simultaneous tasks is computationally challenging, in contrast to other decision problems related to process checking. This study also presents an algorithm to determine if a process can execute a sequence of tasks with specified levels of concurrency, making this decision problem solvable. Further, it shows that deciding process equality and checking if a process can execute a given sequence of tasks with specified levels of concurrency are computationally difficult, even when restricted to sequential processes. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of business process management by investigating the effects of concurrency constraints on process semantics, providing computational complexity results in the process. This knowledge can guide the development of efficient algorithms for process checking and help identify cases where the interactions between concurrency and other process properties can significantly impact their behavior. This recognition may also encourage researchers to investigate more realistic scenarios, like the behavior of business processes in real-world scenarios, with or without restrictions on the number of concurrent operations, to make decisions about process checking that take into account the actual probability of executing simultaneous tasks. This understanding could lead to practical applications, such as advising BPM systems on when to rely on probabilistic or partial process models, based on the likelihood of simultaneous operations, rather than simply adhering to a particular paradigm. This study presents a novel probabilistic model framework that integrates statistical inference and physics-based simulation to model atmospheric light propagation from fires. By optimizing a likelihood function that incorporates measured data and fire characteristics, we can uncover the underlying parameters of fire models. Notably, our approach accounts for measurement errors, making it a robust method for analyzing wildfire-induced light displays. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach using simulated data and a real-world case study involving the 2006 Los Alamos Fire in New Mexico, USA. Our findings indicate that, given accurate fire size and atmospheric conditions, our approach can reconstruct the original fire behavior. However, when confronted with incomplete or imperfect fire and atmospheric observations, our model remains consistent. Our analysis suggests that additional observations or precise fire and atmospheric conditions are necessary to accurately recover the fire's central behaviour. Nonetheless, our results show that it is possible to reconstruct the fire's peripheral behavior, and with sufficient data, the propagation rates in both situations. Our approach provides a flexible statistical analysis of fire propagation and can be applied to other astrophysical transients, such as gamma-ray bursts, using tailored fire and atmospheric models. Our framework addresses differential privacy losses experienced by users of location-based services when sharing spatial data. We introduce a framework that: 1) accurately measures privacy loss by considering the differential privacy guarantee and data dependency; 2) monitors total privacy loss and provides an upper bound; 3) maintains a trade-off between privacy loss and data utility; 4) protects against unexpected data breaches; 5) is applicable to various data types, including spatial, numeric, and categorical data. We evaluated our framework through experiments using real-world location data, which demonstrated its feasibility and accuracy. We observed that our framework successfully prevents significant privacy losses, and the cost of preserving privacy is minimal compared to the benefits achieved. We also identified the upper limit of privacy loss as 10^(-10) being a suitable value for location-based services. We created an open-source implementation of our framework, along with the accompanying data and evaluation code. This implementation is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/CS-UIUC-FP-ISLPADS/PRISM. We intend for our framework to serve as a foundation for future research in privacy preservation, with a particular focus on advancing the state of the art in location-based services. We plan to pursue the following areas of research: 1) developing efficient algorithms for privacy maintenance that are sensitive to data scalability; 2) investigating the effectiveness of alternative privacy guarantees, such as $\mathcal{R}$-differential privacy; 3) exploring the privacy preservation requirements of users when sharing spatial data, with a particular emphasis on data contributors' perspectives; 4) using machine learning to help users understand and reason about the privacy preservation of spatial data; 5) conducting additional experiments with diverse datasets, such as Valparaiso City Buses and Breast Cancer, while verifying the effectiveness of our framework on a broader range of data types. We aim to expand our technical contributions in these areas of research in an extended version of this paper, which will be presented at the IEEE Symposium on Security and Safety in Public Transport. This study investigates how inter-site variability affects brain network reliability in resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data. Using a dataset from the Human Connectome Project, we examined how differences between individual brain connections affect whole-brain networks. Our results indicate that inter-site effects on functional network connectivity can significantly impact the detection of individual and group differences. Furthermore, we found that a site-specific inter-site influence is often present, which is more pronounced in brain networks displaying greater variability in resting-state activity. Therefore, considering inter-site effects is essential for enhancing the accuracy of detecting individual and group differences in brain networks. In functional magnetic resonance imaging, incorporating reference subjects from the same scanning batch as the test subject can help minimize errors and improve the reliability of within- and between-group comparisons. In particular, when conducting between-group comparisons, including reference subjects from both groups can help refine the models and improve the precision of functional network differences. Additionally, we observed that inter-site effects are more significant in older individuals and that age is a key determinant of these effects. In contrast, we did not find significant associations between inter-site effects and average global signal, snappy brain activity, or median age in the pre-processing phase. Notably, including reference subjects from the same scanning batch as the test subject in the analysis is more effective than using standardized data. Therefore, researchers should prioritize using batch-corrected data for within-group comparisons, while also incorporating reference subjects from the same scanning batch for between-group comparisons to increase the reliability of inferences in brain imaging studies. Recent successes of neural machine translation for code-mixed text have been documented. Nonetheless, numerous studies have pointed out that positional encoding poses a challenge during code-mixed translation due to the lack of universal positional symbols. To address this limitation, this research proposes novel positional encoding methods, namely by incorporating word embeddings from related languages or domains. Word embeddings from monolingual sentences have also been explored as an alternative. Utilizing Mexican-Spanish and standard Spanish as a testing case, this study demonstrates that these proposed encoding methods yield superior results when subjected to translation quality assessments. Additionally, the proposed techniques have been validated through the analysis of their effect on the translation task using Hugging Face's Transformer models. It is worth noting that these proposed encoding methods can be adapted for other code-mixing scenarios. Furthermore, this study advocates for the utilization of monolingual sentence positional encoding when relevant language word embeddings are unavailable. Lastly, the possibility of positing a universal symbol for code-mixed positional encoding has also been ruled out. Hence, the proposed methods serve as viable alternatives for enhancing code-mixed translation models. Details regarding model implementation, data collection, and experimental setups can be accessed via https://github.com/omenglezi/OMS_Zheng_CSE_2022/tree/main/Project_2.

H$_{3}$S is considered a prime material for studying superconductivity because of its exceptionally high superconducting transition temperature when compressed. To understand the evolution of its superconducting properties, we studied the isotope effect coefficient ($\beta$) in the low-density low-lying phonon model of H$_{3}$S. The calculations revealed that $\beta$ consists of two components: the compressibility term ($\beta_s$) and the rotational term ($\beta_r$), both of which vary significantly with pressure. Furthermore, $\beta$ was found to be negative and have a non-intuitive growth trend with increasing pressure, suggesting that the phonon rigidness does not strictly govern the superconducting transition temperature as pressure changes the structural dynamics of H$_{3}$S. Additionally, the study's results are consistent with experimental findings and can be used to guide future research into the superconducting properties of compressed H$_{3}$S. Lastly, the study's approach can be applied to a wide range of hydride superconductors to understand their electron-phonon coupling.

This paper presents a novel feedback control approach that accelerates bipedal robot recovery from deviations during gait phase. To mitigate the consequences of discrepancies between the planned and actual gait paths, the proposed controller introduces a closed-loop feedback mechanism. By incorporating measurement data from the robot's inclination sensors in real-time, the controller enables swift and efficient correction procedures. By integrating this feedback into the robot's trajectory planning, the inherent tendency of bipedal robots to experience compliance-related errors is effectively addressed. By evaluating the proposed controller through both simulated and actual experiments, the authors verify its capability to successfully intervene and correct gait deviations in a real robot. Specifically, the simulated results indicate that the controller can effectively correct gait discrepancies within a timeframe of 0.5 seconds, while actual experiments confirm the feasibility and performance of the proposed feedback control approach. Overall, the proposed controller demonstrates a beneficial impact on the bipedal robot's ability to adaptively navigate challenging environments. Details regarding the controller and associated experiments can be found at https://github.com/Fazay/Feedback_Controller. This paper builds upon existing research into geometric camera tracking by incorporating machine-learning based image features, which enhance camera position and orientation calculations. By leveraging these image features, we've developed a simplified framework for geometric camera tracking that outperforms current methods, even in challenging conditions, like those involving rapid camera movements, intense light sources, or highly repetitive scenes. By replacing traditional hand-crafted features with machine-learned ones, we've substantially improved geometric camera tracking accuracy and speed. Notably, these machine-learned features exhibit versatility, successfully adapting to various applications, such as tracking pose in 3D and 2D, as well as adapting to different datasets, like those from industry and robotics. We've tested geometric camera tracking on a range of datasets, like the challenging KITTI dataset, and found that using machine-learned features significantly improved performance in difficult scenarios. By analyzing these results, we've found that using camera pose estimates with support from multiple features significantly improves accuracy. As a bonus, these machine-learned features also enhance related computer vision tasks, like 3D pose tracking. We've released our geometric camera tracking code, pre-trained models, and related KITTI dataset analysis as an open-source resource for the community. This code has been successfully integrated into the popular PIVO framework. As a result of these efforts, we've substantially improved geometric camera tracking accuracy and efficiency, laying a strong foundation for future research into this topic. In particular, we've found that using machine-learned features enables geometric camera tracking on GPUs, significantly reducing computation times. In our worst case scenario, we've found that using geometric camera tracking with machine-learned features still outperforms traditional hand-crafted features by a factor of 20. As a final contribution, we've found that using a simple metric structure from these features greatly enhances geometric camera tracking, particularly in difficult scenarios, like those involving rapid camera movements. This framework exhibits exceptional performance, even when the number of features available for calculation is relatively low. As such, we believe it to be highly adaptable and easily interpretable. As our code has been integrated into the popular PIVO framework, we've made our code, pre-trained models, and related datasets available for public use and future research.
