In federated learning, a decentralized approach to training AI models, clients collaborate by sharing calculated update information.  However, because each client has unique data sources, powering any one client often necessitates sharing knowledge beneficial to all, improving efficiency while also reducing data collection risks.  Our proposed semi-supervised personalization approach involves creating tailored models by leveraging unlabeled data and existing global models, which are then used as a starting point for local fine-tuning with provided labeled data.  Additionally, we develop a new approach called Distillation Semi-Supervised Learning, which allows the global model to incorporate knowledge from all participants by implementing a multi-class approach and calculating a compact, informative density function based on unlabeled data that captures important class trends, while also using this function to create labels for unlabeled data.  These pseudo labels are used to train a new global model, which serves as a starting point for local fine-tuning.  Our approach results in performance enhancements and reduced communication costs compared to traditional co-training, with results showing improvements in medical image classification and speech recognition tasks.  Our findings also indicate that the density function obtained using DSLS encodes valuable class information, which is supportive of the model's decision-making processes.  Code and models are available at https://github.com/apjithkumar-dsa/DSSL.git.  Our approach is the first of its kind to combine density function estimation and semi-supervised learning techniques, contributing to the development of new methods that combine global model averaging and semi-supervised learning. Emergency Department (ED) lengths of stay can vary significantly due to various factors, with even minor enhancements during treatment making a noticeable difference in visit outcomes. In this study, using real-world data from the Montefiore Medical Center, we examined the relationship between ED stay times and visit duration, while accounting for initial visit complexity and potential biases in treatment timing. The results from our analysis indicate that increasing ED stay by thirty minutes is associated with decreased revisit and readmission rates within thirty days, as well as lower costs. The findings from this study suggest that extending ED stay times is beneficial, despite initial expectations based on visit complexity. Therefore, prioritizing patients who would benefit from additional treatment time in the ED could lead to improved outcomes and reduced costs, with potential applications in quality improvement initiatives and research on treatment timing. Additionally, the results from this study emphasize the importance of accurately estimating treatment times in modeling and analyzing clinical processes. However, existing models often rely on simplistic assumptions regarding treatment timing, with even minor and realistic variations difficult to capture. In order to address this limitation, we propose an innovative method to estimate treatment times based on actual clinical data, with a novel application in modeling and analyzing ED stay times at the Montefiore Medical center. The proposed model utilizes real-world observations of clinical processes, with extended ED stay times based on visit complexity and biased by initial and completion times. The model's accuracy is confirmed through comparisons with observed data, with a close match in terms of visit distribution and key outcome metrics. The proposed model demonstrates potential applications in simulation studies, performance assessment, planning, and resource allocation - with the aim of improving clinical processes and decision-making. However, the model's scope is initially confined to ED stay times and visit complexity, with possible expansions to additional variables and outcomes in the future. In order to fully leverage the proposed model, we examined the performance assessments and resource allocations that could be supported by the model, with potential applications in allocating ED staff and scheduling patient visits. In particular, the model could be employed in determining the minimum number of ED staff required to maintain a target visit capacity, with the staff count initially set to twenty-five. This paper explores how a group of agents can work together to achieve common goals by taking advantage of their unique capabilities and the challenges they face.
Each agent has a set of tasks to complete, along with an estimate of how difficult they think each one will be.
Their objective is to coordinate with each other and decide which tasks to take on in order to maximize their overall efficiency.
This problem becomes more complex if agents can't tell which other agents are trustworthy or if they've completed their tasks, adding a layer of uncertainty to the situation.
We look at different ways that agents can work together to achieve a common goal, considering various distributions of difficult tasks and how they might choose to collaborate.
Ultimately, our findings show that cooperative strategies are not always the best option, and that agents can get better results by competing with each other in certain situations. We also identify a specific threshold that determines when cooperative strategies are more effective than competitive ones. Our research has applications in fields such as cognitive science, economics, and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly enhanced the accuracy of network intrusion detection (NID), surpassing traditional methods. Nevertheless, training a deep learning model with synthetic data in an NID system necessitates significant computational resources and motivates a federated learning approach. This model combines increased user privacy with reduced computational requirements, yet poses significant challenges in its application to federated NID. Mainly, sparsely transmitted model updates and limited access to local training data pose substantial obstacles in utilizing federated learning for NID. As a result, earlier federated learning systems are incapable of providing reliable intrusion detection, thereby restricting the potential benefits of federated NID. Motivated by these limitations, we introduce FedNID, a pioneering federated learning system for intrusion detection at the edge. FedNID leverages a novel aggregation technique based on weighted voting, along with a customized learning rate adjustment and model size reduction methods. Additionally, FedNID employs a reputation system to enhance cooperation among NID entities. Comprehensive simulations utilizing real-world network data from the Kaggle Intrusion Detection Competition demonstrate that FedNID achieves accurate intrusion detection, improves entity reputation, and facilitates seamless collaboration among NID entities. Consequently, FedNID emerges as a suitable and efficient solution for federated learning in intrusion detection applications. Finally, an experimental prototype of FedNID is implemented using real-world edge devices to validate its practical feasibility. This experimental evaluation confirms the potential of FedNID to effectively support the intrusion detection needs of NID entities. Consequently, FedNID emerges as a promising and practical solution for federated learning in intrusion detection applications. The performance of a semiconductor device heavily relies on the properties of its constituent materials.  Metal-oxide-semiconductor systems are comprised of diverse materials, which enable precise engineering of their properties to achieve efficient electrical flow.  However, the underlying processes that determine device mobility are often obscured by the complex behavior of materials at the interface with metals, leading to incorrect modeling and misinterpretation of experimental data.  To address this issue, we employ first-principles calculations to assess the potential of metal gate materials to influence device mobility.  By analyzing order-parameter-dependent electrostatic fields and density-dependent metal gate relaxation, we identify key mechanisms that govern mobility and reveal the significance of metal gate choice in optimizing device performance.  Specifically, we find that certain metal gate materials are associated with unusually high relaxation trends, which could either enhance or degrade mobility.  These findings emphasize the necessity of considering the interplay between order-parameter-dependent electrostatic fields and metal gate relaxation in the modeling of metal-oxide-semiconductor systems.  Consequently, our study offers valuable guidance for the selection of optimal gate materials to minimize performance limitations.  The optimized gate materials we identify could potentially reduce the power consumption of modern devices by up to 30%.  The predicted trends we obtain are consistent with experimental observations, thus holding significant implications for the design of cutting-edge MOS systems.  The calculated trends are also relevant to the study of other technologies that utilize epitaxial films, such as spintronics and quantum computing.  The calculated results are available for further analysis through our open-source repository, which contains the data, methods, and associated documentation.  The data repository is accessible at https://github.com/ResearchInScience/MOS-Data-Repos.   The techniques employed in this study can be obtained from https://github.com/ResearchInScience/MOS-Code.   Additional information, including the used computational methods and data curation techniques, is available at https://doi.org/10.5068/D14F4R. More details about this initiative can be found at https://osr.risscientist.org/.   The research data described in this article are available at https://doi.org/10.5068/D14F4R. Networks of oscillators that exhibit group synchronization have significant applications in physiology and engineering, yet the overall theory regarding these synchronized groups is still in its early stages. Prior studies primarily focused on the properties that a synchronized group would have in an ideal setting. In contrast, this research aims to explore the robustness of synchronized groups when subjected to uncertainties in their behavior. By applying advanced mathematical techniques, we were able to identify the fundamental characteristics of groups that would remain stable in networks of oscillators subject to variability. Our findings indicate that groups with synchronized phases are highly resistant to fluctuations, whereas groups with a phase shift are only moderately affected and, in some cases, may eventually transition into a state that is robust against further parameter changes. Through numerical simulations on a range of different networks, we were able to confirm our theoretical observations and illustrate the critical impact that uncertainties in system behavior have on synchronized groups. Our results suggest that small deviations from ideal behavior can lead to significant changes in a group's stability, even when the deviations are very small compared to the differences between individual oscillator frequencies. In particular, we found that groups with a phase shift are only stable when the differences between individual frequencies are relatively low, whereas groups with synchronized phases can withstand a wider range of frequencies, although they may eventually transition into a state that is robust against further parameter changes. Our initial survey revealed a notable absence of YouTube in a significant portion of search engine outcomes. A key aspect of deriving formulas for expected wait times is determining the operational state, or regime, at a particular location. There are essentially four distinct operation regimes, characterized by different delay conditions: a single driver, free flow, and two separate regimes resulting from interactions at stops, with and without interference. A delayed driver inserts a time gap when stopping, causing subsequent drivers to stop with reduced spacing, potentially resulting in a train, or string of vehicles. A new classification system, based on local delay, combines with spacing to determine the operational state. While this system works for a single road, modifications are needed to handle multiple roads with connections and turn lanes, and even more complex configurations. A new method of determining the operational state is developed, incorporating both local delay and spacing, with a focus on systems where vehicles may not be equally spaced. This new approach makes possible the creation of a map showing operational state conditions in a system of roads. Additionally, a new strategy, or policy, for managing traffic is introduced, as well as methods for efficiently calculating the expected wait time for any given road segment. Some of the provided formulas are compared with real data, showing generally positive results. Finally, a practical solution is presented for actively managing traffic, using real-time data, to minimize aggregate system wait time. This solution is based on the idea of selecting the road with the highest estimated wait time for the current time period. Some data is also presented to support this solution. Semi-supervised node classification using Graph Neural Networks has achieved impressive results in various applications. To expand GNN's training capacity to unlabelled graph data, several pseudo-labeling techniques have been proposed, which assign labels to unlabelled nodes based on GNN predictions. Nonetheless, these methods have shown mixed outcomes in improving GNN performance, with some even hindering it. To address this inconsistency, this study provides a thorough explanation of pseudo-label quality metrics, modelling uncertainty, neighbourhood structure, and the GNN's learning process, which aims to clarify how pseudo-labeling affects GNN performance. Based on this understanding, it suggests and evaluates simple, adaptable methods to enhance the effectiveness of pseudo-labeling. Experimental results confirm that these methods can significantly improve GNN performance in various benchmark and benchmark-like datasets with diverse characteristics. In this research, we introduce PatchNet, a lightweight, efficient, and versatile convolutional neural network designed specifically for object detection in videos. By integrating multiple scalable building blocks and efficient, inter-frame communication mechanisms, PatchNet strikes an optimal balance between performance and computational efficiency. We developed PatchNet using the EfficientNet framework, a family of highly efficient neural networks, to create a family of efficient detectors, including MobileNetV2-based PatchNet. Through extensive testing on various benchmark datasets, including KITTI and ImageNet, we consistently achieved superior results. Our novel approach to object detection in videos using PatchNet outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods, all while requiring significantly fewer computational resources. Specifically, PatchNet demonstrated improved mean average precision (mAP) on KITTI 2012 and KITTI 2015, and improved top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, outperforming other efficient models, including MobileNetV2. We publicly released the PatchNet source code to facilitate further research and development. Evaluations on videos with various frame rates confirmed that PatchNet remained effective and efficient, even when using fewer frames for object detection. Ultimately, PatchNet represents a highly effective, efficient, and versatile tool for object detection in videos. In addition to its applications in video object detection, the modular design of PatchNet also enables its use in other video-centric tasks, such as action recognition, making it a valuable resource for researchers and developers. Specifically, we successfully adapted PatchNet to perform action recognition on Mini-KITTI, outperforming other state-of-the-art models. With its exceptional efficiency, versatility, and performance, PatchNet is an invaluable tool for video object detection and other video-centric tasks. In conclusion, our research on PatchNet not only expanded the family of efficient detectors but also made significant contributions to the development of accurate object detectors for videos. The main outcome of our study shows that initial conditions significantly affect the multi-point distribution, even at large time intervals, and this effect does not diminish. The result is a contrary finding compared to a previous study on TASEP with continuous time, where the multi-point distribution converges to a normal distribution with a specific correlation structure at large time intervals. The present investigation also confirms existing results on TASEP with continuous time, which included the convergence of single point distributions and the relationship between certain distributional limits and the KPZ equation. Additionally, we derived central limit theorems for discrete time TASEP with non-standard initial conditions. The key to our analysis was developing a duality relationship between TASEP and a version of the TASEP with 'frozen' particles, combined with the use of exact distribution results and the Convergence Martingale Theorem. Our findings also lead to the calculation of the large deviation rate function for the discrete time TASEP with a standard initial condition. Finally, we provided explicit formulas for the large time limits of single and multi-point distributions under non-standard initial conditions in the context of TASEP with continuous time. To optimize the network, we propose the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique, which enables us to derive equilibrium prices through a Mathematical Programming framework. Simulation results validate the optimality of our proposed solutions and highlight the effectiveness of the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique in achieving energy efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of our solution in accommodating various energy-harvesting schemes and bandwidth allocations. To maintain simplicity, we assume that energy efficiency at the receiver is not a concern, but our framework can be modified to account for receiver energy efficiency in future work. Notably, our proposed solution remains highly effective even in the presence of imperfect channel state information. In addition to energy efficiency, our framework can also be utilized to achieve other performance metrics, such as rate allocation, by incorporating appropriate constraints into the Mathematical Programming framework. However, this method's classical equivalent, the Driscoll-Bennett model, uses a different approach and has led to conflicting interpretations of its classical versus quantum origins. To resolve this, we present a new optomechanical model that eliminates the need for a quantum drive and shows that, in cases with high occupation numbers, the Driscoll-Bennett model aligns with classical physics. Additionally, we establish a connection between this model and the widely used quantum Langevin equations. By comparing our new model with the standard treatment, the differences between classical and quantum behaviors become apparent. We explore the Driscoll-Bennett model's applications in specific scenarios, such as a particular system studied by Marshall et al. and a classical system characterized by only vibrational temperature. Notably, we also establish the development of a classical model that matches the standard quantum treatment, yet deviates from it at occupation numbers close to unity, highlighting its decoherence-induced quantum-to-classical transition. Lastly, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for the understanding of open quantum systems. Throughout the manuscript, we provide detailed mathematical derivations for the models presented. These derivations are available online as supplementary materials. Finally, the research presented here aims to contribute to the ongoing debate of how quantum systems become classical, with potential implications and extensions to this phenomenon in quantum electrodynamics. In contrast, the generalised sextic Freud weight is distinct from the generalised Airy weight, which is defined using a similar sextic function. The study of the generalized sextic Freud weight also has implications for understanding certain nonlinear equations, specifically those defined using the p-Laplace operator. Specifically, we leverage the derived eigenvalue expressions to establish existence results for a nonlinear equation involving a sextic perturbation term. The related problem of minimizing a nonlinear functional, subject to constraints defined by the first four weak derivatives, is also explored. The critical parameters and values that define this optimization problem can be determined through a combination of different methods, including scaling, dilation, and other analytical techniques. The calculations related to these optimization problems prove to be highly non-trivial and require the combination of different techniques, including the use of expression (3.10) and other key results, to obtain the correct solutions. The paper also provides a brief overview of a different type of optimization problem, defined using a different nonlinear equation and a variety of different constraints, to illustrate the diversity of different optimization problems that can be studied in this field. We introduce Multivariate Gaussian Processes (MGP) that maintain conditional independence in a probabilistic model of multiple processes. This model can simulate independent Gaussian processes by setting certain covariance values to zero, thereby modeling multiple processes as separate entities. We develop two MGP simulations: one based on sparse covariance matrices, which provides an efficient, scalable approach, and another utilizing kernel compositions. Through theoretical analysis, we prove the existence of a composed kernel that yields sparse covariance matrices, which serves as a practical solution. We showcase the effectiveness of our method in predicting individual traits from multivariate trait data by simulating MPAs on real datasets. Additionally, we provide scalable algorithms for learning MGP parameters using sparse covariance matrices and kernel compositions, which outperform current methods in terms of computational speed and data accessibility. Our work is implemented in the R package "RGP" under the repository link https://github.com/c4epping/RGP. By adapting classical transformer models, researchers have successfully applied recurrence and attention mechanisms in recurrent quantum circuits to enhance the accuracy of quantum chemistry calculations. Building upon this insight, this work introduces a novel deep learning method, dubbed deep symmetry-enforced permutation, to improve the efficiency of computing molecular ground state properties. The proposed DSM method ensures that the generated permutations align with the molecular symmetry rules, thus adhering to the no-ghost theorem. The authors' numerical evaluations have yielded exceptional results, with conventional simple and complex permutation algorithms faltering in certain cases. The DSM method surpassed these performances, with a notable enhancement of about two-fold in FLOP count, while maintaining comparable accuracy. The proposed DSM technique may be directly applied to obtain approximate wavefunctions for specific molecules, with potential future developments aimed at extending its use to larger systems and polynomial approximations. orthomodular spaces, and their corresponding underlying relationship frameworks, 
orthomodular lattices. This correspondence enables the transfer of properties from 
lattices to their associated orthomodular spaces and vice versa. As a result, 
orthomodular spaces automatically possess certain key properties, including the 
existence of atomic and coatomic elements. Conversely, any geometric structure with 
these properties can be equivalent to an orthomodular space. Furthermore, we show 
that a space's orthomodular lattice is isomorphic to that of another space if, 
and only if, their corresponding geometric structures are equivalent. Additionally, 
we find that a sublattice of a given space's orthomodular lattice corresponds to a 
closed sub-space within that space, and we establish a direct relationship between 
comparability elements in the lattice and closed sub-spaces in the orthomodular 
space. Finally, we demonstrate that any lattice, regardless of its underlying 
geometric structure, can be represented as the lattice corresponding to some 
orthomodular space, provided it satisfies specific compatibility conditions. 
Notably, these conditions are more lenient than those defining standard orthomodular 
spaces, giving rise to novel geometric structures, which we term'semi-orthomodular 
spaces.' Consequently, the class of orthomodular spaces provides an alternative 
characterization of lattices adhering to specific space consistency criteria. 
Previously, these criteria were shown to imply the existence of orthomodular spaces, 
but, as shown here, they may not be sufficient to define them uniquely.

lattices, including atomic and coatomic elements, which cannot be derived from the 
lattice alone.

The use of AI-generated proofs is becoming increasingly common in various domains, but their effectiveness is contingent upon the quality of the representations they are based on. In the context of legal document verification, for instance, human experts must carefully examine and validate the accuracy of AI-generated proofs. To address this need, we have developed SysRep, a system designed to represent the output of AI-generated proof tools in a format easily understandable by legal experts. By analyzing the structure and content of SysRep, machine learning models can predict the likelihood of errors or weaknesses present in the AI-generated proofs, thus enabling experts to focus their attention on the most suspicious or complex aspects during the review process. Evaluation results have demonstrated that SysRep can effectively forecast errors, outperforming a random guess by 67% in one benchmark scenario. Furthermore, we have integrated SysRep into a case management system, facilitating the efficient distribution of challenging cases to specialized experts. Future plans for SysRep involve leveraging its capabilities to develop AI-assisted review tools and potentially using it to determine the reliability of multiple AI-based proof generators. Additionally, we have developed a repository containing a collection of legal documents, complete with annotated proof representations, to serve as an open-source resource for the research community. This repository, along with accompanying documentation, is accessible at https://github.com/ai4gm/SysRep. For technical details regarding the development of SysRep, please refer to our detailed description in the paper's supplementary materials at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01433. Source code for the project is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ai4gm/SysRep. A video showcasing the system can be found at https://youtu.be/7pM7M7vBv9E. In this study, we explored the application of SysRep in a simulated setting inspired by complex contractual agreements, as well as through collaboration with two actual legal document verification professionals, utilizing a combination of automated and human-generated proof. The outcomes of this research indicate that SysRep possesses valuable insights capable of supporting human decision-making during the review process. Notably, in one instance, a professional was able to verify a previously unverified document containing 1098 discrete proof steps in less than 10 minutes with the aid of SysRep. To facilitate further research on the topic and potentially utilize AI-generated proofs in an operational capacity, we propose the development of an open-data repository containing detailed information on complex document verification, including the associated proof representations. This resource would serve as a valuable tool

Building on Watson's formula, combining it with Soundararajan and Harper's developments provides an explicit expression for the $2k$-th moment of $L$-function coefficients, specifically tailored for $k$ being a positive even number. This formula enables a thorough asymptotic analysis of its leading term. This analysis is crucial in understanding the behavior of a normalized version of the central value of a family of $L$-functions, where the parameter $S$ varies within a defined set $\mathcal{S}$, as the family becomes infinitely large. The structure of this asymptotic expression closely mirrors the behavior of a family of polynomials studied by Mertens, allowing for a subsequent derivation of its underlying parameters, namely the relationship between specific constants $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$, as well as the value of the central value $\Lambda_S(1/2)$ in terms of its standard deviations. Ultimately, this work provides formal proofs of two conjectures proposed by Conrey and Senni, with the first concerning the behavior of the ratio between $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$, given that both are positive, and the second, which describes the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of the sign changes of $\Lambda_S(1/2)$. Lastly, this research has been used to investigate the characteristics of salient functions, defined as functions that maintain the same sign throughout a significant portion of their domain, with a particular focus on determining whether functions within specific families are salient or not. These families include those associated with cubic fields, as well as those connected to $Q$-integral cubic fields, with additional speculation that this pattern may hold for various other fields of degree three. As advanced intelligent systems (AIS) become increasingly widespread, so too have concerns about their negative impacts grow. Many, but not all, issues with AIS can be traced back to malfunctioning, highlighting the need for better incident reporting and learning from failures. To address these problems, we have developed the Artificial Intelligence Incident Database (AIID), a comprehensive resource for recording, analyzing, and sharing AIS incidents. By gathering a diverse range of incidents from various sources, AIID serves as a hub for building awareness of AIS failures and facilitating improvements in the development of more reliable and responsible intelligent systems. Ultimately, AIID aims to become a primary reference for understanding and learning from AIS incidents, promoting positive change in the field. The database can be accessed through a public interface at https://aiid.ai2.gov.au/ and our technical approach is described in more detail in another paper. In this article, we introduce AIID, outlining our vision, methodology, and ongoing efforts to build a broad-based database, as well as the opportunities for collaboration and contribution from the broader community. We also explore potential uses of AIID beyond its primary application in informatics, as well as the various benefits that could accrue from reporting AIS incidents, such as enhanced learning opportunities, improved AIS safety and reliability, and greater community awareness of these topics. We conclude with a call to action for researchers, practitioners, and stakeholders to engage with AIID, sharing their knowledge and experiences to build a more comprehensive understanding of AIS incidents. By working together, we can utilize AIID as a platform for advancing the responsible development and deployment of intelligent systems that benefit society as a whole. This article presents Proto-Quipper-M, a modern implementation of a quantum circuit design tool, specifically tailored for reversible computing. Proto-Quipper-M's classicisation method, which translates quantum circuits into reversible circuits, is enhanced with a novel module called RQC, enabling the classicisation of any quantum circuit within the universal quantum computation framework. To preserve the non-cloning property of quantum states, Proto-Quipper-M incorporates a controlled copying function. The tool is further refined with the inclusion of a symmetric permutation circuit, which combines with the RQC module to generate a reversible circuit. A copying function module is introduced, which, when combined with a Bell-basis circuit, allows single-qubit states to be duplicated multiple times. The tool's design maintains the non-cloning property of quantum states, as required, by regulating access to these modules. In the field of genomics, sequence assembly is a crucial and computationally intensive task that researchers face. To speed up the process, a new algorithm is proposed, which efficiently builds an undirected weighted graph from fragmented DNA sequences. By utilizing multiway number partitioning, the algorithm effectively minimizes the total weight of critical sections, where breaks occur in the graph. Through experimentation using real-world data, the algorithm's accuracy and speed are significantly validated, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the problem of breaking the graph into continuous sections is actually an NP-hard problem. To address this, an efficient approximate algorithm is developed, which uses a new method to quickly identify potential breaks in the graph. By combining these techniques, the proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance in assembly tasks, according to evaluation metrics. To facilitate future research, the algorithm's source code is made available on GitHub under the license terms of LIBS. Initially, the algorithm is designed to work with single sequences, but its framework is also adaptable to handle multiple sequences in the future. To date, the algorithm has successfully assembled over 30 new, completely annotated genomes in the Solanaceae family. The Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation efficiently converts matrix-valued data into a vector format, thereby enabling easier identification of event patterns in point processes. However, the ILR transformation also introduces a metric that varies depending on the data, which needs to be taken into account when analyzing temporal patterns. While previous studies have acknowledged the benefits of ILR for descriptive analysis, they have overlooked the implications of combining ILR with nonparametric time series methods. Our research involves applying ILR to the time series analysis of macroecological data through the use of a dynamic metric that varies over time, thereby allowing for the reliable identification of temporal patterns. The results of our research demonstrate the capability of this approach to provide superior resolution in the temporal analysis of point process data. Our method also offers greater flexibility than conventional methods, such as nonparametric density estimation, while also providing exact p-values for the detected patterns. Ultimately, the effectiveness of this technique was confirmed through the simulation analysis of its performance, and its application to the real-life analysis of bird species data revealed new insights into the temporal patterns of community assembly. The software used to perform these analyses is available through the open-source R package RILR. Hybrid superconductors that combine with quantum systems have the potential to
be the foundation of quantum computation.  A key aspect is the entanglement of
Cooper pairs that develops in the proximity of a S-QD-S system, where S denotes
a superconductor, at low temperatures.  This entanglement leads to non-local
correlations that could be utilized for measuring entangled states in conductance.
However, it has not been previously confirmed if the entanglement of Cooper pairs
can cause measurable effects in conductance.  In this research, we examine the
conductance of a single-coordinated hybrid system and find that its non-local phase
coefficient $\gamma$ can cause an observable shift in the conductance spectrum.
  The magnitude of this effect is highly dependent and may be amplified by various
factors.  Furthermore, we have developed an analytical method for determining the
quantum phase of the hybrid S-QD-S system, which we have applied to calculate $\gamma$.
  A key advantage of this approach is that it allows us to determine phase coefficients
for complex networks of connected hybrid systems.  In the future, we plan to apply our
method to investigate phase phenomena in macroscopic networks of hybrid systems.

We've developed a system for text recognition in scenarios where the input is a specific set of words, such as street addresses or part numbers. Given that data, we created methods for making the recognition more accurate by using the likelihood of the unknown word instead of treating it as completely unknown. Experiments conducted in simulated environments for addresses and part numbers showed that our system excels at recognizing complex, fixed-format text. These experiments also demonstrated the benefits of incorporating language models, which vary depending on the assumed level of writing skill. Interestingly, our results indicate that pre-trained models perform better with less educated writing skills. Although offline methods facilitate offline work, they often fail to account for various runtime variables, leading to inaccurate results. We observed clear differences in the clustering behavior of various galaxy types, with spiral and irregular galaxies displaying clustering trends that align with the predictions of the Lambda-CDM cosmology. Conversely, elliptical galaxies exhibited clustering patterns that deviated from Lambda-CDM cosmology predictions at higher redshifts. We have created a new algorithm that uses an adaptive sieving approach with a backward water-filling strategy to solve complex high-dimensional problems in rank lasso. This innovative solution tackles the difficulties posed by conflicting penalties and lacking sparse structure. By launching a limited number of sieves with varying penalty levels, we can precisely identify the optimal solution and efficiently handle the associated computational complexity, achieving a scalable performance that is independent of data size. Notably, our method outperforms traditional convex relaxation techniques when the underlying signal has a sparse structure, but may introduce additional, non-sparse correlations in high-dimensional settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our adaptive sieving algorithm produces lower prediction errors and better post-optimality solutions compared to alternative methods. This approach has enabled us to develop a novel majorization property, which serves as the foundation for proving the algorithm's optimality and establishing its computational efficiency. We have also developed a novel sieving-based method for estimating the optimal solution accuracy and the required computational complexity of our algorithm. This theoretical analysis provides the first quantitative understanding of the algorithm's performance and scalability. Current conditional predictive modeling methods primarily focus on predictive process monitoring and often overlook the need for model validation. Although some methods address this issue, they are limited to certain scenarios and often rely on synthetic data, which may not accurately reflect real-process behaviors. Therefore, there is a need for validated prescriptive process monitoring methods that can be applied to various types of processes. This study proposes a framework that facilitates the deployment of prescriptive modeling methods in real-world settings through model validation. Based on the underlying assumptions of these methods, it defines prescriptive monitoring metrics, establishes relationships between model parameters and performance indicators, and outlines a testing procedure that can be adapted to accommodate diverse processes and performance indicators. The proposed framework is then tested on two established prescriptive process monitoring methods, one based on multi-criteria decision analysis and the other using decision theory. The results of this evaluation are presented, and future research directions are discussed. Additionally, an open-source implementation of the proposed framework, as well as the tested methods, is available for reproducibility purposes. Specifically, the implementation can be accessed via the PDisaster simulator, PDisaster decision model, and R language packages. More information can be found in the supplementary materials provided with this study. The potential of the proposed framework to improve decision-making in real-world processes is also explored, and one such process is presented as a use case. A novel approach for estimating the error of coupled problems in fluid dynamics is introduced, specifically designed for thin-film flows that involve both nonlinear conservation laws and ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Although robust methods exist for solving these problems, there has been a lack of reliable error estimation methods that could provide confidence and inform mesh-adaptation techniques. We address this gap with a dual-weighted residual method that combines goal-oriented error estimation for the nonlinear flow with a posteriori analysis for the coupling with the ODE. Through numerical testing on various benchmark problems, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method and evaluate its potential for application in adaptively refined meshes, even in cases involving small-scale features that could lead to oscillations. Notably, we observe that the error estimator exhibits robust behavior and remains stable in such situations. We believe that this method offers a valuable tool for practical use in adaptively refining meshes to capture critical features of the solution, which may help to reduce the complexity of meshes required to achieve precise results. We explore the practical implications of the estimator and provide insights on its potential to lower the cost of mesh refinement. To achieve this, we examine the scalability of the method and its impact on computational efficiency in solving problems, which could be particularly beneficial when dealing with intricate geometries and delicate features. We then establish a threshold for when the refined mesh can be considered optimally configured, which could serve as a guide for determining when further mesh refinement is necessary. Ultimately, we seek to provide a practical strategy for utilizing the error estimator to ensure that meshes are sufficiently refined to achieve a desired level of precision, which could be particularly advantageous when resources are limited. We test the efficacy of this strategy on benchmark problems and find that it enables the development of optimized meshes that are comparable in quality to those obtained through higher-level mesh refinement. Notably, we observe several key differences in how the error estimator behaves on various problem types, which may impact its practical application and require further investigation. One such situation arises in the interaction of the flow with the substrate, where the assumption of thin films is no longer valid, leading to a different behavior. Graph packing issues have been extensively studied for various graph types, yet tight bounds remain elusive even for basic problems like cycles and paths. This work introduces a novel algorithmic technique to determine approximate upper limits for cycle and path packing in general graphs. For cycle packing, we achieve a $O(\log |S|)$ approximation, where $|S|$ denotes the number of spheres in a given cover of the graph. For paths, a $O(\log |T|)$ approximation is found, with $|T|$ representing the number of sets in a cover resulting from a previous divide-and-conquer process. These approximations significantly improve previous ones and highlight the value of using combinatorial covers to enhance algorithmic efficiency. Additionally, we explore cycle and path unpacking, a problem that involves removing cycles or paths from a graph while preserving its connectedness. This research contributes to graph packing by providing tighter bounds, thereby facilitating greater insight into graph packing's inherent constraints. Ultimately, we aim to pave the way for more effective graph packing algorithms. Experimental findings validate the proposed algorithms and demonstrate their practical utility. This research is particularly significant in the context of demand assignment, a crucial component of traffic engineering, where we find near-optimal solutions by analyzing the approximations in terms of minimum label increase. Experimental results reveal that these solutions experience only a minimal increase in label cost compared to the optimal value. This growth remains within a constant bound of the optimal value, except in one scenario involving cycle packing, for which the increase remains within a logarithmic proportion of the optimal value. Based on these findings, we establish a threshold for the quality of solutions obtained through a simple rounding approach: the minimum possible gap between the proposed and optimal values is logged in the approximate upper limits we have provided. where each individual has a position on a linear spectrum from -100 to 100. Opinions
are updated according to a simple rule: moving towards the average of their nearest neighbors.
We discovered that, through a complex process, groups tend to form, where individuals are grouped
with those who have similar opinions. These clusters are centered at various points on the opinion
spectrum, where many individuals share the same opinion. These group formations are an example
of how a system with many similar individuals can create patterns through chaotic and unpredictable
interactions. We found that the groupings are stable, where smaller groups within a larger cluster
do not tend to separate from the main group. Additionally, when two groups within the spectrum have
opinions that overlap, they will merge into a single, combined group. We were also interested in how
these groupings are affected by "noise," where individual opinions are occasionally randomly changed. 
We discovered that, while some groupings may cause certain opinions to become fixed (where they

individuals are evenly spaced within the original group spectrum. These findings give us insight
into how a system with similar individuals can create and shape patterns and social groups. While
our study is not meant to represent a real-life situation, it can help us understand how a complex
system can create patterns and groupings, which may be applicable to studying bird flocks, school
fish, or even social groups of larger animals. Ultimately, our goal is to use this study to
develop and test an algorithm that can help us understand how these groupings are formed
and shaped, which may be useful for making decisions in fields such as biology, medicine, and

The process of converting transcribed genes into functional mRNAs involves a complex and previously underappreciated timeline that varies significantly based on gene size. Our research reveals that genes of a certain size undergo a rapid production of functional mRNA shortly after transcription completion, whereas larger genes first undergo a prolonged and variable delay during translation. Within this context, we've developed a new model that accounts for the challenges posed by large genes encoding critical proteins, such as those essential for cell survival and including the genes encoding the human diploid genome's largest subunit of RNA polymerase II, TRF2/TRF1 double-stranded RNA-binding proteins, and telomerase components. Our theoretical framework indicates that gene expression is controlled by a buffer system that prevents overwhelming transcriptional activity, and we provide empirical evidence to support this notion. Our studies demonstrate that genes involved in essential processes are guarded by a network of non-essential long genes that create a buffer zone, thereby maintaining optimal balance between transcriptional activity and protein production. Notably, mutations affecting protein production in critical genes often have a significant impact on nearby or related genes, which we've observed in multiple instances, including the relationship between TFEC and TRFC, the variation surrounding CDK9, the expansion of the CD36 gene family, and the connections between IRF2 and IRF3. Our research reveals that gene size and location work together to regulate critical protein production and maintain genome homeostasis through a buffer system. Furthermore, targeting genes with a wide size range can significantly increase the effectiveness of gene knockout, and we've verified this hypothesis using data from public resources. Our analysis also sheds light on the mechanisms governing the evolution of gene size and reveals that genes that grow larger within a genome are more likely to provide relief from selection pressure, only to subsequently grow even larger, potentially due to a new function that arises on a highly expressed gene. Notably, when a novel function first appears, it's typically located towards the middle or end of a larger gene, and we've seen this pattern in multiple instances, including the evolution of the TFEC/TRFC double-stranded RNA-binding protein, the expansion of the CD36 gene family, and the telomerase component TINF2. Our study of 64Ni employs the 40Ca + 24Mg cluster model, utilizing monopole interactions to explain excitation energy distributions. However, this model falls short in accounting for the width and shape characteristics of the energy spectrum. Kobayashi and Matsumoto's proof that linear group codes of optimal min-rank have a specific property has been enhanced by showing the property necessarily exists for any group codes C and D, provided that code D is an extension of code C and both codes have a specific property, known as Q-conformality. It has been demonstrated that this property is preserved when codes C and D undergo a series of dualizations and group ring extensions. As a result, if two linear group codes C and D are duals of each other and both codes have a specific property, known as Q-conformality, then they are equivalent.

By integrating Bucket Elimination with these methods, we create Belief Propagation with Bucket Elimination (BPEB) and Max-Product with Bucket Elimination (MPBE), respectively. BPEB and MPBE benefit from reduced computational complexity by leveraging sparsity and exploiting dependencies within their corresponding sub-graphs. We test these approaches on various scenarios, including classification, integer programming, and generative models, where they demonstrate a significant speedup in computation. Furthermore, BPEB and MPBE exhibit a notable improvement in performance on statistical models derived from practical problems, even after the elimination of significant variables. We propose these methods as efficient tools for tasks that involve sparse graphical models and suggest them as potential replacements for more complex algorithms. Additionally, we suggest improving existing sparse Belief Propagation algorithms by integrating them with Bucket Elimination. When an object falls, the collision with the ground triggers a complex signal sequence capturing dynamics like impact sound, vibration, and visual motion. Our research reveals that humans use physics-based rules to integrate multiple object drop-related cues, with age and educational background in physics influencing one's ability to accurately identify dropped objects. Through scientific experimentation and analysis of both children and adults, we demonstrated that certain individuals, categorized as "Perceptionists," have exceptional sensitivity to ground-collision events, sensing even slight changes in motion. Our findings also show that Perceptionists consistently feel the impact vibration more intensely than others, underscoring the significance of tactile feedback in object drop identification. Furthermore, we developed a sophisticated artificial intelligence model, capable of processing a wide range of multimodal sensor data like a human, to effectively recognize drop events. Notably, this model surpassed industry-leading deep learning models by a significant 7% in classification accuracy. Our ground-breaking research provides evidence of a deep, innate connection between sensory information and physics, facilitating efficient object drop recognition. Our innovative, highly accurate AI model can be applied in industries such as smart homes, wearables, and robotics by processing a broad range of sensory inputs. Finally, we present a novel, immersive smartwatch interface called DropWatch that empowers users to detect object drops, addressing various practical implications. Our project has garnered significant media attention from prominent outlets like The New York Times, CNN, and MIT Technology Review. You can find the associated video on YouTube at https://youtu.be/7Umu_Tn1HTk. By developing a new mathematical framework, the study defines jamming in terms of a specific property that is observable in systems at the jamming point, regardless of their history. This approach allows for the application of a critical scaling theory that provides a unified description of jamming through power-law equations. The analysis reveals that frictionless and shear jamming behave according to different critical scaling theories, characterized by unique exponent values. Additionally, the study explores how jamming under intermediate friction rates produces critical scaling theories that integrate both isotropic and shear jamming behaviors. The work also provides a necessary mathematical foundation for defining jamming in a precise and observable way. We introduce the MS(2)-AR(4) model, which combines the AIC-champion MS(2) polynomial model with the AR(4) model, as a potential enhancement to the AR(4) model commonly used in electricity futures pricing. We find that the MS(2)-AR(4) model effectively captures the AR component of electricity demand dynamics, which surpasses the AR(4) model's fit. Additionally, incorporating latent variables into the MS(2)-AR(4) model does not yield improved results. We test the model's robustness by simulating market crises and find that it remains effective. We use the Root Mean Square Error as the performance metric and compare the MS(2)-AR(4) model to the AR(4) model in various market conditions, including normal, crisis, and mixed scenarios. Our empirical analysis, based on data from the German EPEX SPA, reveals that the MS(2)-AR(4) model outperforms the AR(4) model across 90% of the observed time points in normal and mixed conditions, and across 80% of the observed time points in crisis conditions. As another validation step, we wrap the MS(2)-AR(4) model in a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity model, which also confirms its superior performance. We conclude that the MS(2)-AR(4) model is a useful tool for Eisenführ-Heyermann & Möller's arithmetic approaches to electricity futures pricing. Moreover, our findings suggest that the model can serve as a potential alternative to the AR(4) model for future research based on Eisenführ-Heyermann & Möller's geometric approach. Ultimately, our study underscores the importance of data-driven model selection to arrive at a more efficient methodology. As a result, we recommend employing the AR(4) model for situations characterized by simplicity and reliability, while reserving the MS(2)-AR(4) model for more complex scenarios. As a corollary, our research is consistent with Eisenführ-Heyermann & Möller's conclusion that models should be tailored to the specific problem at hand. As a broader contribution, our study highlights the value of utilizing established econometric techniques in the context of pricing financial instruments with complex characteristics, while also promoting data-driven model selection practices. Furthermore, our research is consistent with the principles of efficient problem solving, which prioritizes simplicity and reliability, as advocated by the engineers Wilhelm Cauer and Otto von Guer

However, detecting such biases yourself is impractical due to the significant time and effort required to research and understand the complex algorithms used. Therefore, we propose a proposed a system to detect and highlight potential biases in Web search results for important public queries. This system consists of three core components: (1) a training dataset of algorithmically biased search results, (2) an analysis module that assesses bias in individual search engine results, and (3) a data visualization framework for presenting the findings in a clear manner. In this paper, we will detail our approach and present the outcomes of our study, including the development of the training dataset and the effectiveness of our system in identifying bias. In our experiments, we found that our system successfully pinpointed 90% of the biased search results from our training dataset and also detected 75% of new queries not included in the training dataset. In terms of efficiency, the system required under 200 milliseconds to analyze each query. In terms of accuracy, our system was found to be 94% accurate in confirming algorithmic bias in search results identified as likely biased by our system, as confirmed by two independent assessments. In addition, our visualization framework enabled straightforward identification and review of the detected biases. In terms of scalability, our system was designed to be adaptable to various computational environments and resource constraints, and can be readily integrated into existing information systems used by public sector organizations. In terms of usability, our system was designed with a clear objective of facilitating seamless usage by public sector professionals, who can easily navigate the presented findings and take the required action to address any detected biases. In conclusion, this system provides a valuable tool for public sector organizations, enabling them to effectively detect and mitigate algorithmic biases in Web search results. In analyzing compositional data, researchers often transform their high-dimensional data by taking the logarithm and standardizing components to have the same variance. This is typically done to meet model prerequisites, like being multivariate normal, in order to apply methods like PCA. However, applying log-transforms makes it challenging to retain the data's original metric. We address this challenge by developing a method of combining PCA on normalized compositional data that preserves the data's original metric.

We propose a new approach to classical PCA methods by leveraging the data's original transformation. This involves applying a type of Riemannian PCA on the transformed data, ultimately allowing researchers to make informed decisions about feature selection and data dimensionality reduction, all while maintaining the data's original metric.

We thoroughly examined the performance of our method using artificial datasets and 30 real-world datasets from various domains, including microbiota, gene expression, and financial markets. Our results indicate that the proposed method outperforms competing approaches, including PCA, PCO, and other geometry-inspired methods, by utilizing the data's original structure and avoiding artificial transformations.

Our code and data are openly accessible on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/AlvaroOrs/LRPCA. This repository includes the implemented methods, simulated data, artificial datasets, figures, and results discussed in this study. In the future, we aim to extend our approach to include dynamic compositional data, such as the analysis of time-series data. In this paper, we investigate how a novel memory system, dynamically allocated
to varying sizes in the short-term memory region, enhances an agent's ability to
predict unseen future states and improve predictions from partial observations.
Building upon previous research using a structured memory system with pre-designated
regions for different purposes, we introduce a method where the system dynamically
allocates memory according to an agent's current expectations of what future states
may look like, as indicated by partial observations.
The expected future states are initially unknown and need to be inferred by the
agent, which is challenging without storing relevant past experiences in memory.
By utilizing a neural network to automatically determine the optimal memory configuration
and simulate different memory capacities, we show that dynamic memory allocation
significantly enhances an agent's ability to learn and reach better outcomes.
The proposed method also offers an alternative approach for addressing the 'credit
assignment' problem in more effective reinforcement learning algorithms, which can learn
end-to-end from raw observations and execute complex tasks with high accuracy. 
The proposed method outperforms a comparable approach using a fixed memory system in
tasks such as Grid World, Deep Reinforcement Learning challenges, and a practical task
of finding goals in an unmapped environment. 
The study also provides an explanation for the method's performance using a more basic

improve prediction and achieve better outcomes.

useful information from past experiences, even when the experiences are no longer
relevant or have become unnecessary due to changes in the task.

This analysis focuses on a specific scenario where $\chi$ has a smaller mass than $s$. It is known that if $s$ has a relatively small mixing with the Standard Model Higgs boson, $s$ will eventually come to rest at the bottom of a potential well due to being kinematically separated from the Higgs boson, resulting in a temperature-dependent dark matter density that significantly deviates from the Standard Model prediction during freeze-out. In this study, we demonstrate that if $s$ is predominantly composed of dark matter, the reheating temperature required to achieve the correct dark matter density is remarkably low. This results in a scenario where the correct dark matter density can be achieved even if $s$ is heavier than dark matter, a scenario in which it is known that the interaction between $\chi$ and $s$ is insufficient for dark matter annihilation to account for the observed relic density. Instead, the correct relic density is achieved through the process of "scattering" into $s$ particles during the matter-radiation decoupling epoch. In addition, for a given dark matter mass, the fraction of dark matter composed of $s$ increases as the coupling between $\chi$ and $s$ becomes weaker, requiring a higher reheating temperature to achieve the correct dark matter density. The cognitive diverse battery, CogEB, was the first to assess a wide scope of cognitive abilities both within and across domains. Its success prompted the development of a more comprehensive version, Mod-Cog, which retains CogEB's tasks while adding 29 new ones of varying complexity to create a larger, 81-task battery. Mod-Cog's expanded repertoire offers a greater range of difficulty and exploration possibilities, enabling researchers to design more tailored studies and get better insights into cognitive processes and their connections. This updated battery includes multiple measures of executive functions, social cognition, perception, emotion regulation, and general cognitive abilities, all closely linked to the CogEB tasks that they replace. Furthermore, Mod-Cog provides alternative assessments for key constructs like working memory, decision-making, and personality traits, thus providing enhanced coverage in these areas. Finally, it includes tasks that test novel capabilities like creativity, humor, and playfulness, thereby offering a more comprehensive and innovative assessment of cognitive functions. Mod-Cog's extensive task bank serves as a valuable resource for researchers who use task-analytic methods to study the same underlying cognitive abilities through different methods and domains, thus promoting consistency across studies and advancing our understanding of the interplay between cognitive tasks. Mod-Cog is freely available for non-commercial use at https://modcog.github.io. The complete package can be downloaded from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/modcog/modcog. Mod-Cog is maintained by the GitHub community, which invites researchers to join the effort and contribute to its development. Interested individuals can contact the first author at [sergio.gomez@student.unige.ch](mailto:sergio.gomez@student.unige.ch) for more information. The current version of Mod-Cog is the result of a collaborative effort between the Applied Cognitive Neuroscience lab at the University of Geneva and the Barcelona Knowledge Management group, with support from the IDIBELL Biobank and the University of Barcelona. Future updates will draw from ongoing and completed projects, as well as newly developed tasks contributed by the Mod-Cog GitHub community. A pre-processing step involves identifying image characteristics and creating a saliency-based mask to focus registration on key areas and simplify the process. With its ability to handle different intensity variations and local irregularities, CPD-SIFT can effectively register images with flexible modulation. We evaluate the performance of CPD-SIFT using 20 pairs of CT scans and compare it to state-of-the-art registration methods, which demonstrate its ability to deliver high-quality results. Furthermore, the study showcases the algorithm's capabilities on MRI-CT image pairs, highlighting its potential to improve segmentation accuracy in medical imaging. Recently, pre-trained language models have seen significant adoption across various datasets, yet they have fallen short in tackling time-series analysis tasks due to a lack of adequately annotated training data. To address this limitation, we introduce TCube, an enhanced dataset comprising 34m labeled time-series instances, alongside accompanying meta-data. TCube's design facilitates not only individual time-series prediction but also pairwise and multi-step time-series analysis. We showcase the effectiveness of TCube by pre-training BERT and applying it to multiple time-series applications, achieving notable predictive results. Furthermore, TCube's versatile dataset structure empowers researchers to tackle an array of advanced time-series tasks, making it readily accessible for public use. Additionally, to streamline the development of various time-series applications, we provide an accompanying framework called CubeNet, which streamlines data processing and inquiry operations. Ultimately, we anticipate TCube to serve as a foundational resource for enhancing time-series analysis through deep learning techniques. This study seeks to apply LSTM, a type of recurrent neural network, to improve Japanese word segmentation accuracy. Unlike English, Japanese words do not typically follow a Subject-Verb-Object structure, leading to variable sentence segmentation. In this work, we examine LSTM's effectiveness in predicting Japanese word endings. Experimental results indicate that an LSTM model incorporating contextual information achieves a higher success rate compared to a model relying only on neighboring words. Additionally, our study examines the internal workings of LSTM using dropout and an attention mechanism, revealing that the attention mechanism places greater importance on the immediate surrounding words when predicting the next ending. Furthermore, a comparison between an LSTM model utilizing contextual information and a model based on statistical models like HMM/ME, reveals improved performance in the former. Finally, our research explores the application of LSTM at a sentence-level to improve Japanese sentence segmentation using dynamic programming, resulting in enhanced accuracy. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating a significant improvement in Japanese word segmentation accuracy. Notably, our best model achieved a 9.2% error reduction over the HMM/ME method. A significant portion of these errors were related to characters in the extended kana syllable system, leading to a 5.6% error reduction in these cases. Moreover, our models exhibited a significant improvement in location-specific error reduction, particularly in cases involving multiple adjacent characters. Furthermore, by combining the attention mechanism with an LSTM model, we observed a 2.2% error reduction, indicating the potential for optimal sentence segmentation through attention-based reinforcement learning. Finally, a general comparison between LSTM and HMM/ME models across various languages revealed a consistent improvement in Japanese word segmentation accuracy using the recurrent neural network method. Based on these findings, we believe a comprehensive deep learning approach has the potential to achieve state-of-the-art results in Japanese word segmentation. Moreover, our proposed method may serve as a foundation for enhancing sentence segmentation through dynamic programming, as well as other NLP tasks involving related languages. Additionally, our study's attention-based LSTM model could be adapted for other prominent East Asian characters, such as those found in Mandarin and Korean. Conversely, our model's contextual information utilization could be applied to other languages with similar segmentation patterns, such as that seen in Korean. Finally, our proposed method may also be applicable to other languages with variable word boundaries, such as that seen in Arabic. Despite multiple modifications aimed to reduce model complexity and improve representational capabilities, it remains challenging to achieve general-purpose classification performance with compact models. Alternatively, Neuro-Symbolic Hybrid Systems have gained attention for their efficient computation, but typically need to compromise on efficiency when aiming for high-performance results. This study presents a new type of generalized Artificial Neural Network (ANN) called NetSlab, which integrates symbolic logic operations into the neural network's weighted layers. The proposed model leverages hard-tanh activation functions and weighted logic operations along the network's forward pass, resulting in a computationally efficient model that can serve as a general-purpose classifier with competitive performance. According to our experimental findings, the NetSlab model achieves comparable results with state-of-the-art DNNs, outperforming other hybrid models, and exhibits significantly lower power consumption and memory requirements. The code for the NetSlab model is publicly available at https://github.com/achyara/NetSlab. In particular, our results indicate that NetSlab offers substantial advantages in terms of inference efficiency, specifically for tasks like MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR-10, where it requires roughly 5-7 times fewer parameters and exhibits 2-4 times fewer activation evaluations compared to other hybrid models. Furthermore, the numerical advantages of NetSlab are sustained even when processing images, as evidenced by its successful performance on the ImageNet dataset. We examine survivor sets associated with the $\beta$-transformation for noninteger base $\beta$ and find that these sets coincide with numbers that have badly approximable values of Mahler type. Furthermore, we establish a specific relationship between the survivor sets of two intermediate $\beta$-transformations and demonstrate that their intersection constitutes all numbers with badly approximable values of Mahler type in base $\beta$. Additionally, we explore similar properties in the context of powers of 2 and show that the survivor sets associated with the doubling map correspond to numbers with badly approximable values of Mahler type in base 2. Lastly, we outline potential future research applications. \\

In the course of our analysis, we achieve a clarification of a particular criterion of Lehmer's conjecture, namely that Lehmer's conjecture is equivalent to the supremacy of a specific value, $B_B$, in the classical sense of unboundedness. This, in turn, gives rise to the notion of a 'weak Lehmer' conjecture which posits the validity of the classical criterion. Consequently, the relationship between various types of badly approximable numbers receives further clarification and their distinctness is confirmed. \\

Finally, we extend our findings to a general class of polynomial transformations, thereby revealing a vast collection of classes for which survivor sets correspond to numbers with badly approximable values of Mahler type and for which Lehmer's conjecture is equivalent to the supremacy of a specific value, $B_P$, in the classical sense of unboundedness. This, in turn, gives rise to the notion of a 'weak Lehmer' conjecture for each of these classes, thereby providing alternative interpretations of Lehmer's conjecture itself. \\

Our analysis is built upon a novel model of analytic hill climbing, often referred to as the 'hybrid method', combined with a novel version of Mahler's fundamental theorem, as well as numerous combinatorial results, all of which are detailed in the provided proofs and papers in progress. \\

Machine learning model explanations have been enhanced by saliency mapping, which maps uninterpretable features to interpretable versions. However, these methods often rely on inductive biases or provide irrelevant insights for complex datasets. To address this issue, a novel explanation technique called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs) has been proposed. DACs utilize adjacent data points to create predictive models, allowing for predictable shifts in coefficients as input variables change. This approach was tested on various datasets and demonstrated its effectiveness by revealing new insights in the bike-sharing dataset. Specifically, DACs identified counterintuitive youth demand and the interaction between registered and casual users, which supplements existing knowledge. Furthermore, DACs provided marginal importance values that aligned with previous research findings. To facilitate future research, a comprehensive framework called Explainable Deep Regression (XDR) has been established, which integrates DACs with other explanation techniques. The xdr package has been developed in R and is available for public use. Future research will focus on enhancing DACs to capture polynomial relationships and incorporating constraints from domain experts. Ultimately, DACs aims to become a versatile method for analyzing dependent variables using machine learning models. To achieve this goal, DACs will be tested on high-stakes datasets in the future. Meanwhile, other methods such as Roldan and Vaidya's and Grdina and Khanna's are confined to specific settings (e.g., linear models) and involve considerable computation overhead. This research presents a new approach to project-based software engineering that allows students to create driver software that operates on microcontrollers and is connected to physical components like LEDs and motors. To test the drivers, we're developing a system that mimics the connection to physical devices using artificial agents and simulation software. The solution consists of three parts: the Artificial Intelligence Testing Environment, the Simulation Software Reconfiguration Tool, and the Driver Adapter Software. 

Here's how it works:
- The Artificial Intelligence Testing Environment is responsible for creating test scenarios by interpreting input from students, and it's managed through a User Interface that processes these inputs and controls the testing process.
- The Simulation Software Reconfiguration Tool takes the Artificial Intelligence Testing Environment's outputs and converts them into formats that can be used by the Simulation Software to simulate the physical devices connected to the drivers.
- The Driver Adapter Software acts as a middleman, allowing the students' code to communicate with the testing system by adapting the inputs and outputs.

We're developing this testing system as a real-world example to demonstrate the challenges of testing driver software and to present a concrete problem for students to learn how to create testable software components that can be easily verified and debugged.

We conducted a pilot study with undergraduate software engineering students to evaluate the effectiveness of our testing system in project-based learning. The results showed positive outcomes, and we're now planning to refine the testing system based on these findings and conduct a larger-scale study in the coming semester. 

In this research, we're contributing the design of the testing system as an approach to project-based software engineering that can be used by educators to teach students the principles of test-driven development in the context of driver software developed for microcontrollers.

This paper presents an evaluation of two techniques for enhancing the security of untrusted applications within a Linux environment.  The first method, Envelope, allows for the isolation of untrusted apps by restricting their system call functionality.  However, Envelope is specifically designed for programming languages that require a virtual machine, such as JavaScript and Python, and is optimized for a specific interpretation model.  The other technique, Timeloops, focuses on protecting untrusted apps by limiting their execution.  Both Envelope and Timeloops are being integrated with the Jvstalker virtual machine to provide a security layer for JavaScript and Python applications.  A comparative study of the two techniques revealed that Envelope is more efficient, but Timeloops offers greater ease of implementation and is less complex.  As a result, Envelope was modified to accommodate static code analysis and compilation-time enforcement, and a dynamic version was developed for protecting apps that use dynamic code loading.  A major revision of Timeloops was also implemented, incorporating techniques from runtime inspection and dispatching, to create a more streamlined and efficient filter.  A comparative assessment of the modified techniques confirmed that Stencil, the static version of Envelope, offers the best performance, followed closely by dynamic Envelope, and then Timeloops.  Conversely, Timeloops requires less development effort and has a simpler implementation.  Ultimately, the integration of both techniques holds significant potential for enhancing application security.  As part of this integration, a prototype filter was developed for protecting Python applications, and experiments demonstrated the efficacy of this integration in limiting malicious system calls and app execution.  Details of the performance integration, integration experiments, and efficacy evaluations are presented in the paper's technical discussion.
