This research introduces a family of compressive ICA (CIICA) algorithms that combine principles of compressive sensing and independent component analysis. These algorithms utilize a single compressive sensing measurement matrix to obtain sparse representations of mixed signals, which can then be efficiently decomposed into independent components using a reduced size of units. We present three CIICA variants based on different updating methods and evaluate their performance in various contexts, including source counting and component recovery, under conditions of complete and partial knowledge of the compressive sensing matrix. Our results show that CIICA algorithms outperform traditional ICA algorithms in terms of memory efficiency, running with lower memory access requirements of $O(M)$ compared to $O(N)$, where $M
  < N$, while achieving comparable to superior performance in terms of correct component recovery rate. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of quantization on the performance of CIICA and observed that even with highly distorted representations, CIICA algorithms remain competitive, demonstrating robustness to this type of noise. We also examined the performance of our algorithms in the context of post-nonlinear ICA and observed that CIICA algorithms remain efficient and accurate even when the sources exhibit nonlinear relationships with the identity matrix. Notably, we found that CIICA algorithms with partial knowledge of the sensing matrix achieve similar performance to their fully informed counterparts. Based on our findings, we recommend the use of a cross-validation approach to select the optimal compression ratio for real-world applications. The proposed algorithms, implemented in the open-source MatLab package, can be accessed at https://github.com/alberto123au/CIICA. Experimental results validate the theoretical performance of our algorithms, showcasing their effectiveness in the simulation-based evaluation. Additionally, we successfully applied the CIICA algorithms to analyze real-world mixed signal data, including EEG recordings from a neuroscientific study and stock market time-series data. Our analysis, which included multiple evaluation metrics, showed that the top-performing CIICA algorithm accurately detects the independent components of the data while achieving correct source counting. In contrast, the standard ICA algorithm was unable to provide a sparse and stable set of independent components. In conclusion, the proposed CIICA algorithms offer a memory-efficient solution for ICA problems, effectively combining principles of compressive sensing and independent component analysis to achieve accurate component recovery at reduced memory costs. Our experimental evaluation validates the performance of these algorithms, which outperform traditional ICA algorithms in various contexts while successfully applying them to real-world data sets. The developed code is openly accessible at https://github.com/alberto123au/CIICA.

We explore how the integration of a coherent feedback loop influences the capabilities of quantum systems to generate entanglement when under the influence of heat. Our study reveals that including a coherent feedback loop significantly enhances a system's ability to produce entanglement, doing so even in situations where it would fail without it. Furthermore, we've developed criteria for both static and dynamic systems that enable the determination of entanglement without the need for precise temperature measurement. Our proposed criteria serve as certifiable bounds for the maximum amount of entanglement that can be achieved in a system subject to varying temperatures. In order to obtain these bounds, we utilize a unified approach to express both the quantum system and the environmental interactions in terms of the linear algebra of the Hamiltonian. This expression enables the analysis of thermal effects in an abstract manner, leading to the realization that certain conditions necessary for embedding the environment into the system's Hilbert space also facilitate the achievement of maximal entanglement. We utilize this unified approach to establish both static and dynamic conditions for entanglement that are robust against fluctuations in temperature and system-bath interaction. In our examples, consisting of both a static system and a dynamic system consisting of two qubits connected via a harmonic oscillator, we demonstrate the significance of coherent feedback loops in the production of entanglement and verify that our proposed bounds accurately certifying the maximal entanglement that can be achieved in these systems. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between robust entanglement and the non-Markovian behavior of the system, discovering a correlation between the duration of non-Markovian behavior and the increased capacity for entanglement. Our study provides significant insights into the production of entanglement through the integration of coherent feedback loops, underscoring the importance of consideration of dynamic system interactions in the production of robust entanglement. Our proposed entanglement bounds also serve as reminders of the limitations of using static conditions to produce entanglement as a general rule. Lastly, our study provides an alternative perspective on the environmental constraints of entanglement, demonstrating how the integration of coherent feedback loops can be used to produce entanglement through the optimization of system interactions with its environment. This optimization is made possible by incorporating the dynamics of both the system and the environment into the production of entanglement. This article presents a unified structure for examining computations performed by quantum, neural, and optical systems, as well as other up-and-coming quantum technologies. The framework is based on an input-output model that evaluates the success of a computation by measuring the correlation between inputs and outputs. However, we find that quantum computations stand out from other physical computation mechanisms due to their inability to perfectly evaluate performance, unless additional irrelevant inputs are incorporated. This finding has practical implications, as it underscores the importance of keeping track of the relationship between inputs and outputs when assessing the performance of computational systems. Additionally, our input-output framework provides a useful tool for exploring the connection between computational tasks and physical systems. Using this framework, we are able to demonstrate how certain computational tasks are implemented in a similar manner by both neural and quantum computers, despite the tasks themselves being fundamentally different. The relationship between computation and the physical systems that perform it is explored further by considering the role of noise, a fundamental characteristic of all physical computation mechanisms. In the context of noisy computations, we identify a clear distinction between errors that affect the relationship between inputs and outputs and those that merely introduce random correlations. As a concrete example, we examine the computation of the absolute value function and show that while it can be efficiently computed by both quantum and neural networks, the associated optical implementation is noticeably different, highlighting the diverse roles of noise in different computational tasks. The optical computations stand out from the other physical computation mechanisms due to their unique property of being completely decentralized and lacking a relationship between inputs and outputs. While this property may seem advantageous, we find that it comes with a cost, as certain computational tasks require a significantly larger number of input-output relationships to be established, which can become impractical. In the context of classification tasks, we demonstrate the importance of maintaining input-output relationships in computational systems, which may be useful for tasks beyond classification. Finally, we explore the potential for classification tasks to be used as a physical mechanism to explore the connection between inputs and outputs, which can serve as a foundation for developing new computational tasks and technologies. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between physical systems and computational tasks, which can guide future research and development in this domain. We consider a d-dimensional random walk with steps of length 1, starting from the origin and lasting for a time T, where the increased step sizes lead to a count of K(T) = 0 + 1 +... + T^(d-1) + T^d sites visited. It's demonstrated that visits to a significantly greater number of positions in d+1 dimensions compared to d dimensions is typical. To achieve this result, we apply a general technique of'multiplying dimensions', combine it with a linear programming technique, and utilize a specific estimate of the number of collisions in a random walk, all of which are new developments. Additionally, we address a related issue by defining a measure of complexity for discrete walks and demonstrating that these walks tend to be more complex if the dimension increases. Finally, we provide an alternative for a long-standing conjecture in the field by establishing that the maximum number of distinct positions visited by a d-dimensional random walk, starting from a single point and lasting for a time T, is generally less than the maximum number of positions in a d-dimensional lattice with a hop distance of at most T. If the dimension is high, this result indicates that the former is typically less than the square root of the latter. We also introduce a new model of walks on a grid with memory, where the path's geometry is influenced by the walker's memory of its previous steps, and demonstrate that these walks tend to be more complex in higher dimensions. The quality of text-to-speech systems can significantly benefit from speech masking during non-blurred, non-pause periods. By incorporating masked speech, the TTS system can learn a more accurate representation of speech, enhancing its naturalness and expressiveness. A novel system called MaskedSpeech is introduced, which utilizes a mask factorization technique to divide speech into blurred, non-blurred, and pause segments. While existing TTS systems only utilize non-blurred segments, MaskedSpeech leverages blurred segments for learning a more comprehensive speech representation. Additionally, MaskedSpeech optimizes its objective factorization to minimize disruption to non-blurred segments. A comprehensive experiment was conducted across four datasets in four languages, demonstrating that MaskedSpeech enhances the naturalness and expressiveness of synthesized speech in all languages. Notably, it outperformed the baseline system by 26.3% on the MOS scale in one evaluation. A comparison with WaveNet, Tacotron2, and FastSpeech2 also revealed that MaskedSpeech can be implemented as a plug-and-play replacement for these systems with little computational overhead. Specifically, it can be integrated with Tacotron2 to achieve improved naturalness and expressiveness without sacrificing synthesis speed. Furthermore, it can be combined with FastSpeech2 to produce high-quality speech with accelerated synthesis speeds. A live demo of MaskedSpeech can be accessed at [www.msdemo.com](http://www.msdemo.com). In neuromorphic computing, the aspiration of achieving efficient learning within hardware is driving the development of novel on-chip learning techniques that differ from conventional software-based methods.  The spiking neural network based on memristor crossbar architecture has gained significant attention in this regard.  The implementation of synaptic training, particularly using analog spike events, within this architecture is well-established, however, the challenge of integrating backpropagation, a crucial algorithm for large-scale deep learning model deployment, still persists.  The existing memristor crossbar based neuromorphic learning frameworks face limitations due to their inability to support end-to-end training of deep learning models due to the one-shot analog symmetry breaking issue.  To address this limitation, a new spiking neural network based learning framework, named Rebergram, has been developed to overcome the mentioned limitation.  The Rebergram framework leverages a novel loss function and data augmentation techniques to enable the end-to-end training of deep learning models based on analog symmetry breaking.  The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Rebergram framework by achieving a 10% error reduction compared to the baseline model.  Additionally, the Rebergram framework, designed for hardware implementation, has been successfully tested on a commercial Field-Programmable Gate Array using a neuromorphic chip specific programming approach.  The results show a 25% improvement in the error rate over the conventional softmax based baseline.  The computational efficiency of the Rebergram framework is also analyzed based on the number of analog bits and neuromorphic cores used.  The analysis reveals that the computational cost of the Rebergram framework is predominantly influenced by the number of analog bits used.  The Rebergram framework offers a potential pathway for future neuromorphic computing applications by addressing the existing hardware limitations.  The key differentiating features of the Rebergram framework are:  1) the utilization of a novel loss function to promote the development of robust global features, 2) the employment of data augmentation to boost the quality of the end-end training, 3) the incorporation of an analog symmetry breaking technique based on in-pipeline data processing, 4) the compatibility with a commercially available FPGA based neuromorphic platform, 5) the seamless integration with a large public dataset, and 6) the development of a neuromorphic chip specific programming approach to facilitate the transition from software to hardware.  The technical discussion of the proposed method is based on the assumption that the neuromorphic computing system employs analog weights and binary inputs

We performed integral field spectroscopy on the young massive cluster Westerlund 2, a region known for its substantial star ejection that may influence the galactic stellar initial mass function. Our study involved mapping the properties of multiple cluster fields, and we found a notable absence of stellar populations in the error budget that could account for up to 30% of the stars being ejected from the cluster at velocities exceeding the galaxy's circular velocity. Despite numerous ejecta candidates, we could not confirm the presence of ejecta cluster members beyond a certain radius due to contamination from the galactic stream and field stars. We found that a fast-ejecta population with properties similar to P940 (a previously mapped star) is present in Westerlund 2, although it may not be the sole origin of this group's stars. Utilizing stellar stratification, we determined that two-component metallicity distribution is required to explain the cluster's overall metallicity, and we found an intrinsic metallicity deficit in the fast-ejecta population compared to cluster-bound stars. Furthermore, we discovered two newly identified blue straggler candidates with high tangential velocities that are likely members of the fast-ejecta group. Our findings support the idea that Westerndon 2 is a supernova-rich environment with multiple star-ejecta interactions each day. Unlike the ejecta in NGC 3603, Westerndon 2's ejecta does not follow the same stellar distribution as its stars, and further studies are required to confirm the uniqueness of these findings. Additionally, we used K-giant measurements to map Westerndon 2's gravitational potential, and our results showed that a flat disc gradient is present in the north-south direction, and a slight radial slope exists in this potential. This study is the first to chart the mass distribution in Westerndon 2, and it may serve as a prototype for future studies of massive star-ejecta populations. Future spectroscopic surveys such as the Roman space telescope may reveal dozens of newly discovered ejecta in Westerndon 2, and potentially other massive star clusters in the galaxy. Based on Westerndon 2's characteristics, it is likely that a significant portion (30-50%) of the galactic stellar initial mass function originates from massive star clusters with high mass distribution. Additionally, a massive cluster like Westerndon 2 plays a unique role in regulating the galactic stellar-by-stellar mass transfer, and its star-ejecta distribution may follow unique patterns compared to less massive cluster like NGC 360

The minimax principle, which establishes a connection between the $\mathcal{H}$-monotonicity property and the existence of solutions in variational problems, is discussed in relation to its applications to first-order and second-order elliptic Dirichlet problems. The minimax principle is reinterpreted in terms of sub/suplinear operators, which in turn allows it to be applied to a broad class of nonlinear elliptic problems. The minimax principle is also demonstrated to be applicable to time-dependent parabolic problems by making connections to related elliptic problems. The applications of the minimax principle are illustrated through examples involving various nonlinear elliptic and parabolic problems. Furthermore, the minimax principle is utilized to prove the existence of multiple solutions in the following problems: the first-order nonlinear elliptic problem, the second-order nonlinear elliptic problem, and the time-dependent nonlinear parabolic problem. Additionally, the minimax principle is used to show that the existence of minimal and maximal elements in the geodesic pseudorelation of a Hilbert manifold implies the existence of a minimum and a maximum of a weakly coercive functional with both sub/suplinear properties. The applications of the minimax principle are extended to the third-order nonlinear elliptic problem, the second-order nonlinear evolution problem, and the third-order nonlinear evolution problem. Finally, the minimax principle is used to establish the existence of multiple solutions for the mentioned problems. Conversely, the nonexistence of a minimum or a maximum in the pseudorelation of a Hilbert manifold for a weakly coercive functional with sub/suplinear properties is demonstrated. The study also explores the connections between the restricted minimax principle, the infinite minimax principle, and the $\mathcal{H}$-monotonicity property. The discussion is complemented by the introduction of a new result linking the minimax principle to the multiple minima property in the pseudorelation of a Hilbert manifold for a weakly coercive functional with sub/suplinear properties. The study concludes by analyzing its contributions to the field. The study is completed by a bibliography listing the references used. Finally, the main results of the study are reprised.

Utilizing handwritten text recognizers in conjunction with Generative Adversarial Networks allows for the improvement of degraded document images. However, handwritten text recognizers are susceptible to inaccuracies resulting from minor image degradations, which can be alleviated through image enhancement. In this research, we develop an image quality enhancement method that utilizes a handwritten text recognizer to provide accurate text input to a discriminator in a Generative Adversarial Network. The handwritten text recognizer is trained to provide hand-written text rather than attempting to generate clean images from degraded input. This approach is complemented by a generator in the GAN that reverses the image degradation process, allowing the discriminator to verify image quality based on both the enhanced images and the original degraded documents. The proposed method outperforms existing hand-written text recognizers and image enhancement methods, producing high-quality images and accurate text output. Additionally, we find that integrating image enhancement with handwritten text recognition improves hand-written text recognition accuracy over standalone handwritten text recognition. The proposed method is denoted as HandWritten Text Recognizer followed by GAN (HWR-GAN) and demonstrates exceptional performance in hand-written text recognition accuracy and image enhancement quality, representing a more effective approach to hand-written text recognition and image enhancement. In a more practical application, we successfully improve a commercial handwritten text recognizer, specifically the Tesseract API, by substituting the API's image enhancement method with our HWR-GAN. The modified Tesseract API exhibits superior performance in both accurate text output and visual image quality over the original version. The performance of the modified Tesseract API surpasses that of the original version by 22.4%, 26.5%, and 60.6% in terms of text output accuracy, image enhancement quality, and visual image quality, respectively. In a comparable evaluation, the modified Tesseract API outperforms other competing handwritten text recognizers, specifically the CROHME Challenge Solution and the HTRDB, by 13.0%, 14.0%, and 6.0% in terms of text output accuracy, image enhancement quality, and visual image quality, respectively. Super-resolution (SR) technology has been successfully applied to various fields, including astronomy. SR techniques can reconstruct high-resolution images from multiple low-resolution images captured under varying conditions. SR methods can be categorized into two main types: learning-based and physics-based approaches, with the latter relying on astronomical point spread functions (PSF) and the principle of image deconvolution. However, the physics-based method may not consistently produce satisfactory results if the captured images are too blurry or if the actual PSF is not accurately represented. On the other hand, learning-based SR methods utilize deep neural networks to achieve SR reconstruction, but they have the drawback of requiring a large dataset of paired high-resolution low-resolution image pairs. Since astronomical images are typically scarce and often blurred, making the PSF a critical factor, combining both methods seems like an optimal solution. In this study, a novel SR method is proposed that utilizes a physics-based approach to pre-process the images and then employs a learning-based SR nodule to enhance the resolution. The physics-based nodule is based on a data-driven estimation of the PSF, using a data-driven model that learns to estimate the blurring caused by the telescope's point spread function, as well as a system that uses a blurriness map to accurately reconstruct the blurriness in each image. This information is then passed on to a learning-based SR nodule, which uses a generated, clear version of the low-resolution image to produce a high-resolution image. The proposed method is evaluated using real data from the Grover telescope at the Big Bear Observatory, with the results showing significant improvements over current SR techniques. In particular, the proposed method demonstrates SR capabilities down to a scale factor of four, with a 40% reduction in noise compared to the reference image, as well as accurately reconstructing the original blurriness in the images. To establish a unified model for training multiple human operators controlling multiple robots, we propose a novel Federated Learning framework. This innovative system facilitates simultaneous learning between multiple robots and their respective human controllers, enhancing their collaborative capabilities. By distributing a unified model across interconnected devices - in this case, robots and human device-equipped heads mounted with augmented reality devices - the framework allows for efficient model training. As each device is responsible for generating local gradients, the challenge of dividing tasks among devices is addressed through an optimized solution. Additionally, we outline key considerations for designing such interaction protocols and demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework via successful simulation studies of multiple robots working together. These experiments reveal the impact of various parameters, including network latency and device connectivity, on the training process. Ultimately, our framework shows great potential for applying ML techniques to complex mhmri scenarios. Here, we focus on two distinct use cases: 1) multiple robots assisting one human, and 2) multiple humans controlling multiple robots. This research opens up new research avenues for applying ML techniques in complex mhmri settings. For more information on this research, please view our full paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17228 and our video presentation at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cpCOTYAoC6I&feature=youtube. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/AUTOPilot-UIUC/FedLearn_mhmri. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation grants 1939592 and 2046572. We have developed a novel approach that employs adversarial training and robust regularization to create deep learning models that perform flawlessly even under extreme scenario predictions. Our framework is the first to seamlessly integrate these two methods, which are necessary for training models that can withstand unknown future threats. Since adversarial training often necessitates knowledge of the specific attack, and robust regularization alone may not suffice for the task, we have modified the process to incorporate an additional layer of protection. By modifying the loss function to include a robustness criterion, simultaneously optimizing both model correctness and robustness, we have achieved a framework that provides confidence in its decisions. Our proposed framework has been successfully tested on various datasets and models, outperforming existing competitors in prediction accuracy and robustness. Notably, we have achieved a remarkable 97.70% prediction accuracy with a robustness score of 93.46% on the challenging ImageNet dataset. Our framework has significant potential for application in industries where data collection and model testing can be costly and time-consuming, particularly for fields such as medicine and law. With our framework, the development of deep learning models becomes notably more efficient, reliable, and safe. Our source code will be made available on GitHub at https://github.com/drumbox/Early-Bird-Robust-Net. Our paper has been submitted to the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition for formal presentation.

Understanding their behavior and spreading dynamics, which are tied to key attributes, can aid researchers in identifying and counteracting online rumors. A data-driven rumor model, incorporating attribute information, enables analysts to gain insights into rumor dynamics and characteristics. Based on a large dataset of Chinese rumors, our analysis focuses on how attribute information influences rumor modeling. The results show that attributes significantly impact rumor analysis, with implications for researchers and practitioners working on online rumor detection and mitigation. The findings highlight the potential for attribute information to guide developers in building effective rumor-mitigation systems. The underlying dataset, which includes information on precursor attributes and locations related to rumors, is also presented. The approach outlined in this paper is applicable to developing and improving existing rumor-mitigation systems as well as similar applications for other social media platforms. This study investigates how well different dimensionality reduction methods can extract and reconstruct hyperspectral image pixels, focusing on the impact of noise levels. It reveals that methods like PCA and t-SNE offer superior reconstruction performance, even with noisy data. Additionally, we demonstrate that a hybrid classifier utilizing a combination of PCA and KNN (nearest neighbor) can outperform classifiers employing more sophisticated techniques like deep neural networks and ensemble algorithms, achieving up to 98.47% accuracy in a hyperspectral pixel classification task. Notably, this hybrid classifier performs well across various dimensionality reduction methods and noise levels, suggesting its reliability and general applicability. Hence, it is recommended as a dependable solution for pixel classification, particularly when combined with efficient methods like UMAP or t-SNE for feature dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, we introduce an open-source Python package, dimreduction_scatter, which efficiently implements dimensionality reduction methods, facilitating the use of scattered plotting for feature visualization. The proposed analytical approach and associated code package can be utilized for numerous applications, including the analysis of large hyperspectral images, where manual feature engineering proves ineffective. The integration of the dimensionality reduction scatters with popular deep learning libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow also enhances their capability to utilize dimensionality reduction methods effectively. In the realm of deep learning, the choice of loss function has often been considered straightforward, with Mean Square Error (MSE) being the de facto standard for regression tasks. However, research has shown that MSE is only minimally interpretable in terms of the underlying data distribution. Consequently, various loss functions have been proposed, yet their underlying theoretical connections to data interpretation are rarely established. A prior investigation found that under-represented loss functions, including KL Diversion, can lead to improved performance despite data constraints. This study builds on this discovery by conducting a comprehensive loss function emigration experiment. First, a suite of 19 state-of-the-art loss functions was evaluated on 21 benchmark regression tasks. Notably, this assessment confirmed that KL Diversion and MSE exhibit distinct minimization points, alluding to potential data manipulation. Furthermore, a large-scale training experiment using GPT-3 revealed that many loss functions are susceptible to evasion tactics, with some even facilitating data manipulation. Interestingly, our findings also demonstrate that multiple loss functions can produce comparable performance on certain benchmark tasks, including MSE and KL Diversion, highlighting their differing impacts on data distribution and performance. A custom tool, LossFinder, was developed to empower researchers in selecting loss functions that align with their objectives and are resistant to manipulation. Overall, this research emphasizes the importance of scrutinizing loss function choices to ensure they conform to the underlying data interpretation principles and achieve the desired outcomes. We used hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy with high spatial resolution to examine the interplay between charge-density-wave (CDW) order and exciton condensation in monolayer TiSe2 on boron nitride. Our research demonstrates that CDW order excites excitons and leads to significant lattice deformation within the ultra-thin crystal structure, as manifested by the emergence of new quasi-particle bands. Our findings offer experimental verification of the exciton-phonon coupling mechanism underlying the soft-mode approach to CDW ordering in monolayer TiSe2. Moreover, our study provides tangible evidence of exciton condensation in a 2D material, thereby opening up new avenues for the investigation of correlated electron systems with adjustable dielectric properties. With the ability to manipulate excitons using light, we propose experimental strategies for either suppressing or enhancing CDW ordering in monolayer TiSe2 via optical excitation. Conversely, pressing the system near the quantum critical point could lead to the creation of exciton liquid droplets due to exciton-phonon coupling, as illustrated theoretically. Ultimately, our research aims for a complete understanding of the excitons in monolayer TiSe2 through simultaneous adjustment of electron, photon, and lattice irradiation. Additionally, our photoemission data featuring $\sigma$ and $\pi$ polarization reveals distinct contributions from CDW quasi-particles and phonons to the spectral weight, thus facilitating a greater understanding of the CDW state through resolution of the quasi-particle momentum space. Emergency call centers rely on text-based incident reports from field personnel to assess risks. We studied these reports, which contain information about incidents such as vehicle crashes, medical emergencies, and fires, and found that related requests varied significantly based on the type of incident. To streamline this process, we sought to automatically identify required details in each report, thus enabling more efficient response times. We began by categorizing incidents in two groups: those involving emergencies and those related to responses. Within these categories, models were developed to predict likely collection points for specific pieces of information. For instance, reports of emergencies might contain information about involved parties, while response-related incidents might contain notes on primary and secondary contacts. We assessed these models' accuracy and found that to predict ten specific points of collection, separate models achieved 91% and 85% accuracy for emergency and response incidents, respectively, while a unified model had an accuracy of 27%. Furthermore, we found that incorporating additional information would improve the classification of certain incident reports. We believe our findings can guide development of risk assessment systems that adjust to the format and content of received reports. Additionally, we have made our code and dataset available online for the purpose of transparency and replication. Specifically, the code can be accessed at https://github.com/krishannad/risk-assessment, and the dataset can be found at https://humboldt university.github.io/risk-assessment-dataset/. We welcome contributions that can expand the capabilities of risk assessment systems. If interested, please reach out to krishannad@humboldt.edu.\\

Keywords: natural language processing, sequence models, transparency, datasets, information collection, text classification.\\

Research has made significant progress in understanding superconductors with unusual Fermi surfaces, characterized by non-trivial topological properties. In contrast, little is known about the mechanical stress-induced modifications to these Fermi surfaces. Using a theoretical model based on a specific type of material known as BCT compounds, our research shows that mechanical stress can significantly alter the topological characteristics of the Fermi surface. The study also indicates that these changes can manifest as a significant increase in the material's magnetic susceptibility at low temperatures, with the amount of increase potentially exceeding orders of magnitude. A prominent method for enhancing model-optimal policies utilizes human feedback
in the form of relative rankings, which can be costly when provided one-by-one.
To mitigate these costs, we investigate ways to optimize human feedback by
grouping comparisons and examining their collective output. Our central concept is
"critical subsets" of comparisons, which contain sufficient information to determine
the optimal ranking. Through mathematical analysis, we have identified instances where
systematic approaches can reduce the number of necessary comparisons. Additionally,
we have created an algorithm that selects high-information comparisons based on
model predictions. In experiments using synthetic and real-world data, we have
observed that our approach can significantly reduce the need for human feedback. 
This efficiency gain enables us to explore more complex decision-making scenarios
and achieve better results in reward learning. Our code and data can be found at the
specified link.  https://github.com/krhng/batch_human_feedback.

We've investigated the problem of reinforcement learning in scenarios where optimal policies might be compromised by corruption. Our study provides a range of algorithms that adapt to the extent of corruption, using at most $\sqrt{\frac{d \log (D+1)}{\Delta}}$ amount of data, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the state space, $D$ denotes the maximum achievable reward rate, and $\Delta$ represents the advantage of the optimal policy over suboptimal ones. Notably, our algorithms exhibit an improvement over existing methods, as the required data efficiency is only sensitive to the dimensionality $d$, as opposed to the much larger search space $S\times A$. The design of these algorithms relies on having an estimate of the corruption level, $\epsilon$, which is not known in advance. As such, we developed a preliminary filter to estimate this $\epsilon$ using an iterative process, resulting in an algorithm that uses a range of $\epsilon$ values and adapts accordingly. Our study provides data efficiency bounds for these algorithms, both with and without knowledge of the corruption level, $\epsilon$. When the corruption level, $\epsilon$, is known, we developed an algorithm that utilizes this information to achieve faster convergence. For the specific scenario of binary corruption, $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$, we developed an algorithm that utilizes the difference in log-likelihood ratios between these policies to determine the corruption level, $\epsilon$. Furthermore, we tested the efficacy of these algorithms in scenarios of unknown corruption levels, $\epsilon$, using synthetic data. Our study provides empirical evidence of the effectiveness of these algorithms in adapting to the extent of corruption, as long as the algorithms can determine that the corruption level, $\epsilon$, is nonzero. This study examines the approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation, focusing on the relationship between impulse approximate controllability and internal controllability. We establish a connection between these two forms of controllability by proving that impulse approximate controllability implies internal controllability under specific conditions. Conversely, internal controllability can be derived from impulse approximate controllability when the controller's duration is extended. Additionally, we explore the relationship between impulse approximate controllability and the localization of the impulse control function in the impulsive heat equation. Our analysis includes essential definitions, the structure of the reachability set, and a comparison between impulse approximate controllability and internal controllability. We provide numerical examples to verify the results and demonstrate the efficacy of impulse approximate controllability in the impulsive heat equation. Finally, we propose future research directions, including the extension of our results to other types of differential equations and the design of optimal impulse controls. The study concludes with a brief exploration of the possibilities for generalizing the impulsive heat equation to include non-Lipschitz coefficients and the relevance of this generalization to the control of electrical impedance tomography. Lastly, the study addresses the practical challenges associated with implementing the impulsive heat equation as a control strategy due to the discrete and non-Lipschitz nature of the impulse control function. Despite these limitations, the study showcases the potential of the impulsive heat equation as a mathematical model for understanding heat wave propagation and the effect of pointwise controls in thermal systems. Furthermore, the study promotes the use of approximate controllability as a viable approach that can overcome the robustness issues associated with exact controllability in the impulsive heat equation. Ultimately, the study aims to encourage further research into the approximate controllability of the impulsive heat equation and related differential equations with Carleman estimates. Additionally, the study finds applicability in the control of thermal systems through the approximation of internal controllability. Nevertheless, the study acknowledges the practical drawbacks of exact controllability in the impulsive heat equation due to its discrete and non-Lipschitz nature. Molecular machines, found in cells and laboratories alike, rely on interactions between structural elements to move, influenced by forces such as friction and steric interference. Dynamic systems, like microtubule transport powered by dynein, and Brownian ratchet models, can be studied together to illustrate how mechanical tensions, maintained by active structures, can create movement from random motion. We introduce a theoretical framework, based on abstract objects called "twists," to describe the formation of mechanical bonds and breaks, both driven by existing forces. This model provides a measurable twist density to describe molecular movement and, in cases of laboratory-built molecular machines, can predict necessary activation energies. We also explore how twists, assumed to be passive objects, can record the history of mechanical tensions within biological systems, affecting their future movement. Our approach is versatile, applicable to various systems, such as dynein-microtubule dynamics and the self-assembly of viral proteins. Moreover, we demonstrate that, in some cases, recording mechanical histories can enhance the efficiency of molecular movement. We utilize the example of the laboratory-built molecular machine, built to transport micrometers-long rods, showing how twists from previous turns in motion can facilitate faster transportation. This innovation offers a fundamental innovation in molecular engineering, potentially applicable to biological molecular machines as well. In a related topic, we examine the feasibility of using molecular machines, capable of transporting macroscopic loads, to tap geological thermal energy. Our detailed studies, centered on a geothermal molecule, designed to transport geologic rocks, reveal a thermal activation energy barrier of 50-70 meV. We conclude that such high-end molecular machines, capable of tapping geological thermal energy, are unrealistic, however, our model is applicable to smaller loads, like ions and atoms, where we demonstrate a theoretical loading capacity of up to 100 pN for such molecules. Furthermore, we noticed a notable decline in loading capacity as the molecule's length increased, opposite to our twists model's predictions. It's an object of interest because it's significantly larger and more massive than typical ice bodies, yet significantly smaller than celestial bodies. Our findings indicate that GJ 229B's atmosphere is gradually disappearing and that the data is best explained as coming from a system with two distinct components: a massive object with a size and mass similar to that of a small star, and an atmosphere with properties similar to those of a hot, small star. This is supported by the presence of indistinguishable magnesium oxide and silicate components in both the upper and lower layers of the atmosphere. Our observations and modeling suggest that the boundary between objects that form via core accretion and those that form via gravitational collapse is not as clear-cut as previously thought. Objects like GJ 229B, which is at a crossroads of planetary and stellar formation, can exhibit complex features. When compared to other intermediate objects, GJ 229B stands out due to its remarkable similarity to the hot, small star HD 176051. This comparison is key as it could provide a unified explanation for the observed phenomena in these objects. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the object's atmosphere is gradually disappearing, a process that is likely to be observed in the coming years. Our research combines stochastic particle fluid dynamics with various microbial transport models, enabling accurate simulation of both turbulent and laminar air systems. In contrast to simpler models like the well-mixed framework, our methods effectively predict aerosol concentration and transport mechanisms. By integrating an airborne virus model with a particle transport system and factoring in breathing patterns, floor tile moisture, and human movement, we simulate various environmental conditions. Our model is validated through comparison with empirical data, demonstrating reasonable agreement. Furthermore, we examine the impact of different model assumptions on transmission risk. Specifically, we investigate and illustrate the influence of factors such as turbulence, breathing pattern asymmetry, and virus stability on transmission outcomes. Finally, our results guide the development of noncontact immunity strategies, including the recommendation that maintaining a distance of at least 5-6 meters from an infected individual is necessary to minimize transmission risk. We examined how the number of parts in minimal periodic decompositions varies with the period, and the results depend on the complexity of the pattern. If the pattern has a complexity that increases at a regular rate, Szabados' conjecture holds. Conversely, if the pattern's complexity increases irregularly, Szabados' conjecture does not apply. Our research provides a new level of insight into the relationships between pattern complexity, periodic decomposition properties, and the validity of Szabados' conjecture. Additionally, we identified specific conditions under which the differences between consecutive terms in the decomposition grow or decline. Our analysis is complemented by the discovery of a new lower bound for these differences. Lastly, we presented an algorithm that enables the precise calculation of a number related to the decompositions, which was previously only estimated. This algorithm has the potential to be adapted for use in computational biology to analyze the evolution of minimal periodic sequences. This application could help determine the probability of obtaining specific minimal periodic sequences with a given period that correspond to the genetic code. A novel kernel-based method has been developed, building on dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), to capture the spatiotemporal behavior of nonlinear systems. This approach, kernel-based dynamic mode decomposition (KDMD), combines the effectiveness of kernel learning and the simplicity of DMD. By applying the kernel trick to DMD, KDMD can capture the underlying dynamics of complex systems, even when the snapshot data is limited to a low spatial resolution. Moreover, the proposed method can adapt to various nonlinear systems of multiple scales by selecting the most relevant kernel. Leveraging the gram-schmidt process, KDMD can be implemented in a closed-form solution, similar to traditional DMD. To evaluate its performance, KDMD was applied to simulated data from a Taylor-Couette flow system and experimental data from a quasicontinuous reactor, producing robust results in both cases. The study demonstrates that KDMD can accurately capture the dominant eigenvalues and modes of various systems, making it a valuable tool for analyzing nonlinear dynamics. Overall, our investigation uncovers the intricate connections between chess strategy and player ability, shedding new light on the world of professional chess. Binary systems containing a compact object such as a neutron star or white dwarf can undergo the process of Accretion Induced Collapse (AIC) if the transferred material triggers stellar collapse.  The possibility of AIC has significant implications for the understanding of supernova events, particularly if the initial and final compact objects have significantly different magnetic field strengths.  In such scenarios, the magnetic field of the initial compact object could be amplified or reduced as a result of the collapse.  In order to investigate this phenomenon further, we have developed a theoretical framework for the interaction of high-density matter with an externally-generated magnetic field.  The framework allows for the simulation of the microphysical processes involved in the interaction, and we have conducted simulations of the merger of neutron stars and white dwarfs with various magnetic orientations and configurations to gain insight into the resulting magnetic field dynamics.  The results of the simulations show that the magnetic field lines tend to align with the jet-like outflow patterns and orientate themselves according to the angular momentum of the progenitor objects.  The final magnetic topology of the AIC scenario is characterised by a complex configuration involving a poloidal magnetic field that gives rise to toroidal substructures.  The findings of the simulations indicate that the magnetic field inclination is primarily determined by the caliper radius and spin angles of the compact objects, rather than the detailed distribution of the accreting material.  The model provides a useful tool for understanding the AIC process through numerical simulations and could be expanded to include other binary system interactions such as the stable coexistence of the compact objects.  The study also paves the way for the potential observation of the electromagnetic counterparts of the AIC process, and highlights the significance of accurately determining the properties of the compact objects and the surrounding disc in binary systems.  The research has important implications for the improvement of numerical models of the compact object collisions and binary system mergers, and could be applied to the understanding of various astrophysical phenomena including quasars, gamma-ray bursts, and super-chandrasehar type gravitational wave sources.  The findings of the research could also be used to study the properties and evolutionary history of the compact objects and their surrounding disc in binary systems through the analysis of the gravitational wave data from the events of the binary system collisions.  The results of the research could also be used to further understand the processes involved in the formation and evolutionary development of the compact objects and their surrounding disc in binary systems through the comparison of the observed phenomena with the calculated results of the binary system collisions.

This paper presents a novel perspective on how intrinsic motivation can enhance reinforcement learning, particularly when combined with extrinsic rewards. Current approaches often prioritize either intrinsic motivation or extrinsic rewards, but we investigate the effects of providing both, introducing a new learning paradigm called Intrinsically-Enhanced Reward Structures (IERS). Our theoretical analysis reveals that IERS can accelerate training, but only under specific conditions. Additionally, we develop a metric to gauge the level of intrinsic reward in learning agents and validate our theoretical findings through simulations and a real-world robotic experiment. Interestingly, our results show that IERS can either boost or hinder learning, contingent on the environment and how much intrinsic reward the agents already derive from it. Therefore, manually adjusting the balance between intrinsic and extrinsic rewards can improve the efficiency of reinforcement learning models. Moreover, our research offers a more subtle interpretation of CRTRL, a learning algorithm that seeks to maximize both intrinsic reward and extrinsic rewards simultaneously. As such, CRTRL can be considered a more adaptable version of its variants, including Q-learning with intrinsic reward and prioritized experience replay. Additionally, our analysis sheds new light on the characteristics of high-level priors in reinforcement learning. Specifically, we've derived new insights into the computational complexity of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) and variable elimination algorithms in the context of restricted planar DAGs, which are a generalization of trees. Our key contributions include: Firstly, we've established a sharp distinction in computational complexity between CSPs that can be solved using the variable elimination algorithm and those that require elimination orderings with limited tree-width. Furthermore, we've derived new integer programming-based algorithmic techniques that parameterized by treewidth, allowing us to generalize current integer programming algorithms used in solvers. Additionally, we've derived new depth-1 arithmetic circuit counting techniques that are also treewidth-parameterized, allowing us to generalize current integer programming algorithms used in solvers. Conversely, we've shown that variational auto-encoders used in the Restricted Boltzmann Machine learning paradigm can be counted within the same complexity class as depth-1 arithmetic circuits, even when restricted to the BPQ class of planar DAGs. Notably, our results can be generalized to the broader BPQ class of DAGs, which includes the well-studied BPQ class of bipartite graphs. This analysis examines how Quantum Mechanics can be formulated using mathematical structures from topology and analysis, with a particular emphasis on essential tools, such as complex numbers, linear vector spaces, and function properties. We look at how these tools can be used in operational approaches to Quantum Mechanics, with a focus on understanding the measurement process. Unlike decision trees that make definitive predictions, Indecision Trees are designed to handle uncertain outcomes and multi-valued predictions, making them suited for handling noisy data and counterfactual scenarios. We show how Indecision Trees can be efficiently combined with probability distributions, and demonstrate their benefits in the context of counterfactual inference and semi-supervised learning, outperforming existing methods in both cases. The Indecision Trees approach can be implemented using a modified version of popular algorithms such as EM, and can be applied to a wide range of problems including missing data recovery, multi-class classification, and reinforcement learning. In our experiments, Indecision Trees consistently achieved better results than existing methods, highlighting their value in machine learning applications. Building on existing single-target approaches, this research introduces an early abandoning mechanism to reduce the search time and number of distance computations in one-to-many searches. The study utilizes the popular Time-Space Distance (TSD) index, modifying it to support early abandoning by sorting index entries prior to search and leveraging partial results. The proposed MODiTSDwea version of the TSD index includes efficient techniques for creating and querying an abandoned Prune Distance Index, with internal pointers that accelerate the search process. Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). While there is a general recognition of over-smoothing, the underlying causes and their implications in machine learning and network architecture are not thoroughly understood. This research provides an in-depth analysis from two perspectives: the theoretical foundation of GCNs and the properties of GCN architectures. We found that over-smoothing is mainly attributed to the properties of GCNs, specifically the eigenvalues of the graph, Laplacian, and mixing matrices. Furthermore, we found that the over-smoothing phenomenon is inherent to GCNs. We investigated the effects of GCN architectures on over-smoothing and found that the choice of architecture plays a crucial role. Based on our findings, we developed algorithms to estimate the effective layer of GCNs, which can guide the selection of GCN layer configurations. Our methods also demonstrate strong generalization performance on various graph classification tasks, according to our experimental results. This study provides simplified limits on dark matter (DM) that can decay into various mediators such as bosons or fermions, leading to signatures like multi-lepton and jet production along with large jet missing transverse momentum. Our limits are based on a dataset of 7.4 fb^-1 of pp collisions at 13 TeV collected by the CMS experiment. A statistical method is used to set limits by modeling the observed number of events under different hypotheses as a background in a 2D matrix of kinematic variables. By comparing the observed data with predictions from different models of DM decay modes, we establish limits on the product of the DM density and decay width of the dark matter, given certain assumptions about the decay of mediators. This study is particularly relevant in scenarios where the dark matter has a relatively small mass compared to the mass of the mediators. For example, we set limits on the decay width of the dark matter for different cases where it decays into heavy bosons or a sum of fermions, assuming the mass of the latter is 50 GeV or 1 TeV. We also set combined limits on the decay width of the dark matter in scenarios where it can decay into various final states via different mediator bosons. Overall, these limits provide significant constraints on theories of ballast dark matter, where the mass of the dark matter is less than the mass of the mediators. Our limits are even more stringent than those obtained in a previous study based on searches for events with a single large jet and missing transverse momentum. Additionally, we present results on the mass dependence of the cross-section times the decay width of the dark matter for different assumptions about its interaction with the standard model particles. This research offers a novel probabilistic approach to estimating the number of shared random trends underlying multiple non-stationary time series. Building on the continuous framework of Johansen's procedure, our methodical analysis assesses the accuracy of the estimator, particularly how it performs in scenarios of limited data, heavy-tailed patterns, and significant market fluctuations, and reveals that it consistently determines the correct number of common random trends in such complex scenarios. Additionally, our findings indicate that the estimator remains precise even when individual series exhibit long memory. To validate these theoretical outcomes, our analysis includes results from extensive Monte Carlo experiments, which support the observed accuracy in real-life data sets, as illustrated by means of several empirical examples. Specifically, our analysis demonstrates that the estimator's accuracy depends on the availability of at least 250 observations per series and a minimal ratio of series to observations of 1/3. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the shared stochastic trends among various data sets can be reliably identified when at least 90% of the individual series exhibit long memory. These outcomes are particularly evident in the analysis of stock price indices. Our research further introduces a associated test statistic along with corresponding critical values to determine whether a given series is driven by a single random trend. This test can be applied individually to assess the shared stochastic nature of a given series within a multiple series data set. Our companion software provides a functional implementation of these methods. Specifically, the R package CCSignal offers a signal extraction procedure that can be utilized to identify the shared stochastic trends underlying a given data set of stock price indices. This test can be compared to three alternative tests for common factors, namely the ccf, urca::pcfgene, and urca::pcf tests, which are all part of the urca package. Galaxy clusters act as gravitational lenses, creating distorted images of background galaxies.
The mass of individual galaxy cluster members can vary significantly, potentially leading to notable distortions.
In addition to main cluster members, various objects such as galaxies, star clusters, and far-off galaxy clusters can act as perturbers due to their non-negligible masses.
The effect of these perturbers on lensing distortions is generally considered minimal.
A recent study has demonstrated that lower-mass perturbers, typically found in galaxy clusters with lower central densities, can induce notable distortions.
The team analyzed the lensing distortions in a galaxy cluster named MACS J0022+0048, utilizing a novel approach to map mass distribution.
The resulting map revealed a pair of galaxy clusters overlapping at a point called the filamentary structure.
The team discovered that lower-mass perturbers in galaxy clusters can significantly affect the accuracy of mass distribution mapping.
The findings of the study will help in improving the estimation of mass distribution in galaxy clusters through lensing distortions by including substructure information.
A model-dependent comparison of the team's map with X-ray data showed a generally good agreement, although the inclusion of substructure revealed certain discrepancies.
The study also highlighted the challenge of accurately inferring mass distribution in galaxy clusters based on lensing distortions alone.

Research has emphasized the significance of skewness and kurtosis in asset returns for option pricing, but a superior approach may be to use cross-sectional returns, which reflect how individual stocks contribute to total market movements. If the cross-sectional return distribution's characteristics mirror those of asset returns, it would imply that option pricing can be informed by capturing the cross-sectional return moments. Specifically, calculating the first four moments of cross-sectional returns may be more practical than computing the moments of asset returns, which are critical for pricing. This study investigates the feasibility of using cross-sectional returns for pricing, evaluating their suitability for pricing options in comparison to asset returns. Using high-frequency data of S&P 500 stocks, it finds that the first four moments of cross-sectional returns match those of asset returns, whereas the fifth and sixth moments differ significantly. This discovery suggests that cross-sectional returns can effectively capture the price-sensitive characteristics of asset returns, making them a more transparent and easily computable alternative for pricing options. Furthermore, combining cross-sectional returns with time series asset returns may enhance the accuracy of option pricing, which is confirmed in empirical tests. This study also explores various applications of cross-sectional returns, including modeling portfolio performance, assessing market liquidity and systemic risk, and helping investors make investment decisions. Additionally, it demonstrates that cross-sectional returns can be utilized for pricing options in both constant volatility and the Black-Scholes models. This research offers a novel approach to option pricing, offering both investors and practitioners a more manageable method for pricing options. Ultimately, this strategy may contribute to both greater option pricing efficiency and better alignment of prices with fundamental market data. We use these twists to construct an equivariant cohomology ring, with an isomorphism existing between this ring and the cohomology ring of a classifying space for the group G, processed through a Galois extension induced by the action of G on T. We identify certain twist families as 'geometric' and 'non geometric', separating the equivariant cohomology into stable and non-stable components. Implementing these proposed initiatives was anticipated to improve the climate, increase collaboration, and produce more research outcomes. Based on the 15 newly suggested ideas, introducing a 'Wellness Wednesday' series was the most favored innovation, followed by 'Departmental Website' and 'Research Spotlight' as other preferred options. Prioritizing and integrating climate, collaboration, and visibility initiatives was recommended to ensure successful execution and achieve the desired impact. By combining and adapting existing and new initiatives, the department can improve its overall climate, foster a more harmonious and productive environment, and enhance its reputation as a welcoming and innovative academic community. Ultimately, a happy and supportive community translates into happy and productive employees and great students!

Through experiments using a virtual reality platform, we observe that sellers who attempt to cheat do not maximize their revenue, due to limitations imposed by feelings of fairness and honesty. Notably, our study is the first to conduct high-stakes auctions in a virtual reality environment, where bidders and sellers wear HMDs and interact with fully immersive auction environments. We find that when the threat of police enforcement is present, but not effectively monitored, it has a minimal impact on preventing cheating. However, the emergence of a voluntary system of auction rule enforcement, maintained through collective action, significantly reduces cheating and maximizes sellers' revenue, even in the absence of external enforcement mechanisms. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of incorporating fair and honest preferences in models of non-credible auctions, which have previously been solely framed as games of strategic manipulation. Based on our results, a voluntary enforcement mechanism is shown to be an equilibrium in which all bidders and sellers refrain from deviating, even when faced with a threat of punishment from a third-party enforcer. Moreover, when sellers are willing to sacrifice their own fairness and honesty values, a system of third-party enforcement emerges as an equilibrium, in which case the voluntary enforcement mechanism is shown to be inferior. Accurate diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperattention Disorder (ADHD) is challenging and often requires expertise along with time and resources. Deep Learning (DL) techniques have shown potential in enhancing diagnosis efficiency, but require large datasets and time-consuming manual label verification. To overcome these limitations, we suggest a novel approach based on the critical Role of Interest (ROI) in ADHD pathogenesis. By training a deep neural network on a reduced set of strategically selected ROIs, we aim to improve ADHD diagnosis precision. We conducted extensive experiments with publicly available ADHD-200 State-of-the-art Challenge data, evaluating models with various architectures and training configurations. Notably, our Modified ResNet-18 model, pre-trained on an autoencoder task, achieved an impressive 70.46\% accuracy when trained on just half of the dataset volumes, and 71.80\% when trained on three-quarters of the dataset, respectively. Validation across datasets revealed that this model performed comparably to state-of-the-art challenges, and sometimes even surpassed them. Notably, our analysis revealed that certain DL features exhibited strong correlations with Full Scale Intelligence Quotient (FSIQ) scores, while others demonstrated connections to ADHD symptom subtypes. These findings underscore the ability of DL methods to uncover valuable clinical insights and improve ADHD diagnosis efficiency. By reducing the necessity for vast manually annotated datasets, our approach has the potential to revolutionize computer-aided ADHD diagnosis and detection. Furthermore, our proposed AL technique, based on ROI importance weighting, enabled precise selection of crucial images for further human evaluation, thereby enhancing ADHD classification performance. Ultimately, our model was successfully tested in a simple classification task, yielding an accuracy of 70.46\%, and demonstrated robust generalization capabilities across various testing conditions. The growth of music usage has led to a need for better music representation, yet existing models are restricted due to the scarcity of multi-modal music datasets. Our new dataset, MusicTM, comprises a vast collection of music videos and accompanying lyrics transcripts, allowing for the development of more effective cross-modal music representation methods. We present VSE-LT, a video-lingual text model that focuses on extracting important musical features, by pairing music videos with lyrics and optimizing a video-lingual similarity objective function. Comprehensive testing on MusicTM-Dataset and the existing AVA and MSCOCO datasets has shown VSE-LT's excellence in similarity ranking and retrieval tasks. Notably, VSE-LT excelled in music retrieval tasks, outperforming current methods by a substantial 10%. Additionally, we analyzed the musical features extracted by VSE-LT and discovered them to be relevant to music theory. This paper shares our experience in using Ontodia, a visual data exploration tool, 
to explore various datasets and enhances it further. We briefly introduce Ontodia and 
its capabilities before highlighting our contributions in refining the platform. 
By sharing methods and results from user-friendly enhancements, we aim to facilitate 
connections within the Ontodia community and promote community-driven growth.

successful collaboration where we utilized Ontodia to visually navigate Wikidata

based on graph data reduction, which preserves key features.

further investigation.

Ontodia as a platform for harmonious human-data interactions and contributing to 
its continued growth and development.

A co-designed algebraic and geometric balancing domain decomposition preconditioner, BDDC(C), is analyzed in terms of its algebraic counterpart, the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC). This analysis provides insights into the performance of BDDC using a model problem. It demonstrates that the condition number of BDDC's preconditioned problem is predominantly determined by a few key off-diagonal elements of the stiffness matrix. Specifically, these elements contribute to the lower bound of the condition number. Furthermore, the preconditioner's performance is largely influenced by the following factors: the connectivity within subdomains, the ratio of subdomain sizes, and the distribution of degrees of freedom within them. This understanding enables the development of guidelines to optimize BDDC(C)'s performance. Notably, the results are presented in relation to the algebraic algebraic multigrid (AMG) method, which is often used as a model for BDDC. However, unlike BDDC, AMG does not suffer from connectivity-related issues. Nevertheless, the conditions derived for BDDC provide upper bounds for AMG's performance, suggesting that BDDC and AMG are complementary methods. Finally, the results suggest that BDDC's potential for improvement is largely encapsulated by the ratio of subdomain sizes, underscoring its significance in optimizing the preconditioner's effectiveness. This study examines how users contribute to content management in collaborative systems by analyzing their behavior when categorizing articles. By identifying patterns in user activity, we uncover methods by which individuals spontaneously create new categories, assign multiple categories to content, and tag beyond established labels. Building on this insight, we propose an automated system for expanding system categories based on user preferences and demonstrate its effectiveness using data from Wikipedia's French edition. Moreover, we develop an approach for categorizing content beyond established labels by identifying interconnected themes among tags and leveraging user roles within a community. By applying this model to Wikipedia's English edition, we increase the number of categories by 26% and enhance predictive accuracy. Our analysis explores the connection between user behavior and content management, offering potential new mechanisms for advanced category development. Additionally, we explore the technical challenges and requirements associated with implementing these changes. Our research provides a foundation for future research into content management, including the potential for spontaneous category development and the interplay between user behavior and content interactions within collaborative systems. Common methods for controlling acoustic waves rely on elastic solid deformation. In this research, we examine the control of long-wavelength acoustic waves using heat and fluid properties, where the acoustic soft meta-material is based on a microscopic micro-sphere structure. The study focuses on the impact of heat-induced movements and fluid viscosity on the operation of the micro-sphere technology. The results show that heat and fluid effects can significantly affect the control of long-wavelength acoustic waves. The study also finds that heat and fluid effects can cause the soft meta-material to absorb rather than transmit acoustic energy. This work presents a strategy called mobile integrated access and backhaul (mIAB) with a reconfigurable massive MIMO (RMMM) technology to enhance mobile broadband connectivity for users in motion, by enabling the backhaul connection and access separation through beamforming. Leveraging RMMM's capabilities, mIAB facilitates multi-user, multi-beam communication with adjustable beamwidths to serve individuals or groups on the move simultaneously. Our proposed model extracts the backhaul connection for each user through a narrow beam, while providing separate access beams to minimize interference between users. By optimizing beamwidths, our mIAB strategy achieves cost-effective implementation. Our simulation results demonstrate that mIAB with RMMM can significantly enhance the throughput capacity and energy efficiency for users in motion, compared to conventional cellular networks. Moreover, our findings reveal the potential for mIAB with RMMM to increase the average throughput by up to 500% and reduce energy efficiency by up to 60%, while reducing the cost per bit by up to 90%. Our research offers novel insights into the mIAB paradigm with RMMM, which can inspire the development of more advanced MIMO strategies to serve mobile users effectively. Our analysis indicates that mIAB with RMMM is highly suitable for applications like high-speed transportation systems, by providing superior connectivity during journeys. Our mIAB with RMMM can potentially transform the future of transportation systems into mobile cities with enhanced connectivity, by addressing the challenges of connectivity through innovative technologies. Our study presents a comprehensive outlook on the potential of mIAB with RMMM to reshape the future of mobile communications, by offering superior performance and cost-effective solutions. Our research can inspire further development of MIMO-based strategies to serve mobile users effectively. Our results can be utilized for optimizing beamwidths based on user positions, by prioritizing the backhaul connection for users in need, by maximizing the throughput capacity and energy efficiency, by minimizing interference and cost per bit. This project aims to examine the relationship between algorithm stability and hyperparameter interaction, focusing on stochastic gradient descent, both with and without momentum. A theoretical model, based on El Karoui and Guillin's stability concept from 2006, is developed to analyze the asymptotic stability of stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, two specific models of hyperparameter space are modeled as discrete graphs, one based on Renyi entropy and another on Tsallis entropy. By applying the above mentioned graph theory framework to both models, the project shows that they are equivalent. A practical method is also proposed to measure algorithm stability using entropy-based metrics, validated through experimental results on the CIFAR10 deep learning benchmark. Finally, the project demonstrates that hyperparameters facilitating individual node stability can lead to slower convergence in node neighborhood changes. This suggests that trade-offs exist between different stability aspects. The project concludes by suggesting that more research is required to achieve entropic stability in high-performance SGD algorithms. The discrete nature of energy in the electromagnetic field, observed in the Balmer series, prompted a historical interpretation of quantum theory by Planck and later by Bohr. Building on this, we develop a simple, consistent theoretical framework, which provides a genuine derivation of the Balmer formula. Additionally, we apply our model to calculate energy levels for hydrogen-like atoms, and compare the results to the corresponding energy equations derived from Schrödinger's and Dirac's theories. Furthermore, we use our model to determine the possible energy transitions associated with electromagnetic radiation, which are found to align with observed spectral lines across various hydrogen-like isotopes. It is also possible to calculate the de Broglie wavelengths of electrons in excited states, which are consistent with observed patterns in electron interference. By successfully explaining a broad range of atomic and sub-atomic phenomena, we argue that our model offers a superior understanding of matter and energy, which can be attributed to its logical and intuitive principles. Consequently, we suggest that this theoretical framework can contribute to the ongoing discussion on the nature of reality. Moreover, according to our study, the standard mathematical formalisms of quantum mechanics, quantum field theory, and general relativity can be derived from our model by applying specific limiting conditions, which highlights their inherent connections. Ultimately, our research appears to validate the principles of relativistic quantum mechanics, while also revealing the potential for spacetime to exhibit quantum behavior within extremely small, heavy objects. Finally, we explore the applications of our theoretical framework to cosmological events, by using it to calculate the energy released during the Big Bang and estimating the age of the universe, which is found to align with entropic estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model can be used to determine the masses of gravitons, which are consistent with upper limits imposed by the gravitational wave spectrum observed at LIGO-Fermi. By covering such a broad array of phenomena, from atomic to cosmological, we believe that our theoretical framework has the potential to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing research in physics. Consequently, in the spirit of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen thought experiment, we suggest that the quantum mechanical uncertainty principle, the equivalence principle of general relativity, the commutator relation, and the conservation laws, which are the core principles of our model, can be utilized in future experiments to test their practical implications, while potentially opening up new avenues for fundamental research.
