Current assessments of reinforcement learning algorithms are typically based on a single, fixed test environment. However, in real-world applications, curricula are often employed to gradually introduce complexities to learning agents over time. To better simulate natural learning processes and adaptability in evolving scenarios, such as robotic systems where new tasks are occasionally added, our research presents a new method for crafting curricula through controlled modifications to problem difficulty. Using this curriculum, we re-evaluated the performance of established RL algorithms and found that they could be significantly improved by tailoring the progression of challenges. Additionally, our curriculum design can serve as a benchmark to test the capacity of RL algorithms for learning from structured educational pathways. By validating the effectiveness of our approach, our findings provide valuable insights for RL method development and inform the design of more challenging future robotic co-adaptive learning scenarios. A video illustrating our results can be found at: https://youtu.be/7e1fj8v1V9E. All experimental data, model information, and evaluation code have been released at: https://github.com/continuous-coadaptation/CCRLBppo. To implement our CCRLBppo method, we combined it with state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., LBppo) and evaluated its performance in curated environments that transition from relatively easy to more challenging problems. By capitalizing on offline RL, our approach can reduce training times from days to just a few hours, akin to observing a learner progressing through a structured curriculum in a natural setting. To create the CCRLBppo curriculum, we leveraged online reinforcement learning to craft a sequence of task difficulties based on performance, thereby offering a roadmap for improved learning outcomes. By capitalizing on the strengths of offline RL, our approach can successfully apply the lessons learned from online training to offline settings, thereby unlocking new potential in robotic learning. The COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant global impact, and South Africa has also suffered from its consequences. As a result, there has been an increased need for accurate and up-to-date information on the pandemic's progression. Available public data has been limited by delays, inaccuracies, and missing values, posing significant challenges for data-driven research and applications. To address these issues, we present an open-source Python tool, SARSgov, which enables users to access and process reliable official government data on COVID-19 in South Africa, including data on daily new cases, deaths, and testing numbers. By leveraging this tool, users can obtain corrected data sets, calculate key metrics such as the reproductive number, and visualize pandemic trends using SARScov2.net. This approach allows for the development of data science models to forecast future pandemic patterns, ultimately contributing to evidence-based decision-making in public policy development. Furthermore, SARSgov serves as a general-purpose tool for accessing and processing official government COVID-19 data in South Africa, and can be adapted for use in other countries where similar datasets are available. All code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/csc4820/SARSgov. To learn more, visit our project website at https://csc4820.github.io/SARSgov. To contact us, send an email to csc4820@covid19.data. Alternatively, join our Discord community at https://covid19.data. to report issues or suggest enhancements. We welcome contributions from the data science community, and appreciate your participation in helping us combat the pandemic more effectively. We are committed to providing transparent, open, and accurate data to support public understanding, research, and action. We aim to promote data-driven decision-making through reliable data analysis and communication, and to promote practical data science skills in handling official government data through education and outreach. We wish to thank our collaborators, especially the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), for their critical role in gathering and disseminating pandemic data, and for their support in refining our SARSgov tool. We would also like to extend our gratitude to the South African Ministry of Health for their leadership in coordinating the national response to the pandemic, and for their vision in recognizing the importance of data-driven decision-making. We hope that SARSgov will continue to contribute to this effort, and will remain a valuable resource for data science research and applications in South Africa. We intend to maintain active development of the project, and to ensure that the tool remains accurate and reliable in the future

This study makes public 12 new feature sets, incorporating multiple information sources, including Inertial Magnetic Field, Sun direction, and visual inertial pose, retrieved from iPhone devices. We examine the impact of sensor fusion techniques, including hierarchical, intermediate, and early fusion methods, utilizing the provided feature sets. Notably, hierarchical fusion distinguishes itself by incorporating source information at varying levels of detail, whereas intermediate and early fusion methods involve more straightforward combinations. We illustrate the efficacy of hierarchical fusion through a comprehensive training-testing process on four datasets, demonstrating its competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of using hierarchical fusion in addressing data imbalance, much like ensemble methods, and illustrate its application in predicting individual iPhone device orientations using data from a single user. We anticipate that the released feature sets and accompanying code will foster the development of innovative late fusion techniques, thereby contributing to a broader range of applications. The world still grapples with the COVID-19 pandemic's enormity, exacerbated by an overwhelming number of critically ill patients in ICUs, a scarce resource. To effectively utilize and allocate these limited ICU beds, accurately predicting ICU admission from routine medical facility admissions is crucial. Although machine learning models have shown potential in this context, their sensitivity and accuracy have been hindered by the inclusion of numerous irrelevant features. By using COVID-Net, a vast dataset of 1.4 million patient features, our study showcases the effectiveness of targeted analysis on specific, relevant features. By focusing on admission-related features instead of comprehensive patient features, our models achieved exceptional performance. Specifically, the best-performing model, developed using the MIMIC-III dataset, demonstrated an impressive 94.8% AUC when predicting ICU admission. By leveraging COVID-Net's diverse range of features, our work sets the groundwork for enhanced machine learning models, maximizing efficiency in ICU resource allocation. Moreover, our research highlights the significance of feature engineering and selection in machine learning, streamlining models towards better clinical applicability. Finally, our models, available upon request, can aid clinicians in forecasting ICU admissions and making data-driven decisions to combat the ongoing pandemic. To our knowledge, our study is the first to showcase the potential of machine learning models built using COVID-Net's features. Building upon existing knowledge, our work builds a foundation for utilizing broad feature sets, specifically COVID-Net, to predict specific outcomes, paving the way for practical clinical use. By targeting various clinical predictions, our models can achieve greater accuracy and efficiency in feature utilization, ultimately enhancing healthcare decision-making. To this end, our study contributes two key insights. Firstly, a novel approach to feature engineering, consisting of iterative feature selection and analysis, was utilized to derive the Admission Time Features. Secondly, our models demonstrated that temperature and age-related features are crucial for predicting ICU admissions, their importance is to be noted. Our research provides a foundation for leveraging machine learning in COVID-19 feature sets, specifically COVID-Net, to forecast a wide array of clinical outcomes. By building upon existing knowledge, our work sets out to enhance the practical applicability of these models in clinical decision-making, utilizing broad feature sets to predict specific, high-stakes outcomes. To this end, our study contributes two significant insights. Firstly, our models showcase the potential of COVID-Net feature sets in predicting non-mortality outcomes. Secondly, our models achieved exceptional performance in forecasting ICU admissions and mortality, solidifying the practical utility of these feature sets

This study examines the localization of transmission eigenfunctions in a $N$-dimensional space ($\mathbb{R}^{N}$) within a ball with smoothly changing medium properties. We investigate how the transmission eigenfunctions are distributed, under the assumption that a constant coefficient ($\beta$) governs the transmission and a variable coefficient ($\eta$) represents the density of the medium. Our research shows that the localization of these eigenfunctions occurs at the boundary of the ball, given that certain conditions are met, including that the coefficient $\eta$ is not equal to 1, and that the coefficient $\beta$ is not equal to 1 or 0. In contrast, the authors of ["A new approach to the Subgroup Fixed Point Property" (2021)] introduced a property known as the Subgroup Fixed Point Property (SFP), which can be defined as follows: A group $G$ possesses the SFP if for every function $f: \mathcal{S}_G \to G$, where $\mathcal{S}_G$ denotes the set of all subgroups in $G$, the equation $\biggl(\bigvee_{H \in \mathcal{S}_G} f(H)\bigg| H\bigg) = e_G$ implies $f(e_G) = e_G$. In the aforementioned paper, it was proven that a solvable group of order $n$ has at most $n^{\frac{7}{4}+\varepsilon}$ subgroups, for any positive $\varepsilon$. In the present paper, we provide further evidence that a solvable group of order $n$ in fact has at most $n^{\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon}$ subgroups, for any positive $\varepsilon$, thus refining the previous result. Additionally, it is shown that a solvable linear group of order $n$ has at most $n^{\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}$ subgroups, for any positive $\varepsilon$, thereby confirming a conjecture put forth by E. Breuillard and B. Green. Our work presents a new approach to proving the SFP through the use of nilpotent groups, which also yields further results, such as a refinement of the bounds given by Breuillard and Green for the number of subgroups in a solvable linear group, as well as an alternative proof of a recent theorem by Breuillard and Green regarding the nilpotent SFP, our presentation of which is entirely novel. Our methods also allow us to extend our findings to locally solvable groups, which we accomplish by introducing the concept of the Upper Subgroup Fixed Point Property (USFP). Inspired by our previous Efficient Negative Sampling technique, we have developed a new strategy called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which centers around optimizing the proportion of balanced negative samples in the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) task. By leveraging a balanced histogram, BNPS identifies the most critical sub-ranges where the model's accuracy can be most effectively enhanced. BNPS then focuses on sampling negative proposals from these selected areas to refine the model's optimization. Through numerical analysis, we discovered that the conventional Uniform Negative Proposal Sampling method tends to concentrate on easy sub-tasks and dismisses more challenging ones. In contrast, BNPS adapts a "crab-bow" distribution to counter this issue by allocating more importance to sub-ranges containing difficult proposals. Our comprehensive experiments, conducted across three datasets including VRD, and combining the effectiveness of BNPS with the synergy of Dual Relationship Matching (DRLM), noticeably boosted the model's accuracy on semantic relationship detection. Notably, the integration of BNPS and DRLM achieved a remarkable 4.3% improvement in precision at 80% recall compared to utilizing the standard Dual Relationship Matching (DRM) method alone. Furthermore, the newly developed model based on BNPS demonstrated a 0.4% improvement in AO (Average Overlap) metric on the VRD dataset and outperformed state-of-the-art models by 0.6% and 0.3% in terms of mAP and recall@50, respectively. Our thorough ablation studies, meticulous analysis of sampling methods, and thought-provoking discussion on negative sampling best practices solidify the robustness and efficacy of the proposed Balanced BNPS strategy. Implementing neural network architectures on massive graphs remains computationally intensive due to its costly memory and time requirements. To tackle this problem, we developed GINDY, a graph neural network inspired by Inverse Graph Theory. GINDY employs an adaptive sampling strategy that focuses on selecting crucial graph nodes, thereby reducing the dependency on comprehensive node feature extraction. This approach capitalizes on the correlation between neighboring nodes, allowing for efficient extrapolation and estimation of missing features. To achieve this, GINDY adapts the Laplacian matrix of the graph, effectively utilizing the Inverse Laplacian to sample key nodes. This method is versatile and can be integrated with various neural network architectures, such as Inverse Graph Theory-based models and deep learning models. We evaluated GINDY on numerous graph datasets and demonstrated that it outperforms existing graph neural network methods in terms of accuracy while significantly reducing the computational cost. Notably, GINDY successfully streamlined the research of Inverse Graph Theory-based models by effectively sampling nodes from large graphs. In order to optimize Error-Correcting Decoders that utilize Constant Multiplication circuits, researchers proposed various approaches to reduce the cost of these circuits. Despite this, there has been no established framework for quantifying the benefits achieved through cost reduction strategies. To fill this gap, this paper introduces a formal analysis of error propagation rules that facilitates the efficient design of Low-Density Parity-Check Decoders utilizing Constant Multiplication circuits. By developing a framework for evaluating propagation rules, researchers can accurately measure the impact of cost reduction strategies, thereby enabling further optimization. Utilizing this framework, we evaluated the effectiveness of existing Constant Multiplication circuit approaches and discovered that applying certain error propagation rules results in significant cost reduction - up to 50% in some cases. Furthermore, we proposed a novel approach that directly utilizes error propagation rules, yielding a substantial reduction in cost and total amount of error propagation. By integrating this approach with existing circuit optimization methods, we achieved further improvements in cost and error propagation. Through comprehensive experimentation, we validated the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed framework and approach. Notably, we observed that integrating error propagation rules with circuit optimization methods leads to better performance and energy efficiency, while simultaneously enhancing the decoder's reliability. Lastly, we investigated the potential of error propagation rules to facilitate the integration of Constant Multiplication circuits into Field Programmable Gate Arrays. Our findings indicate that the sequential nature of error propagation rules poses challenges in mapping these circuits directly onto FPGAs. Nonetheless, we identified various error propagation rules that can be effectively implemented on FPGAs using existing resources, thereby enabling the direct integration of Constant Multiplication circuits into FPGAs. By combining all proposed framework and approach contributions, we achieved the best performance compared to existing optimization strategies. Specifically, we demonstrated improvement in area efficiency, marked by a percentage reduction of 10%, along with decreased error propagation, accounted for in terms of flip-flops, amounting to 15%. Lastly, the proposed approach resulted in a considerable delay efficiency enhancement - up to 25% - due to reduced error propagation. These efficiency gains paved the way for performance improvement through area optimization, thereby facilitating the achievement of error-free decoding at reduced delay for Low-Density Parity-Check codes utilizing Constant Multiplication circuits. To underpin our findings, the proposed approach was open-sourced under the name CM-HPSK, facilitating the design of Constant Multiplication circuits aligned with error propagation rules. Moreover, the cmhpsk tool has been established on GitHub at the provided link to support the design of Constant Multiplication circuits

In the field of visual parsing, a new few-shot parsing (FPS) model has been developed with the ability to adapt to unseen categories with limited annotated data. The model, called Few-Shot Parsing from Images (FPIO), utilizes a combined framework of iterative conditional inference and self-supervised learning to create a universal parser. The parser's output is then refined through a convolutional conditional autoencoder (CCAE) to produce accurate results. The experiments show that FPIO requires significantly fewer annotations to achieve high accuracy, outperforming existing FPS methods. When trained with just 125 annotated tree branches, FPIO matches the accuracy of a model trained on the full AnnData dataset. Additionally, the model's universal parser can be used to produce parsing results for any image without requiring category information, making it a versatile tool. However, the model's reliance on complex iterative methods causes a significant decrease in performance when dealing with medical image parsing. As an alternative, a new few-shot parsing method (FPIO-S) is proposed by incorporating the parsing results of a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) into the model. The results show that FPIO-S outperforms FPIO and other FPS methods, demonstrating that combining CNN features with iterative methods can lead to improved accuracy. The experiments also show that both FPIO and FPIO-S demonstrate categorical shift robustness, a key advantage over existing FPS methods. We investigate the potential of upgrading standard color-based labels with precise hyperspectral data within the $[700,~1100]\, \mu m$ range, without the necessity of reannotating images. Object-based change detection (OBCD) techniques have become the method of choice for comparing multiple versions of the same area. Typically, supervised methods use manually created training datasets to teach systems what to look for in changing images. However, creating these training datasets is time-consuming, making supervised methods impractical for areas with limited resources. This study evaluates the capabilities of unsupervised change detection (UCD) methods that don't need any training, and compares them to supervised methods. We looked at 30 years of data from the Landsat archive and found four relevant image pairs, along with corresponding manual change maps. To create change maps, we used an unsupervised object-based change detection method and compared the results to 11 supervised methods. We measured how well the methods did by counting the number of correctly identified changed areas, and found that unsupervised methods didn't do as well as supervised methods, but did a lot better than random guessing. We also found that supervised methods need more accurate training data to do well, while unsupervised methods can do a lot better with no training at all. However, unsupervised methods still can't beat supervised methods that use perfect training data. Finally, we found some limitations of the studied unsupervised methods, including their inability to identify small changes and accurately identify complex change patterns. Overall, while supervised methods are the best for areas with reliable training data, unsupervised methods may be more suitable for areas with limited resources or big changes. However, more work is needed on improving the performance and accuracy of these unsupervised methods. Finally, we concluded with some suggestions on potential future research on this topic, including combining supervised and unsupervised methods and using more advanced AI techniques to identify image changes.}

This research paper calculates the transitivity degree of algebraic varieties $X$ where the morphism $\sigma: X\to X$ has $d$-fold axial symmetry and is defined over a number field. We also derive a formula for the maximum number of independent orbits resulting from the action of the Galois group on the set of points of $X^{[d]}(R)$. This formula serves as the foundation for our subsequent investigation of the number of non-intersecting geometric orbits in the set $X^{[d]}(R)$. As a specific demonstration of our transitivity findings, we provide a detailed analysis for the symmetries of certain del Pezzo surfaces. Additionally, we offer a new explanation for the proven fact that the symmetries of hyperbolic varieties have minimal $d$-fold axial symmetry. Our research also establishes that the symmetries of projective space and quadric have minimal $d$-fold axial symmetry, provided that $d$ is not a multiple of the dimension of the variety. Finally, we offer a new demonstration for the fact that the symmetries of rational varieties have minimal $d$-fold axial symmetry. We are thus able to confirm that the symmetries of most varieties are inherently intrinsic. We further leverage our research to study the geometric significance of Galois invariance in algebraic varieties. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between Galois invariance and the properties of hyperbolicity, the presence of rational connectedness, and the existence of minimal rational connections in del Pezzo fibrations. Online misogyny has become a pressing issue, with its expression often wrapped in neutral language, making it difficult for traditional methods to detect. To tackle this problem, researchers have explored the potential of pre-trained language models, which have shown promise in improving classification performance. However, most existing approaches rely on a pre-trained model's overall capabilities, assuming a perfect adaptation to the misogyny identification task. In our study, we introduce MARBERT, a variant of the multilingual BERT model, fine-tuned and adapted specifically for identifying misogyny. By leveraging a large web scroll dataset comprising diverse online comments, we demonstrate that MARBERT achieves exceptional accuracy in classifying both English and German misogynistic content. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that MARBERT's performance excels when compared to a BERT model lacking adaptation, indicating a substantial improvement in accuracy. Additionally, our work highlights the benefits of adapting pre-trained models to specific tasks, emphasizing the significance of dataset collection and domain-specific modeling for successful applications. Our source code and dataset are publicly available for future research purposes. To our knowledge, MARBERT is the first model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in detecting both English and German misogynistic content. Our study's findings have far-reaching implications for developing more effective automated misogyny detection systems. We suggest introducing a framework that incorporates a variety of natural language processing techniques, including sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, and categorization of online comments. Our analysis shows that this strategy may enhance the quality of misogyny detection by incorporating additional features, potentially, as our research demonstrates, doubling the accuracy of detection when combined with other techniques. For German, we observed a notable increase in accuracy from 40.9% to 51.4%, indicating the potential benefits of this approach. Recent research has demonstrated the potential for learned dynamics models to
streamline autonomous systems design by enabling learned controllers to withstand
model uncertainty. Nevertheless, relying solely on a dynamics model can be
inherent in inaccuracies, which become exacerbated when the model is Inferred
from real-world data. In this paper, we examine the effect of incorporating a
maximum likelihood error threshold on learned controllers and models. We find
that implementing this constraint results in a robust learned controller capable of
withstanding model uncertainty, and that doing so outperforms traditional
approaches based on model prediction alone. Notably, our method exhibits
transferability across model paradigms, and that incorporating real-world data
can enhance the robustness and performance of controllers designed using model
system data. These findings are substantiated by multiple controller design
experiments in simulated robotics systems. When applied to actual quadcopters in
real-time, our method has successfully enabled the robust implementation of a
learned controller. Specifically, our method permits the successful
implementation of a learned controller when the model error rate exceeds 15%,
while conventional approaches based on model prediction alone become

This paper presents a novel framework for developing more efficient collision avoidance systems for mobile robotic arms. By integrating spatial considerations into collision detection, our method reframes the problem as a narrow-phase physics engine technique. This approach enables us to leverage existing broad-phase acceleration structures, such as k-d tree, to speed up collision processing. We evaluate the performance of our framework through simulations and compare it to a temporal collision avoidance model. The results show that the new strategy significantly reduces computation time, leading to improved efficiency without sacrificing safety. Consequently, this framework can be applied to a variety of mobile manipulation tasks where a robotic arm's spatial relationship is crucial for collision avoidance. For example, consider a scenario where a robot is reaching over a person; traditional collision avoidance methods might fail, but our framework could help. Language diversity presents significant challenges to natural language processing due to the myriad written and spoken forms across different languages. Furthermore, similar surface structures can conceal differences in meaning, making translation more complicated. To tackle this problem, researchers are developing innovative solutions focusing on thorny translation tasks. One such approach involves incorporating additional task instructions to enhance translation quality. Although this technique is successful within the realm of machine translation, its applications are limited to relatively simple tasks. To tackle more complex translation challenges, such as addressing the ambiguity of source forms, we propose using demonstrations to guide the reader's understanding. Building on the success of demonstrations in other areas, such as gesture recognition and generative modeling, we apply demonstrations to translate complex source forms. However, accurately capturing demonstration data is costly, so we aim to supplement genuine data with artificially created demonstrations. We employ artificial demonstrations with intentionally flawed meanings that resemble common errors in translation, which are learned from a small amount of labeled data. This approach enables the development of an effective neural model for translating complex source forms. To evaluate our method, we created a new dataset with high-quality translations, benchmarking our model against a range of competitive baselines. Interestingly, our results show that the quality of translations can be improved by incorporating demonstrations with basic proficiency, even surpassing the performance of the top baseline model. Moreover, our approach has the added benefit of reducing the complexity of source form ambiguity, as confirmed by expert analysis. To facilitate future research, we are making the data and model code available for download at https://github.com/ghu-neo/auxiliary-task-for-translation. In the future, we aim to apply our method to more challenging translation tasks that demand higher translation quality. To this end, we are exploring ways to enhance the quality of demonstrations available for these tasks. If successful, this could pave the way for using demonstrations as a viable solution for a broader range of translation challenges. To achieve this goal, we are working on creating demonstration data with more sophisticated gestures that better reflect the nuances of human gesture, which will involve collaborating with both professional translators and general language users to gather high-quality demonstration data. This collaborative effort will necessitate a careful examination of the existing demonstration data, with a critical assessment of its quality, along with the incorporation of innovative sampling and editing techniques to enhance the overall quality of the resulting demonstrations. Building on this experience, we aim to establish a comprehensive dataset of high-quality demonstrations that can serve as a benchmark for translation quality, while also providing valuable insights into the complexities of translation. Notably, this method surpasses the theoretical quantum-limited precision of traditional Ramsey interferometry, particularly when considering nonlinear effects in the light matter interaction. In the study of polynomial systems, Gröbner basis algorithms have become fundamental tools. However, these algorithms often consume significant computational resources, making them capable of taking advantage of any available processor cores. This document explores how utilizing multiple threads in these algorithms can significantly boost computational efficiency. The text introduces thread-based adaptations to key Gröbner basis algorithms, highlighting SAGEBEZ through a case study, which demonstrates notable speed gains when applied to various problems in combination with parallel processing techniques. The results show notable savings in time, ranging from almost 5 to over 200 times the original computation time. The success of these adaptations is consistent with the principles of Amdahl's law, where the gain in performance increases significantly as the proportion of parallel work grows. The research concludes by outlining future directions for further enhancing Gröbner basis algorithms, including incorporating distributed computation and applying these techniques to solve other mathematical problems. The software described in this work is available for public use at https://git.tu-berlin.de/eb/sexu@pr4.0. Additionally, the grbez package mentioned in Section 5 can be downloaded from https://www.prpr.org/bez/. Both versions are compatible with Windows, macOS, and various Linux distributions. Moreover, the fundamental thread-based adaptations presented in this work can be easily integrated into other Gröbner basis libraries to achieve similar speed improvements. In the long run, these modifications are expected to contribute to the development of computer algebra systems like GAP, Singular, and SARACEN. Lastly, the researchers express gratitude to Prof. Zhi Lü for his guidance and support throughout the project. The work was financially supported by the DFG through the project PR 1945/3-1.

The PHENIX Collaboration has discovered that photon production in Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV shares a direct proportionality with charged particle density in Au+Au collisions at the same energy level. This relationship holds across various photon transverse momentum ranges, from 1-4 GeV/c, both in central and non-central collisions. Notably, photon production in Cu+Cu collisions at lower energies does not adhere to this pattern, as it is found to be consistently lower than expected when compared to Au+Au collisions at the same energy. This research presents new data indicating that the photon yield in medium-sized collision experiments depends on the interaction density of particles, whereas factors such as the size of the medium and energy loss by photons through collisions with particles must be further investigated to understand their effects. Additionally, photon production in Cu+Cu collisions has been found to exhibit an energy and collision size dependence similar to that found in Au+Au collisions at the same energy level. This energy and collision size dependence is most pronounced for photons with a transverse momentum range of 2-4 GeV/c. This research has expanded our understanding of photon production in nuclear collisions and will contribute to the development of new theoretical models. Furthermore, photon measurements in Cu+Cu collisions at higher energies such as 54 GeV and 62 GeV using the PHENIX detector will provide crucial information for investigating the properties of dense nuclear interactions at these energy levels. Additionally, photon data will be compared to the results from p+p collisions at the Large Hadron Collider to further understand photon production in nuclear interactions. This paper investigates various counting functions associated with specific types of hypergraphs that exclude a particular substructure, and explores relationships between these functions that are similar to those found in extremal combinatorics. Different methods are employed to derive distinct approaches for calculating exco_2(n,H), the maximum number of edges in K_4^3-free hypergraphs on n vertices that contain no three intersecting triangles. A fundamental combinatorial argument is used initially, but a subsequent extension of the Szemer\'edi's decomposition lemma allows for a more efficient calculation, and further applications of this lemma help to refine the estimate. Ultimately, a probabilistic approach is used to obtain a precise formula for exco_2(n,H), and this involves introducing a new property of hypergraph tiling. The paper also explores and generalises this property to obtain a new framework for calculating exco_r(n,H), the maximum number of edges in K_r^3-free hypergraphs on n vertices. The results obtained through this general approach are comparable to the best known upper bounds found elsewhere in the literature. The paper also introduces a new concept, called the asymptotic covering number, and designates a symbol for this new parameter, denoted as hass(n), where ass(n) is the maximum number of aspects in n-vertex covering graphs. The researchers also identify an application of this new concept in the study of K_r^3-free hypergraphs. The results obtained for exco_2(n,H) have potential implications in the study of projective planes over finite fields, and the researchers discover a new general inequality involving exco_r(n,H) and potential applications in the study of higher degree abelian varieties over finite fields. The researchers also identify a new theme for future research, where the goal is to establish a relationship between hass(n) and the maximum number of edges in K_r^3-free graphs on n vertices. This research introduces an innovative algorithm for drawing digital line joins, enhancing the aesthetic of handwritten text. The standard approach to creating smooth joins incurs a time cost that's quadratic in relation to the size of the letters, leading many to simplify these as straight lines. However, this simplification neglects the aesthetic appeal of beautifully connected handwriting. By breaking down the drawing process into discrete stages, our algorithm allows the rendering of even the most intricate fan-shaped joins at a linear cost. Additionally, the proposed method includes efficient techniques for creating uniform thickness, adapting to varying letter connections, and incorporating kinetic dynamics for a more realistic drawing experience. Comprehensive testing has demonstrated that the new algorithm significantly outperforms existing solutions, resulting in visually superior outcomes. Key performance enhancements include a notable speed increase of up to 10 times for basic draws and as much as 20 to 40 times for more complex kinetic effects. Further details can be found at the project website: https://segdevs.github.io/segpro. 

Keywords: Digital Hand Drawing, Kinetic Effects, Line Joins, Real-time Performance, Sketch Rendering.

Although significant progress has been made, the connection of text lines still presents an unresolved issue. The traditional approach involves ignoring this aspect as a line join expense variable, but this comes with compromised visual quality. Conversely, super-sampling, while effective in general cases, is ineffective for sketched-like joins as it introduces jagged lines. Conversely, kinematic drawing methods produce aesthetically pleasing results but are too slow for real-time applications. Building upon these ideas, we introduce an innovative algorithm that allows for the seamless connection of text lines while maintaining real-time speeds. The core idea involves breaking down the sketching process into discrete stages, resulting in a sketch style that can be achieved at a linear cost. Additionally, we have developed techniques for uniform thickness adaptation and kinetic dynamics, resulting in aesthetically pleasing drawings. A novel interpolation formula based on radial basis functions will be introduced in this presentation. This method employs a positive definite sequence of RBFs with an affine linear combination that ensures convexity and monotonicity. A key characteristic of this interpolation technique is its ability to approximate smooth periodic or bounded data while maintaining these crucial properties. Due to its local nature, the support of the interpolation weights is limited to a specified radius, $\delta$, which makes it suitable for handling data with gaps. A fundamental aspect of this algorithm involves solving a small scale linear least squares problem. To enhance its efficiency, the method can be modified using a separable approximation of the matrix, reducing the computational time to a linear scale. These modifications will be showcased through numerical experiments that demonstrate the efficacy of the novel interpolation technique. Additionally, the presentation will cover applications of this new algorithm in solving partial differential equations and volume fractional differential equations. The underlying theory and numerical tests reveal that the method offers exceptional stability and accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, the algorithm's convergence rate far surpasses that of related RBF-based interpolation techniques for solving differential equations. Finally, the presentation will cover the development of a fast adaptive algorithm based on the moving least squares method, which utilizes the pre-computed weights and matrices to rapidly solve interpolation problems as new data becomes available. This recursive algorithm demonstrates excellent potential for reducing computational time, as evidenced by the numerical tests. The presentation will conclude with promising future directions for the method. The accompanying software will be made available on the repository https://git.uq.edu.au/141895/faster-rbf-interpolation/-/tree/master/SOPT. If you would like to obtain the software, please reach out to [rchen100@g.uq.au](mailto:rchen100@g.uq.au). Additionally, the related MATLAB package can be accessed at https://git.uq.edu.au/141895/MATLAB-rbf-interpolation/tree/master/SOPT. Improving Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) accuracy with augmented data is a well-established strategy. By using transmission masks to isolate diverse image features, we can enhance the information content of the training data and thereby improve accuracy. In this study, we examine how varying the size and density of masks influences the accuracy of a classifier. We discovered that even seemingly uniform images can be accurately classified only when certain features are highlighted, and observed a systematic improvement in accuracy as mask sizes decreased. Notably, our results show that CNNs can learn meaningful distinctions between classes even when nearly all image features are obscured, and that the effects of mask densities are highly dependent on the specific classifier and classification task. Our research suggests that using augmented data can be a highly effective way to improve image classification accuracy. In a practical application of this finding, we successfully improved the accuracy of a melanoma vs. non-melanoma lesion classification task by using transmission masks to isolate key features from the images. Our results show that even small changes in mask density can have significant effects on accuracy, and provide a clear framework for how augmented data can be used to improve machine learning outcomes. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the features that differentiate classes are encoded in the high-frequency components of images, and provides a practical example of how transmission masks can be used to improve the performance of CNNs. Their stellar populations, which can significantly affect the observed spectral features, have been estimated for the first time. By assuming a broadband spectral shape, we have removed the effects of lensing in a study of six high-redshift quasars. Their observed spectral features, between 1.2 and 1.8 micron, exhibit a broad band shape. It was observed that five out of six quasars display a general agreement in their spectrum, fitting a broken power-law model, with a break at 1.5 micron. This break is associated with the differential path length effect caused by the absorption of light by molecular oxygen and/or dust. Furthermore, our results suggest the presence of dust in the vicinity of these quasars, extending to the highest known redshifts, with a characteristic feature consistent with the far-ultraviolet tail of dusty quasars. By comparing the data with theoretical models, we found that the observed spectrum is primarily determined by the properties of highly luminous quasars, rather than the effects of gravitational lensing or the broad band spectral shape. Consequently, our results imply that the spectrum of the far-ultraviolet tail is primarily determined by the quasars themselves. Moreover, our results imply that the standard cosmological model is consistent with the observed evolution of dust content in quasars up to a redshift of 6, but further investigation is required to determine their dust content at higher redshifts. Lastly, our method developed in this research can be applied to various astrophysical phenomena, including galaxy clusters and gravitational lensing systems. This study presents a modified Lite-ProSENet model, which combines the strengths of LiteNet and ProSENet, for survival time analysis. The modified model has achieved superior performance, surpassing existing models, including ProSENet and LiteNet, as well as a range of other relevant methods, such as ABC-SD, Competing LiteNet, Lite-Cox, and Lite-RiskNet, in a benchmark competition. Specifically, Lite-ProSENet outperformed the next-best model, Lite-RiskNet, by 11.1% in terms of concordance, and significantly surpassed it in terms of clinical utility, as measured by the continuous net reclassification improvement metric. Furthermore, Lite-ProSENet provided accurate and clinically relevant predictions for individual patients, which were validated through comprehensive analysis and assessment by experts in the field. In particular, its predictions were found to be highly consistent with existing clinical guidelines, and it identified novel subtyping associations that may inform future treatment decisions. Notably, Lite-ProSENet achieved these results while exhibiting a significantly lighter computational footprint, with its parameters being 55% to 85% more compact than those of LiteNet and ProSENet, respectively. This makes Lite-ProSENet an attractive option for wide-ranging practical applications, and highlights its potential as a leading method for survival time analysis. In addition, code repositories for Lite-ProSENet are publicly available, providing a valuable resource for the research community. Specifically, the repository at https://github.com/Lite-PROSENet/Lite-ProSENet can be accessed for implementation details, while the repository at https://github.com/Lite-PROSENet/ProSENet_canalier can be accessed for reference code. Additionally, data for the study can be found at https://osf.io/7j9cp/. Lastly, the corresponding author for this study can be contacted at [xuechen.zhang@ai4health.org](mailto:xuechen.zhang@ai4health.org).

To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach, Rostering from Dialog History, which enables a dialogue system to learn role specifications by analyzing past conversation interactions. By doing so, we have created a pioneering external memory mechanism that enables a dialogue system to access and integrate historical conversation memories into its current conversation context. Through thorough evaluations, we have consistently found that our proposed model outperforms a baseline model using role specifications and achieves competitive results when compared to models with heavily annotated data. Notably, we have achieved up to 75% accuracy in predicting roles from conversation histories without any external inputs. In addition, we have achieved 65% accuracy in predicting roles in unseen scenarios using only the current conversation context. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made our model available on our website at https://dahua.ai/rdh/. Additionally, annotated data used for evaluation can be accessed through https://dahua.ai/role-specification-annotation/. This research focuses on examining the Seidel matrix' spectral properties in various types of chain graphs. It is proven that in a connected chain graph consisting of repeating blocks with at least three vertices each, the eigenvalue -1 is exclusively singular, and there is a corresponding eigenvector with entries of alternating 1 and -1. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Seidel matrix's second largest eigenvalue is -1, and this eigenvalue is uniquely occurring. When the graph is a straight line, it is shown that the Seidel matrix's remaining eigenvalues can be obtained by combining the eigenvalues of its irreducible blocks through the Perron-Frobenius theory. Additionally, four specific types of chain graphs are analyzed, for which the Seidel matrix's eigenvalues can be precisely determined. Finally, two new upper limits are established for the Seidel matrix' spectral radius in these chain graphs. Our findings supersede previously reported results in several aspects. For example, it was previously shown that in a connected chain graph with vertices of alternating colors, the Seidel matrix' spectral radius cannot exceed 3/2, but we now know it can reach as high as 5/3. Our research also extends the applications of the Perron-Frobenius theory in graph theory, as well as Kaashoek's theorem. Conversely, our results are less impressive than those of Tutubaliev's theorem. The theorem itself has been shown to be less impressive than even the above-mentioned results in several aspects. Lastly, our research has been successfully presented at the 12th International Conference on Algebra and Related Topics in Kazakhstan.

This study examines the stochastic control of a log-optimization model that accounts for delays in information processing and consumption. Both inherent and exogenous delays are explored. The problem is initially framed as a continuous-time finite-dimensional open-loop optimal control issue, which is challenging due to the non-affine nature of the dynamics. By leveraging a specific change of measure related to Girsanov's theorem, the problem is simplified to a closed-loop finite-dimensional control problem. For both types of delays, this approach yields the existence of optimal controls. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the mean-square stochastic process to the optimal trajectory. Additionally, taking the limit of these optimal trajectories, we obtain a deterministic solution to the open-loop problem, which serves as the optimal feedback control strategy. The findings are demonstrated through several numerical simulations, which are also accompanied by an analysis of the impact of delay on the optimal consumption policy. The results show that processing delays can lead to overconsumption, whereas under-processing delays may result in under-consumption, which highlights the complex nature of delays in investment and consumption planning. The study extends and adapts techniques from the works of Bahlia et al. (2022), Pham and Quenez (2022), and Pham et al. (2022) to the log-optimization model. The results are also similar to the studies by Borkar and Jain (2001) and Boudou and El Karoui (2006) on the optimal control of log-normal models. The study is based on the PhD thesis of Pham (2022) and the preprint article Pham (2022) by the same author. By recognizing this connection, we enhance DB3 by combining it with pseudo-labels, yielding an improved distillation method. Objectness is first increased through a semantic object detection method, and then object shapes are informed by an anatomical model of human object interactions. Orthonormality constraints are subsequently used to object shape hypotheses, generating distinctive templates that distinguish occluded from non-occluded objects. By combining multiple template samples, we can accurately track objects across complex interactions, even when partially occluded. Experimental results show that our approach significantly surpasses baseline methods in hand-object interaction tracking. Specifically, our approach achieves tracklets of length 0.55 seconds, compared to 0.29 seconds for the second best method. In particular, our approach has shown considerable improvement in hand-object interaction tracking, as well as when focusing on object or background regions. To address the challenge of occluded regions, we propose three additional enhancements: enhancing objectness, object shape constraints, and background-occluded region detection. The current weak-lensing analyses rely on a standard galaxy shape measurement technique called ShapePipe, a multi-step process including image processing, galaxy selection, and shape measurement, all of which are critical for a thorough measurement. This pipeline has been extensively used in recent surveys, such as the KiDS, CFHTLS, and DES, and has been refined to address various image noise patterns and image processing techniques. Due to its importance in weak-lensing research, we now release ShapePipe as a publicly accessible software package, allowing for consistency across different projects and enabling users to track changes made to the code. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the updated internal algorithms within ShapePipe, including a new algorithm for measuring galaxy shapes called NGmix, which utilizes a more efficient method called Bayesian estimation and approximation (BEA). Our analysis of multiple datasets reveals that ShapePipe's standard measurement technique closely matches the results of NGmix, with the difference in measured shapes being minimal and only slightly decreasing with larger galaxy sizes. Notably, both methods demonstrate robust performance even in the presence of severe image noise, allowing for accurate shape measurements down to magnitudes $i_{AUTO}=24.5$ in deep field datasets. By combining these advances in galaxy shape measurement with recent improvements in galaxy separation and shear estimation, we have developed a state-of-the-art pipeline for weak-lensing analysis that will play a crucial role in future surveys, such as LSST. This study presents a first-in-depth examination of the dynamics and structural evolution of Cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin in particular, and Cryptocurrency Exchange Markets. Researchers analyzed data spanning 2019 to 2021 on Cryptocurrency transactions, Exchange Market trading, and Online Retail trading. An advanced statistical analysis combined with Complex Network Theory was applied to understand the patterns of Cryptocurrency transactions. The analysis revealed fluctuations in Cryptocurrency popularity among Online Retail traders and Shifts in Trading Strategies among Exchange Markets. The probability distribution of Cryptocurrency prices and returns exhibited two distinct components - a stable normal distribution and a unstable heavy tail distribution. The proportion of the heavy tail distribution increased over time, particularly in the first half of 2021,corresponding to higher activity and growing complexity in the cryptocurrency trading network. Notably, the proportion of the heavy tail distribution showed seasonal fluctuations, peaking in summer months and decreasing in winter months, and this pattern correlated with the daily trading volume of the Online Retail segment. The correlation between Cryptocurrency prices and the trading volume of the Online Retail segment was positive, while the correlation with Exchange Markets was initially negative but turned positive in 2021, indicating a changing trading strategy among Exchange Markets. The average clustering coefficient of Cryptocurrency prices showed a declining trend, whereas the average clustering coefficient of Trading volumes displayed seasonal fluctuations. An inter-episode analysis revealed the duration and frequency of Trading episodes and Online Retail transactions, and the results indicated stability in Trading patterns. Ultimately, the findings highlight the increasing influence of Online Retail traders on Cryptocurrency Market fluctuations. Additionally, the research suggests that Exchange Markets initially responded conservatively but eventually became more involved, and the Trading activity of Online Retailers contributed to the growth in Cryptocurrency price fluctuations. Furthermore, the study discovered that the probability distribution of Cryptocurrency prices exhibited two distinct components, and the growing share of the heavy tail distribution correlated with higher activity and complexity in the cryptocurrency trading network. Additionally, the results indicate the potential for Online Retailers to disrupt the Cryptocurrency Market, potentially impacting the stability of Trading episodes. Based on these findings, the research suggests that the growing share of Online Retailers in the Cryptocurrency Market may lead to price volatility, potentially impacting the stability of Trading episodes, and the growing influence of Online Retailers may continue to contribute to price volatility in the future. The research offers a comprehensive understanding of the structural and dynamic changes in the Cryptocurrency Exchange Market, and the findings can guide traders and investors in making informed decisions while also contributing to the development of risk management models for Cryptocurrency trading.

This research focuses on evaluating the effectiveness of the GAN training from a geometric perspective. By introducing a geometric approach to analyzing the space of group-equivariant non-expansive operators, we can determine the conditions under which this space can be isometrically embedded within a compact topological space. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the learned generator in GAN training can be viewed as a continuous function from the compact space to the target data set. Building on this insight, we propose a modified approach to GAN training, commencing with embedding the operator space into the compact space and subsequently employing continuous functions from the compact space to the target data set to estimate the data distribution. Our research is motivated by the observation that non-identifiable models often pose challenges in training GANs. Conversely, our approach is capable of generating compact and weakly-coherent representations for data sets such as USPecies, CelebA, and CIFAR-10 when employed in conjunction with the GAN algorithm. Notably, the representations generated by our approach exhibit lower energies and distances to the target data set compared to those produced by the GAN algorithm. Our research is further validated through experiments on image de novo drawing, image generation, and supervised classification tasks, which reveal that the one-shot learning capability enabled by our approach is effective in generating realistic images from minimal examples. The particles moved randomly, driven by a thermal motion, and the temperature varied significantly across different positions. This led us to explore the diffusion process in a two-temperature environment, where the Einstein relation may not hold. To understand the thermodynamic properties of the system, we calculated the mean squared displacement of the particles and derived the hydrodynamic equations governing the diffusion process. Additionally, we identified stationary profiles for the particles' velocity distribution and demonstrated that the Einstein relation is not valid under conditions of spatially varying temperatures. In order to make diffusion theory self-consistent, we derived a generalized Einstein relation by incorporating temperature fluctuations. This approach is anticipated to contribute to the development of diffusion theories in complex thermal systems. The diffusion of molecules with temperature-dependent mobility is analogous to our study, and the derived equations can be compared with existing models in the field. Regularizations such as parameter norm regularization, used during the training of deep learning models, aim to reduce overfitting by limiting the model's complexity. However, the effectiveness of these regularizations declines as models become more complex, leading to the question of their optimal application. A novel method called Parameter Anti-Correlation Learning (PAL) is introduced, which not only reduces overfitting but also promotes generalization through the elimination of redundant parameters. PAL is based on an alternating optimization algorithm that minimizes a loss function with an additional term, encouraging anti-correlated weight updates. Theoretical analysis confirms the algorithm's convergence to a critical point and its ability to eliminate unnecessary parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of PAL on various benchmark datasets compared to traditional regularization techniques. The research also provides a theoretical framework for understanding the effect of regularization in deep learning models. This approach yields a $B_s^0$ lifetime of 1.410 pb$^{-1}$ with a 95% confidence interval, matching standard model expectations. Furthermore, we've calculated the branching fraction of this decay as (9.1 pb$^{-1}$ ± 2.2 pb$^{-1}$ (statistical error) ± 2.3 pb$^{-1}$ (systematic error)), consistent with standard model predictions. Our results on the $B_s^0$ decay rate and branching fraction remain consistent with past studies. Additionally, we've set upper limits on rare $B_s^0$ decay modes into a Higgs boson and a photon and into a pair of photons, aligning with standard model forecasts. These limits will be crucial in informing future research into these decay modes. Lastly, we've determined the $B_s^0$ mixing phase $\phi_d$, finding no significant deviation from standard model predictions, ultimately imposing upper limits on certain CP-violating asymmetries. These results will contribute to the understanding of CKM unitarity tests and input parameters essential for future flavor anomaly investigations. Our analysis remains open to interpretation due to potential improvements in reconstruction algorithms and experimental design. Additionally, we've calculated the $B_s^0$ mixing amplitude and determined the limits on its asymmetrical counterpart, influencing expectations for direct $B_s^0$ decay into a Higgs boson and a photon. Lastly, we've investigated the $B_s^0$ decay into a Higgs boson and a photon, setting the most stringent experimental limits yet on this process. However, these results are predicated on the Higgs boson's characteristics as posited by the Standard model, and we've also explored alternative scenarios in which this assumption is invalid. Furthermore, we've studied the $B_s^0$ decay into a pair of photons, and while this analysis remains subject to uncertainties, for the most part, these results align with Standard model forecasts for both investigations. Conversely, the Standard model foretells notably distinct limits for the $B_s^0$ decay into a Higgs boson and a photon and for the $B_s^0$ mixing

To effectively utilize machine learning models for automated essay grading, it is crucial to create diverse datasets representative of various writing styles and topics. However, since most educational institutions grade the same essays across different classes and time periods, there is a common set of essential questions that appear repeatedly in various forms. Building upon this insight, our approach employs data augmentation to enhance the reliability of model performance. By incorporating multiple, subtly varied versions of existing essays into the training process, we can ensure our model remains accurate in grading diverse types of essays. Specifically, we explored three such methods: the replacement of specific words within an essay, the alteration of a particular section at a time, and the generation of new essays based on a given sample through text manipulation. When tested using hold-out validation, our results demonstrate that each of these techniques improves model performance. Moreover, by combining the augmented dataset with its original counterpart, we achieved an average 15% improvement in overall accuracy compared to training with the original dataset alone. Ultimately, our strategy enables the creation of a highly effective model capable of accurately grading essays that differ significantly from one another. As such, this method serves as an essential tool for tackling various writing assessment tasks. Additionally, our findings suggest that data augmentation has the potential to be utilized in a wide range of applications where gathering abundant, varied data becomes feasible through means of augmentation. Lastly, our codebase and the augmented datasets developed in this study are openly accessible at https://github.com/ideogram/augment for the benefit of the community.

However, both methods have underutilized theoretical analyses in the context of graphical models. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of both techniques in high-dimensional graphical model estimation, offering improved guarantees and a more efficient minimax estimation method based on penalized likelihood. The results are further generalized to the context of multi-task learning, where both approaches are compared in the context of predictive bias and risk. The theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments and an in-depth case study of text topic modeling. The study ultimately leads to a proposed new minimax estimation method, called "Lasso LME," for learning latent variable models, which outperforms existing methods in various numerical experiments. The distribution of opportunities within a society often determines the socio-economic outcomes not just for individuals, but also for future generations. The unlimited, diverse opportunities presented to people from an affluent background are reminiscent of a exploration problem known as the Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) in fields like Reinforcement Learning. While traditional MAB settings are designed to facilitate choice, our research introduces a novel variation called the Socio-Economic Bandit, which incorporates a paternalistic concern for a child's future. The goal in this variation is to ensure that the child is not deprived of opportunities due to the parent's sub-optimal actions, which are influenced by the current action and the child's reduced perspective. The Socio-Economic Bandit setting presents two core challenges: first, it is an MAB exploration problem that is harder to solve than standard MAB due to the lack of choice, and second, it is a hard to learn Markov Decision Process (MDP) because the child's state is only partially observable. To address these challenges, we developed a model-free algorithm called CESA, which uses the child's average reward over time to gauge available opportunities and combine this information with upper-confidence bounds for the parent's rewards to ensure a balance between exploration and adherence to the child's interests. The result is an algorithm that achieves a $O(\sqrt{T}/A)$ regret, which is close to the theoretical limit, along with a provable guarantee that the child's allocated opportunities increase over time. We also tested our algorithm in a simulated economy and found that it performs significantly better than baseline comparisons, such as the child simply mimicking the parent's actions or the parent making random choices, in terms of allocated opportunities. The code used for these simulations can be found at https://github.com/sharvashankar/SES_Bandit. The paper's main contribution is the introduction of the Socio-Economic Bandit setting, which is the first variation of MAB that is concerned with a future generation's opportunities and outcomes. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm's regret performance is the first to solve this variation, and we confirmed its efficacy through experimental testing. The research presented here addresses the practical issue of ensuring that a child's socio-economic status improves over time, which is a common concern for parents and societies. The work is also relevant to fields such as public policy and economics because it indicates that the allocation of opportunities has a direct impact on future generations' socio-economic outcomes. We introduce an improved variant of RingCT, called Delegated RingCT, which significantly increases the efficiency of cryptocurrency transactions by reducing reliance on costly cryptographic protocols. In a standard RingCT, each participant is responsible for contributing encrypted transaction amounts from a hidden address. This necessitates the costly protocol of Safe-Cash to verify the integrity of each contribution. Delegated RingCT mitigates this by enabling designated "delegates" to collectively provide encrypted totals for a set of transactions, thereby eliminating the need for Safe-Cash in the majority of cases. Instead, a Centralized Delegated RingCT relies on a centralized authority to sign a single delegation batch, whereas an Off-Chain Delegated RingCT relies on a consortium of public keys from trusted wallets. We showcase the implementation and validity of Delegated RingCT in Bitcoin, while also highlighting potential applications and improvements. Furthermore, a proposed decentralized alternative to Delegated RingCT is outlined as Future Work. In terms of security, Delegated RingCT retains the robustness of its predecessor, RingCT. With regards to anonymity, Delegated RingCT offers a more robust form of anonymity than RingCT, as well as Standard RingCT. By leveraging a combination of delegation and batch encryption, Delegated RingCT achieves the strongest possible anonymity. Specifically, in a Centralized Delegated RingCT, an adversary's ability to learn information is restricted to the set of involved delegates, whereas in Off-Chain Delegated RingCT, a consortium of public keys protects user transactions from scrutiny. By leveraging a robust form of delegation, Delegated RingCT significantly enhances the anonymity of its users. Moreover, Delegated RingCT retains the capability for transparent and public transactions. Finally, Delegated RingCT is backward-compatible with Standard RingCT. With its robust form of anonymity, efficiency in terms of costs, and compatibility with existing systems, Delegated RingCT presents a compelling solution for enhancing the scalability and speed of cryptocurrencies. From a technical standpoint, Delegated RingCT offers a strong candidate for a scalable and efficient anonymous payment network. From a practical standpoint, Delegated RingCT presents a feasible approach for upgrading Bitcoin and similar cryptocurrencies in the future. Additionally, Delegated RingCT presents an opportunity for further research into a decentralized variant, as well as other potential applications. Recent studies using the few-shot in-context learning method have shown that language models can excel with minimal training data, often using the existing language data as a basis for fine-tuning. Building on these studies, our research examines how language modeling performance, measured by perplexity, affects the likelihood of a few-shot learning task succeeding. We analyze the relationship between in-context examples, task output, and task success in the FLAME dataset, a collection of 12 tasks that incorporate AG News, IMDB, Yelp, Amazon reviews, and Wikipedia articles. Our findings suggest a significant relationship between low perplexity and high success rates in few-shot learning tasks, but only when accounting for task complexity. However, this correlation does not necessarily imply a direct connection, and task-specific factors likely play a significant role. Notably, we discovered that Wikipedia tasks consistently demonstrated high success rates regardless of the model's perplexity. Our research also explores the distribution of in-context example usage in fluents and non-fluents and reveals a significant difference, where fluent in-context examples tend to have more non-edge words than their non-fluent counterparts. To facilitate reproducibility, we make our code and dataset available for public use. Additionally, we include FLAME dataset annotations to aid researchers and developers in understanding the intricacies of few-shot learning techniques. With the growing interest in few-shot learning, we anticipate that the FLAME dataset will play a vital role in the ongoing development of related methods and theories. In the long run, our dataset aspires to contribute to the creation of more accurate and efficient language models in the future. In accordance with this goal, we also make our code accessible on GitHub at the link provided. Our team is willing to engage in collaboration if you have any questions or suggestions regarding our research or dataset. In the realm of few-shot learning, researchers still require a comprehensive theoretical framework and set of guidelines to ensure consistency in evaluating and applying this technique effectively. To this end, our study seeks to make several significant contributions that can facilitate the advancement of the field in the future. Firstly, our research aims to establish a clear understanding of the relationship between low perplexity and high performance in few-shot learning tasks. Secondly, we strive to identify practical implications for using language models through in-context learning. The formation of galaxy clusters has been studied using magnetic field dynamics in a self-gravitating, cold-core cluster model. A study found that if thermal conduction has a direction-dependent effect, it can slow the cluster's core growth, but if conduction is uniform, it has little impact. Additionally, a phase with enhanced star formation has been added to the model, but its influence was minimal on core growth and phase development. However, if conduction is not uniform, it can slow the cluster's core growth, making it a necessary process for maintaining balance in the model. This paper explores the potential for significant energy reductions in edge computing facilities by implementing more efficient resource management techniques. Firstly, we will examine how to extend the life of edge computing equipment by scheduling tasks across multiple devices. This will involve developing an optimization strategy that maximizes service time while considering constraints such as device capacity and energy consumption. Once the equipment lifespan extension plan is established, we will determine the optimal time to replace or upgrade each device. This will involve calculating the cost of replacing or upgrading equipment at various points in time and identifying the most cost-effective time to replace or upgrade each device. Finally, we will determine the optimal time to upgrade the capacity of edge devices and the number of devices to upgrade at each time. This will involve developing an optimization strategy that maximizes the cost-effectiveness of upgrades and identify the most cost-effective time to upgrade the capacity of edge devices and the number of devices to upgrade at each time. We will use a real-world dataset from a major technology company to test our proposed strategies and evaluate their effectiveness. Specifically, we will use the dataset to determine the optimal time to replace or upgrade 2000 edge computing devices and the number of devices to upgrade at each time. We found that by scheduling tasks across multiple devices and extending the life of edge computing equipment, we can reduce the average energy consumption of each device by 37%. Additionally, we found that by upgrading the capacity of edge devices and the number of devices to upgrade at each time, we can reduce the average energy consumption of each device by a further 24%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed strategies in reducing energy consumption and extending the life of edge computing equipment. Specifically, we found that scheduling tasks across multiple devices and extending the life of edge computing equipment can reduce the average energy consumption of each device by 37%, and upgrading the capacity of edge devices can reduce the average energy consumption of each device by a further 24%. Furthermore, we observed that the energy consumption of edge computing facilities follows a power-law distribution, with a small number of devices consuming a large proportion of the total energy. We found that scheduling tasks across multiple devices and extending the life of edge computing equipment can reduce the energy consumption of devices at the tail of the distribution, and upgrading the capacity of edge devices can reduce the energy consumption of devices at the head of the distribution. The proposed method exceeds the performance of the renowned Supreme Bouvier clustering algorithm and matches the efficacy of a more complex dynamic clustering method. This paper presents an efficient motion planning approach for multi-limbed robots that significantly reduces computational costs. Traditionally, planning the movement of multiple limbs is treated as a single optimization problem, leading to prolonged computation times. Our proposed framework divides this process into multiple stages, enabling rapid solution computation. By leveraging precomputed options and adjusting variables between stages, we ensure the validity of our results. Additionally, computation time is substantially reduced by applying batch optimization techniques across stages. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation studies involving a two-armed robot, achieving near-optimal results in less than 10% of the original time required by standard optimization methods. Real-world performance is also verified through successful planning of a multi-limbed robotic system consisting of two arms interacting with multiple graspable objects. Clinical trials investigating treatments for rare disorders often use a fixed basic period to monitor a subgroup of patients from a larger population, exchanging information between these groups to adjust the trial duration.
We've developed a model to determine the optimal trial duration, taking into account the cost of misjudging treatment differences and the expense of maintaining the trial.
Borrowing information between groups enhances the trial's power, necessitating a smaller sample size to achieve the same results.
However, this benefit comes with a price: the increased risk of detecting a false positive treatment effect, necessitating careful consideration of the balance between these competing priorities.
We've introduced a metric to quantify this trade-off and demonstrated that the optimal sample size can be significantly reduced, saving substantial costs in certain scenarios.
For instance, if the trial can reasonably expect treatment differences in one group, doubling the trial duration for the intergroup comparison is not necessary; in this case, the sample size can be cut in half, saving 50% of the costs.
These cost savings translate to valuable clinical and financial benefits, allowing for more trials, which can lead to earlier detection of treatment differences.
Ultimately, our approach may enable the conduct of more cost-effective trials, promoting better resource allocation in rare disease research.
