In our research, we explore the underlying structure of a population's genetic makeup by examining the effects of mutations on a finite population of Amino Acid sequences over time. By utilizing a mathematical framework based on random loops models, previously developed by Brouder et al., to model the mutation process, we demonstrate how the population's genetic organization evolves over a specific time period. Our analysis reveals the distribution of genetic lengths within the population, both for general mutation types and specifically for the case of non-polar amino acid substitutions. According to our findings, even in the long-term limit, the population's genetic structure does not converge uniformly. Instead, the distribution of genetic lengths still exhibits significant variability, albeit much reduced, compared to the initial time point. Furthermore, our research identifies the number of Loops-Blocks formed as a prominent characteristic of the population's genetic makeup, where each Loops-Block representing a sequence segment resulting from multiple mutations. We also establish an explicit formula for the sum of squares of the lengths of these genetic segments, known as Squares-Loops, valid for all types of mutations. Additionally, for non-polar amino acid substitutions, we determine the mean number of Loops-Blocks, known as Mean-Loops, which serves as an essential statistical quantity to assess the homogeneity of a population's genetic makeup. Our mathematical calculations are further enhanced by the creation of two open-source computer programs, capable of simulating the mutation process and estimating the resulting genetic organization within a population. These simulations complement our theoretical models by allowing for the adjustment of various parameters, such as the mutation rate, sequence length, and types of amino acids involved. Our ultimate goal is to apply our mathematical framework to investigate practical problems, such as determining the likelihood that two individuals in a homogenous population share a genetic segment, and to examine how a mutation rate that varies across time affects the population's genetic organization over multiple time periods. These topics of investigation will be addressed in up-coming research papers. A widely-used attention-based model in spoofing countermeasures has been re-examined to understand its effectiveness in detecting speech artifacts. Originally, this model incorporated global attention to aggregate contextual information from the entire input speech waveform, then subsequently utilized local attention to focus on individual overlap segments. Nevertheless, its efficacy relied on an overly broad context, potentially including irrelevant segments that could hamper its artifact-detection performance. Furthermore, its dependency on overlap segments made it incapable of identifying artifacts in non-overlapping regions. In response, a novel context-aware model was devised, capable of enhancing the attention mechanism's effectiveness while keeping its complexity minimal. In this context-aware model, a context mask was designed to selectively enable or disable the broad context, enabling the focus on only the nearby segments when applicable. A comparative study was conducted across multiple datasets, comparing the proposed model with the original attention-based model, as well as two additional baselines that incorporated global context with a fixed duration or integrated global and local attention. The study revealed that the proposed context-aware model exhibited a significant 10.8% enhancement in detection accuracy compared to the original attention-based model, as well as outperformed the other two baselines by 14.4% and 6.1% respectively, in detecting speech artifacts across diverse frequencies. In addition, the proposed model demonstrated a high macro-F1 score of 0.942 when classifying speech artifacts, exhibiting a substantial 7.7% improvement over the attention-based model, as well as surpassing the performance of the baselines by 5.3% and 4.4% respectively. Subsequent ablation studies, coupled with an insightful analysis, suggested that the enhanced performance of the proposed model originated from its ability to dynamically determine the breadth of the context, rather than relying on pre-defined signals. As a result, this context-aware model represents a more efficient and effective approach to improving the detection of speech artifacts in spoofing countermeasures. In addition, the proposed architecture exhibits versatility, enabling its application to a broad spectrum of convolutional neural networks and attention mechanisms. Therefore, the proposed model serves as a valuable resource for future research in audio classification tasks. The proposed model has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/asriram/CACM for the benefit of the research community. Experimental results have been uploaded to https://asriram.github.io/CACM/index.html for reference. Additionally, the datasets utilized in this research can be accessed through https://github.com/adv-comp-free-speech

In this study, flexible MOSFETs were fabricated on both ETCSi and BOESi wafers to compare their electrical properties. XPS and SIMS analysis revealed that ETCSi possessed a higher concentration of carriers and oxygen than BOESi, while ETCSi also exhibited a stronger MOS capacitance. As a result, ETCSi demonstrated better electrical properties and greater stability on a flexible substrate, making it a more suitable material for constructing MOSFETs on a curved surface. Consequently, ETCSi offered enhanced performance and reduced leakage current compared to BOESi. A comparison of the MOSFETs' electrical properties on flat and curved BOESi substrates also confirmed the influence of surface curvature on carrier generation. Both ETCSi and BOESi showed promise as viable substrate materials for creating flexible MOSFETs. Meanwhile, we collect information on short-term reversal traders through academic research. The results indicate that both groups of traders benefit from engagements with each other, with commodity trading advisors gaining valuable market insights from short-term reversal traders and using their recommendations to inform trading decisions. In return, the short-term reversal traders profit from commodity trading advisors' investments, allowing them to scale their strategies. This research explores the behavior of magnons traveling through a combination of
a waveguide system and superconducting strips, feature-sized for optimal performance.
Using advanced simulation methods, we studied how these magnons interact with capillary
waves and found a new method of controlling them by applying a magnetic field. This
approach enables the selection and direction control of two distinct types of magnons,
the zero-line and Breithaupt-Carlin modes. Our investigation also examines how these
strips influence magnon propagation and finds that this interaction can lead to a
system in which the magnons become localized along the waveguide. This discovery
holds promise for the development of magnon-based computers and devices, where
precise control over magnons is crucial for efficient operation. Ultimately, we
demonstrate a theoretical mechanism for reading out magnon states using a Josephson
interference pattern, where a usable signal can be produced with current technology. 
The efficiency of this reading process was found to be on the order of 10^-3 eV per
magnitude change in the current interference pattern. Furthermore, we identify
the limitations of this magnon system, including heat loss and magnon scattering,
both of which can be mitigated through the careful design of the superconducting
strips. By doing so, we find the maximum Q-factor to be around 1000, within
reach of modern technology. Finally, we find the minimum operational frequency to
be approximately 100 GHz, an area where electron spin resonance technology
operates. Last but not least, we explore the potential of using neutron
scatterers to control magnon propagation, where the application of a neutron
beam can dynamically alter the magnetic properties of the superconducting strips. 
This research discovers a new method of controlling magnons, where the combination of
superconducting strips and a waveguide system can be used to select and direct two
distinct types of magnons, while also localizing them along the waveguide. The use
of superconducting strips enables the independent control of magnon propagation,
where strips of varying lengths can be used to create magnon splitters, while also
enabling the detection of magnon states using a Josephson interference pattern.
Furthermore, we find multiple mechanisms for improving the efficiency of this

mitigate heat loss and magnon scattering, where the maximum Q-factor can be

This study analyzed various aspects of local news in Germany, focusing on the amount of coverage and topics discussed during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. Notably, areas with high COVID-19 mortality rates initially received less local news coverage, and news content varied greatly in terms of topics such as the economy, culture, and politics. The researchers also explored how local news in major newspapers differed from that of smaller publications and found numerous interesting patterns. This large-scale study provides a comprehensive understanding of local news in Germany, shedding new light on the country's media landscape. In addition to examining the content of local news, the researchers also looked into potential correlations between local news and public opinion, including how it was affected by government measures, such as curfews and travel restrictions, and how it varied in areas with high COVID-19 infection rates. Finally, the study considered the potential impact of local news on public perception of the pandemic, including how it influenced attitudes toward government action and vaccine uptake. Overall, this research offers a wealth of new insights into local news in Germany, offering a framework that can be applied to future studies of local news in other contexts. Additionally, the study's findings highlight several practical implications for local news and public communication efforts during crises. Deep learning approaches, specifically those employing Neural Network Language Models, have found significant success in enhancing neural machine translation performance. Despite significant gains, a crucial challenge remains, as existing models' translation quality degrades severely outside their initial training data range. To address this, we develop a novel neural machine translation model that facilitates seamless extrapolation beyond its initial training domain with minimal supplementary data. By integrating a dense autoencoder, the proposed Translational Similarity Model (TSM) captures domain similarity characteristics and uses them to facilitate efficient extrapolation. TSM's translation ability is bolstered through a likelihood- and similarity-driven search process. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the proposed model's capacity for successful domain adaptation with minimal additional data, and it outperforms baseline models in zero-shot and limited-data translation scenarios. Notably, our results show that TSM achieves a significant 11.0 and 3.0 BLEU score improvement over GPT-2 and Seq2Seq models, respectively, in zero-shot translation scenarios. Furthermore, with only 2000 sentence pairs in the target domain, TSM exhibits comparable performance to GPT-2, trained on 16 times more data. TSM's source code will be made available.

We introduce xor filters, a type of Bloom filter variant that can be constructed 
using basic operations and is highly amenable to construction and query operations 
on data streams. Our findings reveal that xor filters consistently use less memory and 
are significantly faster than standard Bloom filters, all while maintaining similar 
false positive rates. We also demonstrate the existence of false negatives, unlike 
Bloom filters, and show that xor filters can be rebuilt from a sequence of Bloom filters. 
A novel, efficient algorithm is developed for constructing a xor filter from a series of 
Bloom filters, utilizing at most O(n log n) time and space complexity. Additionally, 
a proposed variant, called xor filter with hash, is presented, offering further reduced 
memory usage and speed improvements. A real-world use case is presented where xor 
filters can be applied to optimize disk I/O operations. A publicly available C++ library 
known as libxfilter is made available for these new types of Bloom filters.

We offer a geometric, model-independent and local explanation for the Alexandrov embedding of a positive closed $(1,1)$-class $T$ on a projective variety $X$. This involves the formation of the Alexandrov body, which is the closed subset of the projective space of all closed $(1,1)$-classes on $X$, consisting of classes that are numerically nonnegative and whose pullback to any curve is nonnegative. Our analysis also provides a geometric interpretation for the numerically trivial class and gives a local model for the decomposition, as well as J-positivity. Additionally, our method allows for an algorithm to calculate the pull-back of a closed $(1,1)$-class from a nearby projective variety, which has applications in solving equations of hypersurfaces in relation to a given class. Finally, our work offers an alternative proof and explanation for the soft and hard Lefschetz theorems, as well as a geometric interpretation for the decomposition theorem of Bogomolov-Skoda. The study explores the notion that market trends in financial markets are characterized by distinct periods of stability and change. It suggests that past market movements have an inherent time frame during which their significance influences future market behavior. To determine this time frame, the research develops an algorithm grounded in statistical principles from the Kolmogorov information theory, which is thoroughly tested using real market data. Specifically, the analysis employs EUR/USD currency exchange rate data obtained from a leading financial institution. By employing the information-theoretic algorithm, the research successfully identifies the optimal time intervals at which market trends become apparent, thereby confirming the idea that these trends occur within specific periods. Notably, the longest time intervals, exceeding 10 minutes, are found in volatile market conditions, while shorter time intervals, less than 5 minutes, are more prevalent in calmer markets. Furthermore, the study reveals that past market movements up to 20 minutes are significant in determining future market behavior, which aligns with existing knowledge. Additionally, the research finds that market trends in both rising and falling markets are characterized by distinct time intervals, thereby confirming their diverse nature. The growing sophistication of deepfakes leads to more plausible media that can incite public unrest and financial losses. As deepfakes become more convincing, identifying manipulations becomes increasingly crucial for maintaining truth integrity in society. Although various methods have been developed to detect deepfakes, they often fall short by neglecting to consider the inherent semantic inconsistencies present in manipulated content. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages large-scale video understanding models to detect deepfakes based on semantic coherence. By utilizing video embeddings generated from pre-trained semantic models, we establish a robust deepfake detection framework that surpasses existing methods in performance, as demonstrated by our experimental results. Additionally, we release DeepFake Semantic Embeddings (DFSE), a comprehensive video dataset containing both authentic and deepfake samples with expert annotations for future research. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/muhammad-muhammad/DFSE. For data access, please contact muhammadmuhammad@gmail.com.MFSE stands for MuMu-DFSE.

The atmospheric retention of massive gas giant planets is well-documented, but much less is known about smaller planets that still maintain a substantial atmosphere. To study these intermediate-sized planets, researchers investigated atmospheric properties of planets with masses similar to those of Earth and Super-Earth. Using high-resolution simulations of planet formation, scientists modeled the atmospheric compositions of planets with masses ranging from that of Earth to that of Uranus. These simulations identified two distinct atmospheric profiles. Planets with small atmospheres contain equal amounts of carbon and nitrogen gases, with trace amounts of hydrogen. In contrast, planets with massive atmospheres contain more hydrogen than carbon and nitrogen gases, with water vapor present in large quantities. To explain these differences, researchers considered two scenarios. In the first, carbon and nitrogen gases are stripped from smaller atmospheres due to insufficient gravitational pull to retain these gases. In the second, massive atmospheres of larger planets are enriched with hydrogen and water vapor from surrounding dust and rocky particles. The results of these simulations indicate that planets with masses between those of Earth and Uranus exhibit varied atmospheric properties. To confirm these findings, researchers applied the results to known exoplanets. These studies demonstrate that small and massive atmospheres differ not only in temperature and pressure but also in chemical composition, with implications for future observations of exoplanets. In particular, researchers found that temperate planets with small or massive atmospheres may be suited for different types of studies. Small atmospheres might be best investigated through spectroscopic analysis of their transmission spectra, while massive atmospheres may be better understood through the observation of their emission spectra and the behavior of internal heat and water clouds. Further research is necessary to accurately model and observe the atmospheric properties of intermediate-sized planets. To this end, researchers suggest conducting additional simulations that take into account various atmospheric opacities, ice clouds, and the incorporation of future instruments, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, that will be capable of observing the atmospheric properties of small and massive planets. With these observations, researchers will be able to constrain the models of small and massive atmospheres and gain a more comprehensive understanding of the atmospheric properties of intermediate-sized planets. With these new findings, researchers will be able to test and refine the models of small and massive atmospheres and make more accurate predictions about the properties of unobserved planets. Ultimately, future studies will allow researchers to use observational data to constrain the theoretical models of small and massive atmospheres, thereby expanding the knowledge of exoplanet atmospheres and improving the accuracy of future predictions about planetary systems. Detecting sudden changes and identifying underlying causes in real-time data streams is crucial for responding to anomalies. However, change detection and diagnosis often require improved efficiency and adaptability, especially in limited-resource settings such as IoT systems. To address these challenges, we developed an efficient online monitoring system that reduces data dimensionality, detects changes, and isolates the root cause. To reduce resource usage, we utilize a balanced tree data structure to enable efficient querying of univariate statistics. Utilizing the Pruned Tree Monitoring system, we leverage multiple techniques, including adaptive sampling, approximation algorithms, and diagnostic methods, to achieve high-accuracy outcomes. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted comprehensive testing, comparing its performance to existing methods, and demonstrating significantly better results, specifically up to $37\%$ improvements, validated through detailed case studies across various fields. We publicly release our open-source system to facilitate future research. \href{https://github.com/alegbert/pruned-tree-monitoring}{Pruned Tree Monitoring} can be downloaded from this link. Experimentally verified improvements in performance, specifically $37\%$ to $55\%$ reductions, were achieved, as demonstrated by diverse case studies across multiple domains. To facilitate future research, our open-source implementation, \href{https://github.com/alegbert/pruned-tree-monitoring}{Pruned Tree Monitoring}, is publicly accessible.

We've performed detailed analysis on newly discovered metallospectrum members of two ancient globular clusters, Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1, incorporating data from the LAMOST survey. Our research reveals that these clusters have striking similarities in their velocity distributions, metallicity patterns, and age of star formation - all of which closely match the findings from earlier studies. Specifically, we found evidence that star formation in these clusters lasted for approximately 1 billion years in the case of Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and 300-700 million years for Wukong/LMS-1. Our results also show that multiple second-generation stars in these clusters had extremely low central densities, which may have led to the development of unusual and complex pattern formations early on. Notably, we discovered a low-frequency oscillation in velocity distribution for the 2nd generation of Gaia-Sausage Enceladus at approximately 0.8 muHz, which could be induced by a 4-million-year harmonic resonance caused by a dark, unseen companion star. Our research suggests that this phenomenon might be a common occurrence in distorted systems like NFW 1 and may offer valuable clues for the study of other disrupted clusters in the Milky Way. In the case of Wukong/LMS-1, we discovered that its 2nd generation displayed a notable lack of calcium-rich and alpha-element-rich stars, which may indicate a reduced supernova II contribution to its development. Based on simulations, we found that these stars likely originated from an irregular ring structure that formed early on, which can explain their distinct distribution patterns and metallurgical characteristics. Our research suggests a new timeline for the development of these stars, which began approximately 2 billion years ago and continued until 300-700 million years ago. Notably, we discovered two particularly ancient white dwarf stars in the metallicity range of -1.20 < [Fe/H] < -1.15 within this cluster, which may indicate that these stars formed through a merger of two WDs approximately 200 million years ago. Our research presents a new, comprehensive view of the metallicity, velocity, and age patterns of these disrupted clusters, which may serve as important references for the study of other disrupted clusters in the Milky Way. Our results also highlight the significance of photometric data in pinpointing calcium-rich and alpha-element-rich stars and encouraging further research into the photometric characteristics of these disrupted clusters. Our results indicate the significance of spin-orbit coupling on the interface electronic structure, with implications for understanding magnetism within InAs/EuS heterostructures. To boost the efficiency of models via hardware acceleration, researchers have been searching for a balance between model's accuracy and computational cost for years. A common technique to achieve this goal is model pruning. However, most existing model pruning approaches focus on reducing the model's size but often overlook the challenges associated with actual deployment. Our innovative tool, ClickTrain, addresses these deployment issues by enabling accurate model pruning from the training stage. ClickTrain utilizes a novel criterion-based method to eliminate unnecessary model parameters by identifying the least important ones for the prediction outcome. By integrating ClickTrain with various pruning techniques, models can be effectively downsized while maintaining their original accuracy. Moreover, ClickTrain's deployment engine further enhances the model's performance by reconstructing sub-networks for accurate hardware-inference, resulting in a notable improvement. Our experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain achieves remarkable results, boasting an astonishing 10.4 times efficiency gain over the original model, accompanied by a 9.2 points improvement in top-1 accuracy relative to the state-of-the-art pruning methods. Our comprehensive evaluations encompassed pruned ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, and YOLOv3 models on the ImageNet and MS-COCO datasets. This paper introduces a relational semantics for substructural modal logics that prioritizes cut-free proof theory. The proposed relational semantics builds upon existing duality-based approaches, adapting them to accommodate both endo- and exo-structural rules. A corresponding Kripke model is presented, along with a demonstration of sound and complete cut-free sequent calculus for the underlying logic. The developed methodology is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of substructural modal logics, including those with additional axioms such as Kratzer's axiom or FDE semantics. Furthermore, we demonstrate a dual interpretation of pregroup assignments, thereby providing a new perspective on pregroup logic's axioms and semantic types. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate a pregroup approach to modal logic and its associated programming and proof assistants. The merger of two compact stars, including a neutron star, can be observed through multiple channels, including gravitational and electromagnetic waves. A neutron star coalescence simulation produced relativistic jets, which interacted with the surrounding matter, forming particles that emit synchrotron radiation. This process produced distinctive X-ray and gamma-ray signatures that were observed in the simulated data. By analyzing the spectral properties of this emission, astronomers could gain valuable insights into the behavior of jets near black holes. Furthermore, incorporating gravitational-wave data could provide independent constraints on the density of neutron star material, potentially validating models of nuclear physics. Our approach leverages quadratic safety constraints and incorporates a safety-aware filter, known as the $\mathcal{F}$-return criterion, to increase the likelihood of tasks being completed safely. Moreover, our approach emits fewer and fewer unsafe actions as training progresses, resulting in a more efficient training process. Our results demonstrate that this new technique outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods in scenarios involving quadratic safety constraints, with notable improvements of 75% in some cases. Our approach also compares favorably to state-of-the-art techniques by increasing the likelihood of completing tasks safely by up to 90%. Ecologists use presence-absence data to understand species distribution patterns across different environments. They employ clustering methods to group species based on their occurrence patterns. Notably, two approaches - Bayesian switching models and the Isolates algorithm - have received significant attention for clustering such data. While these methods are effective, they can face challenges related to the specification of prior distributions and the efficiency of computational methods. To address these issues, we developed a new clustering method that uses the Isolates algorithm within a Bayesian framework and incorporates a non-informative prior on the clustering probability. Additionally, we introduced an early stopping criterion, enabling users to determine the optimal number of clusters without excessive computation. We tested the proposed method on various real-world and simulated datasets, comparing its performance to other popular clustering methods. The results demonstrated that this new approach yields consistent and efficient clusterings, which can be accurately validated through multiple replications. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of the variance of the estimated cluster probabilities, indicating the likely number of clusters can be the square root of the number of specimens. To facilitate easy application of this new method, we created an open-source R package, named ClustPMA, which includes the necessary functionality. We have created an efficient storage system that reduces memory needs for producing weighted three-nucleon interaction matrix elements, crucial for ab initio many-body calculations. These elements are critical for developing three-nucleon interactions from first principles. We utilized a custom C++ program to generate and store these elements, which were then applied to an ab initio many-body calculation based on the coupled-cluster method with an explicit treatment of two- and three-nucleon interactions. We found that the proposed storage system led to a significant reduction in memory usage, allowing the computation of more intricate three-nucleon interactions that were previously unfeasible due to memory constraints. As a result, we were able to calculate matrix elements of a more refined three-nucleon interaction that are relevant for nuclear force development, whereas previous studies could only compute less sophisticated forms. Moreover, we discovered that the ground-state wave function generated by CCSDT(2+1) includes sufficient information to also compute matrix elements of a more refined three-nucleon interaction that are relevant for nuclear reactions, which would otherwise require a higher many-body method, such as CCSDT(q=3), to compute these elements. We believe the proposed storage system can be adapted for computing higher-order many-body interactions, making more sophisticated many-body methods, such as CCSDT(q=4) and beyond, computationally feasible in the future. We discuss the potential for such applications. In deep learning, allocating memory on the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is an essential but complex task. Current GPU memory allocators, typically embedded in Deep Learning Frameworks, often lack transparency in their allocation methods. Understanding these allocators can hinder the development of optimized deep learning models for memory efficiency. We introduce DynaSOAr, a dynamic memory allocator designed for modern GPU architectures. By employing a space partitioning technique, DynaSOAr efficiently maps memory addresses at varying sizes, outperforming state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators while providing clear allocation logic and easy adaptability for developers. We showcase DynaSOAr's benefits in optimizing memory usage during deep learning inference. Additionally, DynaSOAr's modular structure enables its adaptation for other GPU workloads, such as training, tooling, and hardware testing. The source code for DynaSOAr is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/mdbm/DynaSOAr. A benchmarking suite can be found at https://github.com/mdbm/DynaSOAr-benchmark. We believe DynaSOAr's innovative approach will inspire future GPU memory allocators, leading to improved design and optimization of GPU memory allocators, deep learning frameworks, and associated software tools. A highly resistant and adaptable temperature sensor IC has been created using a standard CMOS process, designed for use in temperature measurement and calibration in microelectromechanical systems and IoT devices. The device's temperature measurement accuracy is comparable to that of high-resolution temperature sensors available in standard CMOS processes. The proposed sensor IC features a compact 30 micrometer x 30 micrometer x 3.6 micrometer layout, incorporating on-chip clock oscillations and data storage. The demonstrated circuit achieved a measurement resolution of 0.029 degrees Celsius, far exceeding the specifications of industry-standard temperature sensors. A measurement accuracy of 5.4 percent was also achieved, surpassing the specifications of industry-standard temperature sensors. The total power consumption of the circuit was found to be 10.3 microwatts, enabling its use in battery-powered devices. Current one-round online algorithms for constructing spanners yield a competitive ratio of O((d log n)/r), but this ratio has limitations, exceeding a quadratic factor of the degree r in d-dimensional space. We investigate whether this limitation holds in higher dimensions, considering two scenarios: (a) constructing optimal t-spanners, and (b) forming near-optimal 2-spanners. To address these questions, we present online algorithms for both scenarios that achieve competitive ratios of O((d log n)^2/r) and O((d^2 log n)/r), respectively. These results demonstrate the complexity of online algorithms in higher dimensions, showing that the increased competitive ratio of O(d^2) is inherent for two-hop spanners. We also explore the feasibility of using Steiner points and establish lower bounds, stating that any two-hop online algorithm for forming a near-optimal 2-spanner must have a competitive ratio of at least Omega(d^1.5 log^1.5 n / r^0.5) in d-dimensional space, and at least Omega((log n)^2 / r) in Euclidean space. These findings indicate that using Steiner points cannot improve the competitive ratio to within a logarithmic factor of the current bounds. We also present lower bounds for one-hop online algorithms in Euclidean space, showing that any such algorithm with a competitive ratio of epsilon must induce at least (1 + epsilon)^2 times the minimum spanning tree of the graph. These findings complement previous work on lower bounds for two-hop online algorithms. We also present the first constant-factor 2-spanner in Euclidean space, constructed through a random two-hop approach, demonstrating that both random Steiner points and two-hop algorithms have potential in forming near-optimal 2-spanners. These findings contribute to the development of constant-factor 2-spanners, while also providing insights into the feasibility of one- and two-hop online algorithms in higher dimensions. It is also revealed that an attacker can exert significant influence over the cost-matrix, potentially harming a classifier's performance. Previous studies have examined the performance of parametric aligners such as
AlignMF, which uses a small corpus for training, and compared it to established
tools like GIZA++ trained on a large corpus. To provide a more accurate comparison,
this study re-ran the experiments from Section 4 of the paper "Finding paths of
minimum average cost in weighted directed acyclic graphs using dynamic programming"
by Heffernan et al., using the same data and configuration, to assess the impact
of training AlignMF on a small corpus. The results indicate that AlignMF trained
on a small corpus outperforms GIZA++ in terms of alignment speed and scaled
accuracy, but not plain accuracy, and excels at providing the optimal alignment
path. Furthermore, the study discovered that the efficient AlignMF implementation
using dynamic programming exhibits similar time complexity to Heffernan et al.'s
dynamic programming aligner. Additionally, the study examined the performance of
non-parametric aligners like GIZA++ and giza-++-dp, and an earlier version of
AlignMF, and analysed the strategies for improving their efficiency. The findings
show that the efficient AlignMF implementation using dynamic programming is the
fastest among the compared aligners. Finally, the study explored the potential
of combining AlignMF's optimal cost path module with other aligners like GIZA++ and
SNOWBALL, and verified its scalability using larger datasets. The findings
indicate that the hybrid approach outperforms the individual aligners in terms
of alignment speed, while scaling accuracy and plain accuracy remain comparable. 
In addition, the study investigated the potential of replacing the LM used
in the optimal cost path module with one trained on a larger corpus, and found
that the hybrid approach still excelled in alignment speed. The study also
identified other areas for further research and improvement. Overall, the results
confirm that the efficient AlignMF implementation using dynamic programming is
the fastest among the compared aligners. The combined approach presents an
interesting alternative, especially for situations involving limited data.

This research paper proposes an asynchronous strategy for solving large-scale nonsmooth optimization problems. To this end, we present an algorithmic framework inspired by Spingarn's 1975 paper, which applied Lagrange multiplier theory to analyze asynchronous block-iterative decomposition methods. Our approach leverages a more generalised version of Brouwer's fixed-point theorem to derive sufficient conditions for the convergence of our proposed method. We then test the efficacy of our technique using standard optimisation benchmarks, as well as a nonlinear operator that mimics the Lipschitz continuous case, all while comparing its performance to leading optimisation algorithms. Furthermore, we apply our method to a nonlinear programming problem derived from a real-world fluid dynamics model, which illustrates the potential of this technique to solve complex, discipline-specific nonsmooth optimisation problems. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that the asynchronous strategy can yield comparable or even better performance than its synchronous counterpart, while delivering significant speed-ups in certain situations. Specifically, we observe average speed-up ratios of 1.5 to 3.0 for various standard optimisation benchmarks, as well as a substantial speed-up of nearly ten times for the asynchronous method in its application to the nonlinear problem of Euler equations. We thereby validate the efficacy of our proposed asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm for solving large-scale nonsmooth optimisation problems. In addition, we provide open-source code for the implementation of our method, which is available through the link https://git.uq.edu.au/cafle/codes/-/tree/async_bid.fle2022. We also provide an implementation of Spingarn's 1975 algorithm in the link https://git.uq.edu.au/cafle/codes/-/tree/sync_bid.Spingarn1975.ToFle2022. Both of these implementations can be found in the above-mentioned links. A new technique called quantum imaging has made it possible to non-interactively image sensitive materials by utilizing the ability of projective measurements to delete information. This has led to the development of two separate approaches for optical quantum imaging: one based on the elimination of information and another on the reinforcement of information. Both of these methods, however, rely on the availability of a large number of identical photons from a single source, which is often not the case in practice. This study presents an improved method for optical quantum imaging using a single photon source that overcomes this limitation. By utilizing fast switching capabilities and rapid modulation of a double-layered diffraction grating, this method enables the rapid scattering and reconfiguration of a single photon, simulating the emission of multiple photons from a single source. This technique facilitates the efficient optical quantum imaging of sensitive samples even with low fluorescence from a subject, and has the potential to improve the performance of future optical quantum networks. This method has been verified by successfully implementing a basic information deletion approach to image a 50-micron wide silver wire. We introduce a novel characterization of surface roughness in emulsions and foams based on how their fluids flow. This characterization, derived solely from visual observations of climbing and flowing materials, is applied to both liquid foams and droplet microfluidic emulsions with varying surface modifications. It shows that roughness factors from dynamic observations match those estimated through static measurements, revealing the impact of surface texture. Furthermore, we use this characterization to investigate the scaling of emulsion and foam durability as surface roughness increases. Additionally, we provide a framework for exploring the interplay between material surface roughness and emulsion or foam stability through controlled microfluidic experiments. We investigated electron-hole pairs within the LDA+GW framework applied to a sodium crystal. Our results show significant mass suppression of dipolar electron-hole pairs relative to monopole pairs, suggesting a substantial effect of Na's dielectric constant. Additionally, we found that the mass enhancement of these pairs closely follows the expected quadratic relationship with the reduced dielectric constant. Furthermore, we identified two distinct coupling mechanisms for the dipolar excitations: longitudinal coupling, which is strongly influenced by the macroscopic electric field, and transverse coupling, which is primarily governed by the Na's dielectric response function. These findings are supportive of recent experimental research in this area.

Initially, this class was thought to be circulant when k was an even number. However, a counterexample demonstrated that A[14,6] is not circulant. Subsequent reasoning shows that for any given k, graph class A[n,k] is not circulant if it contains a prime number n. Furthermore, if n is a composite number, we provide a procedure to determine whether A[n,k] can be classified as a circulant graph. Our results indicate that the graph class A[n,k] is circulant when k is 1, as well as in scenarios where n is 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, or 9. However, a computational approach was used to find that A[6,3] and A[10,5] are not circulant graphs. Consequently, there are distinct graph class A[n,k] instances that are circulant graphs despite sharing the same value of n. Our research delves into the underlying mechanics of DINO, examining how it contrasts with other self-supervised methods like SimCLR. We are introducing a user-friendly interface called Stable, which makes it possible for individuals without advanced knowledge of programming to utilize the capabilities of SDGAN, a generative adversarial network that can create high-quality images based on prior artistic experience. Our interface enables users to create custom images by adjusting control values associated with specific artistic effects, such as changing the color of eyes in a portrait. By doing so, users can craft unique images that reflect their intended artistic visions. Our study investigated the capabilities of users familiar with traditional art but inexperienced in using computers, which demonstrated the potential of SDGAN in facilitating creative tasks through intuitive input. We observed users completing drawing tasks, which revealed that while basic images were generated quickly, more intricate sketches required substantial adjustment time. Notably, users were able to produce high-quality images with artistic styles and adjustments, such as changing hair colors, using our interface. These findings indicate that our interface effectively enables users to control the image generation process and produce images with specific characteristics. Based on these results, we believe that the Stable approach can enhance the capabilities of users in controlling the image generation process and producing accurate images. Our study also explored the potential of using artistic experience to guide image generation and the performance of users in utilizing our interface to control image generation. These results will contribute to developing more user-friendly and intuitive interfaces for image generation. Deep neural networks excel in making predictions, but how reliable are those predictions? We can measure the uncertainty of a prediction by comparing it to a set of similar predictions made by a related network of varying complexity. By using the differences between these networks to estimate uncertainty, we can develop accurate models of uncertainty from scratch, without needing any external data or assumptions, and apply these models to a range of uncertainty quantification tasks. Additionally, our method allows us to determine whether a particular network is a reliable predictor, and can even help to improve the accuracy of a existing model by selecting the most reliable training examples. We can also use our method to develop new, more accurate models of image classification, and to discover the most influential examples for a particular classification task. Finally, our method allows us to predict the likelihood of a particular example being misclassified, and can even help to discover the most unreliable examples in a particular classification task. Research onto dark matter-nucleon interactions that relies on direct detection methods cannot rule out a significant contribution from the $J/\psi$ decay channel, as calculated in a 2023 study. This calculation shows that using only the visible $J/\psi$ decay into muons can lead to overly restrictive limits on dark matter-scattering cross sections. The new calculation takes into account the non-visible decays of $J/\psi$ that involve hadrons, which have a cross section nearly ten times larger than the muon decay. As such, properly considering all $J/\psi$ decay modes is vital for properly inferring dark matter properties using data from direct detection experiments. The updated calculation has far-reaching implications for dark matter studies involving $J/\psi$ and certain nuclear recoil events observed in direct detection experiments. In particular, the revised calculation indicates that even an extremely abundant dark matter population would still not be detected in direct detection experiments, as even a substantial portion of $J/\psi$ decays would still be unaccounted for.

Three years of data collected from the SDO satellite, specifically the SMIIF camera, gathered images of magnetic bright points in the quiet sun. Using these images, the characteristics of magnetic bright points in terms of their positions, movements, and associated magnetic fields were studied. Analyzing 1-minute images produced the following key findings: (1) magnetic bright points were found to be evenly scattered across the solar surface, (2) their motion followed a uniform pattern, with some components distributed lognormally, while others followed a normal distribution, (3) the number of magnetic bright points remained relatively stable over time and averaged around 5000 per minute, with each representing a magnetic field of approximately 1000 GS. Furthermore, the area of these bright points decreased exponentially in a time-dependent manner. Additionally, statistical research revealed correlations between the magnetic field strength and the areas of magnetic bright points, as well as connections between their movements and the associated magnetic field strength. Lastly, the research showed that the number of magnetic bright points detected varied depending on the camera's resolution and the duration for which they were observed. As such, the study suggests that the resolution of observations plays a key role in understanding the characteristics of magnetic bright points in the quiet sun. Human motion analysis plays a significant role in understanding human movement patterns and how the human visual system processes movement information. By studying minimal videos, scientists can gain insights into human eye movement patterns and how these are linked to recognition processes. Current eye trackers are capable of accurately recording human eye movements, allowing researchers to use this data to develop models of human motion analysis. Building on existing knowledge of human motion analysis, our team created a database of eye movement information recorded while watching video clips of human locomotion. The database, consisting of 288 minimal videos, showcases diverse walking patterns, including slow and speed-adequate representations, as well as scenarios of human interaction, such as walking alongside another person or while carrying items. The videos were viewed by 108 individuals, resulting in a comprehensive dataset of eye movement information that can be utilized to develop models of human motion analysis and to solve various computer vision problems, including activity recognition, similar action search, and personalized recommendations. The eye movement information recorded by our eye trackers allows for a deep understanding of how these movements relate to specific task requirements and how they can be utilized to solve the mentioned computer vision problems. The theories we studied include the SU(Nl) gauge theory on the spacetime of a sphere, as well as on the spacetime of a sphere with a hole, known as an A1 (Nl-1) quiver theory. The bound monopole ground states in these theories exhibit Debye screening behavior in an external magnetic field. However, the monopole charge remains the same. The monopole-dyon bound state energy was calculated in an external magnetic field, revealing that the energy increases linearly with the magnetic field strength. Additionally, the monopole-dyon mass was found to decrease slightly as the magnetic field strength increases. The results were confirmed through both mathematical calculations and computer simulations using Seiberg-Witten theory and the Higgs mechanism. The findings provide further confirmation of the duality between the Higgs mechanism and Debye screening in the constrained N=4 SU(Nl) gauge theory on a compact spacetime. The research sheds new light on the interplay between magnetic monopoles and the Higgs mechanism in the context of the constrained N=4 SU(Nl) gauge theory on a compact spacetime. The monopole-dyon interactions were found to be consistent with the duality between the Coulomb phase and the Higgs phase of the theory, as well as with the duality between magnetic and electric screening charges in the constrained N=4 SU(Nl) gauge theory on a compact spacetime. To compare and evaluate weather forecasting models, researchers typically assess their predictive capabilities against observed data, typically using measures such as mean absolute error or relative absolute error. However, we've identified two key challenges with this approach. Firstly, weather datasets are inherently uneven, with certain areas recorded more frequently than others, which creates bias in the evaluation process. Secondly, weather models often produce probabilities rather than specific weather conditions, making traditional evaluation methods less effective. In response, we've introduced an innovative technique to normalize and balance weather datasets, matching the distribution of actual weather data. We've also developed a novel evaluation method, Relative Absolute Difference, to compare probabilistic weather forecasting models more effectively. By employing NORMA, a dataset normalization tool, and RAD metrics, we were able to conduct comprehensive comparative studies of weather forecasting models on multiple datasets. Notably, normalizing the datasets and using RAD metrics revealed significant discrepancies in the performance evaluation of previously established models, indicating that these methods offer valuable insights into probabilistic forecasting capabilities. Moreover, models that were previously considered ineffective by traditional measures were revealed to be competent when evaluated using RAD metrics. This research underscores the importance of utilizing normalized datasets and probabilistic evaluation methods to gain more accurate and comprehensive insights into weather forecasting models. The proposed techniques have real-world applications and can be adapted for use in the prediction of other phenomena, such as climate risks. The developed tools, specifically NORMA and RAD, as well as the normalized datasets and corresponding results, are being made available open-source to facilitate future research and improvement. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/daniel-pankowski/NORMA/tree/main/utils and https://github.com/daniel-pankowski/RAD, respectively. The normalized datasets can be found at https://zenodo.org/depositories/495928/. The existing datasets used in this research must be accessed through their respective links: https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/ and https://www.ecad.eu/. Note that the Met Office dataset is subject to a 12-month embargo, resulting in the observations from January to June, 2021 being unavailable. In contrast, the ECMWF dataset is available under a more permissive license, but is still subject to a 1-year delay in real-time. In our research, we accounted for the embargo by evaluating the Met Office dataset up to December, 2020. Similarly, we used the ECMWF dataset up to November, 2020. The PPT conjecture is assessed in terms of its predictive power among density matrices, with a focus on quantum systems with a finite number of dimensions. It is demonstrated that in such systems, the PPT conjecture is equivalent to a more complex theory involving structural properties. As a result, if the PPT conjecture is disproven, it will be countered by a more sophisticated theory. This more complex theory is shown to be applicable in infinite-dimensional systems as well. In addition, a more refined version of this structural theory is proposed, which is stronger than the PPT conjecture and includes previously published work by Kielpa\v{s} and Saalsch\"uter. This refined version has been independently verified by other researchers. Furthermore, a method is introduced to test the PPT conjecture in systems with a finite number of dimensions by analyzing specific protocols related to entanglement swapping. These methods can be extended to systems with a finite number of dimensions by utilizing available computational tools. In the end, some positive findings regarding the PPT conjecture are presented, including its confirmation for systems with at most four parties and a total of 10 dimensions, as well as its confirmation in systems with two parties and a total of 11 dimensions. These results were obtained using a new algorithmic approach. In the conclusion, the relationship between the PPT conjecture and existing theories is summarized, including stochastic local measurement complexity theory, which is the subject of a previously published paper. In particular, it is shown that these two theories are equivalent if the PPT conjecture is correct, but are distinct and independent if the PPT conjecture is disproven. In the latter case, stochastic local measurement complexity theory is shown to be more robust and versatile. In the end, some open questions regarding the PPT conjecture and related theories are presented. In particular, a stronger version of structural theory is proposed, which is not known to be equivalent to the PPT conjecture but is believed to be so. In the event that the PPT conjecture is disproven, this stronger version is anticipated to provide alternative insights. Finally, a discussion is presented on how the PPT conjecture, as well as structural and complexity theories, can be extended to quantum systems that are indistinguishable but not necessarily mutually exclusive. In particular, a generalization of the structural theory is not known to be weaker than this broader class of theories. In the event that the PPT conjecture is disproven, this general structural theory may offer independent and more refined perspectives.

Banking fraud detection is becoming increasingly vital due to the rising cases of cyber theft. To identify fraudulent transactions, researchers use graphical models called banking graphs, which consist of nodes representing various items including accounts, locations, and items purchased, and edges that connect nodes in significant ways. Present methods for creating banking graphs fall short due to their inability to guarantee valid models, leading to incorrect conclusions in analysis. To address this challenge, we introduce the Hybrid Generation Equivalence algorithm (HGE), an innovative approach that ensures valid banking graphs. By combining the principles of graph isomorphism and graph embedding, HGE minimizes the loss of information in model translation. We evaluate HGE's effectiveness through experiments, demonstrating its capacity to recognize patterns in banking data and maintain data integrity in the process. Notably, HGE outperforms current methods in accuracy, according to our findings. The code for HGE is freely available on GitHub for public use. To our knowledge, HGE is the first algorithm capable of generating valid banking graphs, showcasing its potential in practical applications through case studies involving real-world banking data. We also introduce a tool called BG-ISOM, which calculates the isomorphism similarity between two banking graphs, thereby facilitating the identification of equivalent patterns. The code for BG-ISOM is freely available on GitHub, providing an alternative to existing solutions. The HGE algorithm, the BG-ISOM tool, and associated experimental data are jointly presented in this research, contributing to the continued development of banking graph representation. To this end, we introduce a new benchmark called BG-Sim, which serves as a benchmark for evaluating isomorphism similarity between banking graphs, presenting challenges in pattern recognition. The code for BG-Sim is freely available on GitHub, offering twelve diverse scenarios for researchers to test their algorithms against. The total number of instances in this benchmark amounts to 470 datasets. To our knowledge, BG-Sim represents the most comprehensive collection of benchmark datasets for banking graph isomorphism similarity, serving as a valuable resource for researchers in this field. Additionally, our work delves into the theoretical aspects underlying hybrid generation equivalence, presenting various formulations in the context of graph theory. Notably, we prove the intractability of deciding if two banking graphs are isomorphic, classifying this problem as an NP-complete problem in conjunction with co-NP complete properties. To address these complexities, we introduce heuristics for practical use, including node embedding, random node matching, and hybrid generation based on graph homomorphism. The code for these heuristics is freely available

We investigate a family of metric models, the symmetric Tversky ratio, where the parameters influence the distance between pairwise dissimilar items. The structure of these metrics is well understood when the parameters are non-negative, forming a compact, convex space. However, when allowing the parameters to take on negative values, the distance metric becomes semi-metric. In this study, we identify the extreme points of this parametrized space and demonstrate that its boundary is comprised of finite, distinct sets. We also establish that each set corresponds to a specific type of metric, which combines equal distances between similar items and large distances between dissimilar items. These extreme points serve as pivotal angles in a graphical representation of the parametrized space. In a particular scenario, the parameters take on the form of differences between item labels, resulting in a geometric interpretation of the boundary sets. In this context, the extreme points are equivalent to the labels of 'hard' and 'easy' decision boundaries in a series of binary decisions. Moreover, the labels that correspond to 'difficult' decision boundaries are precisely those that lie on the opposite side of the metric's gradient direction. In addition, we show that any metric within this family can be decomposed into a combination of 'hard' and 'easy' decision boundaries, where the weights are flexible and non-negative. Conversely, the 'difficult' decision boundaries are inherently incorporated in the metric, making the replacement with 'hard' or 'easy' boundaries necessitate a non-zero weight for any non-zero weight for the 'difficult' boundary, thus highlighting their essential role in the metric. Finally, we apply our findings to the realm of similarity search, where the objective is to determine whether a query item is similar to any item in a collection. In this context, we demonstrate how the metric can be utilized to efficiently design query optimization techniques, resulting in a reduction of runtime to $O(\log n)$, where $n$ denotes the collection's size. Additionally, we protect against errors by introducing a probabilistic version of the technique, which yields a high accuracy rate and allows for the control of errors. By analyzing the metric's properties, we are able to devise this algorithm, the RSMSearch, as the first query optimization technique to achieve this efficiency. In recent years, a key focus has been on accurately quantifying and comparing the computational efficiency of different machine learning models. However, the traditional approach of benchmarking models is flawed due to various factors, leading to misleading conclusions. As a result, our methods for training and selecting models are in need of improvement. To bridge this gap, we suggest utilizing the resources typically wasted on redundant model training to create inferences of benchmarking data. We then develop and implement a novel method called pseudo-benchmarking, which leverages lightweight model executions to generate predictions of systematic benchmarking results. Our pseudo-benchmarking outcomes display strong parallels with actual benchmarking results, both in terms of overall trend and detailed analysis. To substantiate the reliability and general applicability of our method, we conducted extensive experiments involving seven diverse machine learning models and various data sets from multiple domains. Our pseudo-benchmarking framework has been open-sourced under the terms of the permissive MIT License, allowing for free public access at https://github.com/google-research/pseudo-benchmark. Furthermore, our findings are presented in a public repository (https://github.com/google-research/pseudo-benchmark-results) for reference by the research community. We anticipate that our pseudo-benchmarking approach will enhance the precision and validity of future benchmarking studies in data-driven science. Our research is inspired by previous efforts in benchmarking, such as the influential CoOp system (Elsken et al., 2019), the extensive learning from subgraphs paper by Vlachos et al. (2020), and other related studies that have significantly contributed to the field. To differentiate our work, we focus on developing a versatile pseudo-benchmarking technique that is adaptable to various domains and scalable for large datasets, which distinguishes our approach from the specialized distribution learning approach presented in Zhang et al. (2020). Moreover, our research diverges from the recent efforts of pseudo-benchmarking for specific tasks, such as language modeling, as detailed in Choudhary et al. (2020), and instead aims to make enduring contributions to the field of benchmarking. To achieve this, we propose a general pseudo-benchmarking strategy that is applicable across multiple domains and can be implemented in various environments. Our approach is based on the premise that training numerous models in parallel generates side information, which can be utilized to inform systematic benchmarking. To enhance performance on complex natural language parsing tasks, researchers have long employed self-training techniques, which utilize a model's predicted outputs as input, often resulting in considerable gains. Nonetheless, these methods are only successful when integrated with an existing strong parser, highlighting their dependent and supplementary nature. We propose a novel self-training approach, Deep Contextualized Self-Training (DCST), which capitalizes on contextual representations from pre-trained Deep Contextualized models like ELMO, ULMFiT's pre-trained language model, or BERT. By incorporating context-dependent self-training, DCST addresses limitations of prior methods and achieves enhancements with models like BERT, while also offering an ensemble-like average improvement. We evaluate DCST's effectiveness on datasets from the CoNLL 2006 Parse Tree Banking shared task and the WAVE shared task, yielding consistent and substantial parsing improvements, averaging 1.1 and 1.5 F1 levels respectively, with gains largely outperforming existing self-training methods. Furthermore, DCST's effectiveness extends to enhancements in unlabeled parsing accuracy, with improvements quantified as F1 levels. We also present an adaptation of DCST to neural models, demonstrating its compatibility and effectiveness. Through comprehensive analysis, we validate the significance of contextual self-training and its superiority to prior methods, while also exploring its potential limitations and dependencies. Ultimately, DCST serves as a versatile tool, enhancing both transition-based and dependency parsing models utilizing contextual representations from pre-trained models. We publicly provide the code used in this research on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alevassal/DCST. For additional information, please refer to the document titled 'DCST_Information'.

Eliminating these, enabling or disabling options can lead to performance enhancements, reduced memory usage, and better compilation times in succession. Therefore, an efficient, accurate method called ORE (Optional Runtime Eliminator) is presented, capable of detecting and removing all non-conditional options without human involvement. ORE's approach involves modeling the system's configuration using the Optional Monoidal Automaton formalism and leveraging recent theoretical discoveries to identify and remove redundant components in its structure, effectively eliminating all non-conditional options. Developing robust, multilingual language models necessitates addressing two key challenges: ensuring these models are not exploiting zero-shot translations for unsolved tasks, while also catering to multiple languages. To this end, we introduce a novel framework, Adversarial Multilingual Model Exclusivity (AMME), which is designed to counteract a broad range of language model biases, including zero-shot translations. This framework operates at test time to identify individual input predictions derived from multiple languages that are uniquely related to those inputs. It achieves this by generating exclusive predictions through an adversarial training process at the pre-training stage. To overcome the limitation of labeled data, which is often in scarcity for high-resource languages, we implement a novel data labeling strategy. This approach utilizes data from low-resource languages paired with high-resource languages to label diverse language models on a large scale. Evaluations across diverse datasets demonstrate that AMME significantly mitigates model biases, with significant enhancements in downstream task performance by 6.36% on average. The code for AMME is available at https://github.com/ercling/AMME. Journal papers detailing the method's adaptations for specific tasks, such as neural machine translation, are listed in the supplementary resources. In multi-objective reinforcement learning, a scenario where a single agent tackles various task objectives, our research reveals that utilizing a singular learned dynamics model frequently results in an undesirable phenomenon where knowledge from one task transfers negatively to another task. 
To address this challenge, we have developed a new method where the learned dynamics model is adapted using contextual information, leading to improved performance in tasks that were previously interferent with each other. 
Our proposed approach was tested and validated through experiments on several complex multi-objective reinforcement learning environments, and the results clearly demonstrate its efficacy. 
Specifically, it allowed us to take advantage of a highly efficient neural dynamics model, resulting in significantly faster training and better performance compared to deep reinforcement learning algorithms that learn reward functions separately for each task. 
Our proposed approach achieved an average of a 35% improvement in overall performance and provided up to a 270% faster training time, leading to the creation of efficient neural dynamics models, which can be shared across a wide range of tasks without compromising their quality.

Therefore, our research may promote the development of techniques to create more robust and transferable models of action dynamics in such scenarios. A heat engine's efficiency can be significantly enhanced by tapping into the thermal energy gradient between its heat bath and a source of quantum coherence. To study the dynamics of this coherence, we used a paradigmatic setup based on equilibrium coherence properties, applying it to the Clauser-Horne inequality to measure engine performance. By influencing the coherence with a scaling parameter, we showed that the output power could be adjusted. Furthermore, our findings demonstrated that the optimal point for the scaling parameter lies within the intermediate coherence regime. Notably, when the coherence is extremely high or low, the engine performance peaks at a lower value. This behavior can be attributed to the decreased temperature difference between the two heat baths, resulting from the influence of coherence. Our results are consistent with previous studies on non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, where intermediate coherence often led to superior engine performance. To deepen our understanding of this phenomenon, we performed a detailed analysis of the source of the temperature difference, as reported in the study titled "Probing Paradoxical Coherence Properties with Engine Performance" arXiv:2205.04429 (2022). In it, we established a connection between the coherence-induced temperature difference and the degree of classical correlation, as expressed by the CHSH inequality. By calculating the temperature difference in terms of the correlation, we confirmed that the coherence must be diminished for the thermal gradient to increase, thereby illustrating the intricate relationship between classical correlations, paradoxical coherence, and the temperature difference. This study serves as a bridge between quantum thermodynamics and Bell-test experiments to investigate the impact of coherence on heat engines. Importantly, our findings underscore the importance of considering Paradoxical Coherence Properties in quantum systems, especially when connected to Bell-test experiments. Hurricanes pose a substantial threat to communities in the US, particularly in terms of their effects on the power grid. Forecasting the impact of future hurricanes on the grid is crucial for enhancing resilience. By leveraging historical hurricane data from 1938 to 2008, obtained from the National Hurricane Center, and advanced satellite imagery from 18 transition seasons, a model-based framework has been developed to evaluate the likelihood and severity of damaged transformers. Integrated with weather forecasts, this framework enables quantification of the total cost of potential outages. The proposed method has been tested and validated using a simplified power grid model based on actual network configurations from the IEEE Gridwise Testbed, specifically through scenario analysis of Hurricane Ian, which made landfall in 2021. The study demonstrates the capability of the framework to rank critical nodes in the power grid susceptible to damage, predict the probability and cost of outages for main power lines, and estimate the probability distribution of damaged transformers. Notably, the framework shows that Hurricane Ian was likely to cause significant damage to power lines and transformers in the Houston area, with the majority of damaged nodes concentrated in Harris, Fort Bend, and Brazoria counties. The study also indicates that the method can be refined to account for various uncertainties, such as the trajectory of landfall, by employing probabilistic forecasting, which may lead to reduced expected losses by reducing the probability of extremely damaging scenarios. The expected losses from a probable scenario of 20% probability, for instance, decreased from $120 million to $76 million when incorporating multiple trajectories. To address these issues, we introduce the DyGED model, a deep learning-based method that utilizes the graph itself to generate event timelines with minimal annotations. The model employs a generative adversarial process, balancing the creation of accurate event sequences with the graph's structural features. Through its convolutional component, DyGED captures graph patterns, and its sequential generative module predicts event onsets, which it then refines using the graph's structural characteristics. The model is then evaluated on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority to current best practices, and its effectiveness even when only a small number of annotations is available. The knowledge gained from these experiments shows that the precision of event change detection increases with the availability of annotations. Notably, the DyGED model also captures valuable information about graph auto-encoding, and its capability to generate event-driven graph sequences proves useful for understanding graph event changes. Recent advancements in deep neural networks have improved medical image diagnosis, including classification and grading of colorectal adenomas. To enhance accuracy, network training needs to be refined by incorporating various techniques, such as data augmentation. However, applying this strategy on endoscopic images of colorectal adenomas is limited due to the resemblance of augmented images to real ones. Therefore, we aim to introduce an efficient data augmentation method for these images. By analyzing the structure of these images and potential issues with augmented pictures, we have developed a systematic and comprehensive approach called 'Basic-Image-Augmentation', which involves six techniques applied to the basic unit of an image - a pixel or a character. This method allows the generation of unique augmented images that do not falsely resemble real ones. Moreover, we found that reducing the size of images does not necessarily impair the recognition of distinct features in colorectal adenomas. Therefore, we integrated our efficient augmentation method with size-reduced images to improve training convergence and classification accuracy. When tested with a large dataset of endoscopic images, we found that our approach substantially enhanced the convergence of the model and its internal features, ultimately leading to superior performance in classification and grading of colorectal adenomas. Notably, our method excelled in comparison to alternative strategies, resulting in a remarkable improvement of at least 4% in accuracy in various tests. Based on these outcomes, we recommend using our Basic-Image-Augmentation method to enhance deep neural network training for classification and grading of colorectal adenomas. This approach may also be applied to other medical image diagnosis tasks. Additionally, we have introduced a novel tool called 'AugCo' to facilitate the detection of incorrectly augmented images that resemble real ones. This utility may be useful in identifying potential issues in data augmentation methods. You can access the code for 'AugCo' at https://github.com/Chen-Research-AI/AugCo. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm holds promise for efficiently solving NP-hard issues. However, its variational optimization component, which is critical, may cause inefficiencies. We've modified the approach to utilize Bayesian optimization to discover a more efficient solution for the objective function. By replacing the quantum circuit's variable rotation parameters with Bayesian optimization, the efficiency of the algorithm has been significantly improved. Specifically, we've found that using Bayesian optimization to find key parameters in the QAA for the Monotonic Lipid Blayer issue reduces the number of iterations required to reach a satisfactory solution from 100 to 25, representing a 250-fold improvement. A comprehensive study on ellipses is presented, focusing on identifying their intersections, calculating the maximum distance between their centers, and determining if they touch. Three algorithms are introduced to solve these problems for general ellipses, even when they do not intersect, touch at a single point, or have two distinct intersection points. For ellipses with two distinct intersection points, the maximum distance between their centers is found through a polynomial decomposition and the application of five established methods. Additionally, the study includes code implementations for each algorithm, along with over 30 numerical tests to validate its efficacy. It is shown that the applied methods match the solutions obtained by other approaches, including algebraic and numerical techniques. All code can be found on the Ellipses GitHub repository: https://github.com/lzhang42/ellipses. Key words: intersection points, distance, intersection algorithms, polynomial decomposition, GitHub.
